But something shifted while I was living in Maui throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. During those high-stress months, I found tranquility staring at the night sky. Each night, I’d retreat to the hammock strung between two palm trees in my backyard and watch the stars pop to life like silent fireworks in the heavens. Each evening provided a show far more entertaining than anything I could watch on television. Observing the constellations, the faint glow of distant planets, and the occasional shooting star left me with a sense of awe. And that awe did more than silence my racing thoughts—it felt as if it reset my entire nervous system. A growing body of research confirms that what I felt wasn’t just some island reverie. We’ve long known that being in nature is good for us. However, most research has focused on daytime behavior; more recently, experts have started to look at nighttime behaviors. Inherently, the night is quieter and stiller than the day. “It naturally encourages us to shift into a different mode of awareness,” says Mark Westmoquette, an astrophysicist and meditation teacher who runs mindful stargazing retreats across the UK and Europe. “When the light fades, our other senses are heightened, helping us awaken vividly to the present moment.” Studies have shown that losing yourself in the night sky can help calm the nervous system and increase happiness. It also stimulates curiosity, and curiosity leads to wonder, says Westmoquette. “And wonder is the precursor to feeling awe,” he says. “Awe is well known to have a powerful positive effect on mental health.” Awe also produces a measurable ego reduction, says Heine Rasmussen, a Danish-born astrophysicist and co-owner of Bliss and Stars, a new retreat in Cederberg, South Africa. This psychological mechanism even has a name: the small self effect. “Your problems, your self importance, your mental chatter all briefly contract when you stargaze,” he says. Astrotourism, meet wellness tourism Emerging research on the night sky and health has helped fuel the intersection of two of the biggest trends in travel: wellness and stargazing. New wellness resorts such as Bliss and Stars Retreat and Kosmos Stargazing Resort + Spa in Colorado’s San Luis Valley market the luxury of their light pollution-free, pitch black, star studded skies. And star bathing parties, solar hikes, and moonlight meditations have become the hottest offerings at spas, resorts, and retreats around the world. Cal-a-Vie Health Spa in California calls it galaxy wellness. The property recently introduced mindful solar hikes led by local astronomer Tim Lewis that conclude at the on-property observatory which houses a state-of-the-art Takahashi telescope. “My goal is to stimulate wonder,” says Lewis. “So often we just look and keep walking, but I encourage guests to dwell on the beauty of the sky.” The observatory at Four Seasons Resort Lanai in Hawaii boasts a high-tech, PlaneWave PW1000 telescope used for identifying celestial bodies such as planets, star clusters, galaxies, and nebulae. But the telescope isn’t used for astrowellness programs, like meditation under the stars. “The experience is less about identifying stars or constellations, and more about reconnecting with the light within,” says Caroline Reese, wellness supervisor at Four Seasons Resort Lanai. Through moments of opening and closing the eyes, participants experience the changing layers of the starry night while entering a space of reflection, stillness, and presence, she explains. Whether you use a telescope or the naked eye, you still get benefits, says Dominc Vertue, Project Lead of the Astronomy for Mental Health Project at the IAU Office of Astronomy for Development in South Africa. “A telescope narrows attention and may add learning, discovery, and engagement,” he says. “Naked-eye viewing gives a broad, immersive sense of the sky and may better support awe and restoration.” And while actively trying to identify objects can create more focus, letting the mind drift can be more contemplative and calming, he says. “A good session might combine both: a little guided noticing, then some quiet open-ended looking. This fits with attention restoration theory, where ‘soft fascination’ can hold attention gently without demanding too much effort.” Cultural storytelling in the stars For centuries, cultures around the world have harnessed the power of the night sky. More and more spas are tapping into those cultural connections. On Maui, Kilolani Spa at the Grand Wailea, a Waldorf Astoria Resort is named for the stargazers of ancient Hawaii who used the skies to navigate. The spa’s concept centers around Hawaii’s three lunar phases, and treatments range from new moon Aires somatic sound healing sessions to a full moon sound healing and cacao ceremony. “For native Hawaiians, one aspect of wellness is grounding and connection and the stories in the night sky help keep us grounded,” says Kalei Uwekoolani, Director of Culture at Grand Wailea. “And while the eyes can see the stars, moon, and maybe some planets it’s what they cannot see in the cosmos that creates that universal connection.” For the Maya civilization, the sky was a sacred space filled with spiritual meaning and knowledge, says Jimmy Herrera, a member of the Quintana Roo Astronomy Society who leads a Maya stargazing experience at Maroma, a Belmond Hotel, Mexico’s first Starlight Accommodation certified by the Starlight Foundation. “Stargazing allowed the Maya to understand the cycles of life and maintain a deep relationship with the universe,” he says. “Today, stargazing can be considered a wellness practice partly inspired by this ancestral vision. By stepping away from daily distractions and focusing attention on the vastness of the universe, individuals can experience a sense of calm and connection with their surroundings.” Celestial glamping expeditions from Santa Fe's Inn of the Five Graces are timed to rare astronomical events, like the Perseids meteor shower, and take place in some of the American Southwest's most sacred and protected landscapes, including Chaco Canyon and the Taos Plateau, both International Dark Sky sanctuaries. Run in partnership with operator Heritage Inspirations the trips feature stargazing experiences led by a Cultural Astronomer who connects the ancestral significance of the night sky. All the starbathing bells & whistles Storytelling, gentle guidance, breathing, or calming sound could deepen the stargazing experience for some people, according to Vertue. “The best enhancements are those that help people slow down, feel safe, notice carefully, and make meaning from what they are seeing,” he says. Resorts and retreats are getting creative. At Six Senses Kanuhura in the Maldives, moonlight meditations are accompanied by a soundtrack of singing bowls and ocean waves and the star bathing experience at Eden Roc Cap Cana in the Dominican Republic takes place inside the property’s natural cenote and includes energy work. In the Scottish Highlands, star-bathing parties organized by Cairngorm Excursions feature a spirits tastings of gins and whiskies from a local distillery. And in the Florida Keys, Little Palm Island’s new $50,000 Moonlit Soak experience includes a Champagne sail aboard a 36-foot Hinkcley beneath a waxing gibbous sky, lunar-inspired baths soaks, and a moonrise photography session. But galaxy wellness doesn’t have to break the bank. All you need is a clear, dark sky, says Westmoquette. DarkSky International has a searchable database of the world’s starriest skies and glamping company Under Canvas has six DarkSky-certified camps throughout the US. “I’d say put aside the telescope, binoculars, star maps, and constellation guides; lie on a blanket or sun lounger; and open your senses to what’s around you—sounds, smells, feelings, and sights,” says Westmoquette. It takes around 20 minutes for your eyes to fully adjust to the dark, so start with eyes closed and listen and feel, he says. Then open your eyes and observe. If you have trouble concentrating, try listening to one of Westmoquette’s mindful stargazing meditations. “Like all mindfulness practice, the longer you do it and the more often, the greater the effect,” he says. “And when you find awe on a regular basis, you feel connected, and it reminds us of our true place in the cosmos.”

item.title: Panama's Pensionado Visa Is One of the Cheapest Ways to Retire Abroad—Here's How
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.11
Forget Florida—what better place to spend your golden years than Panama’s storied Casco Viejo district or idyllic San Blas Islands? The Central American country has becoming increasingly popular amongst international travelers, consistently ranking as one of the best places to retire in the world. Its wide appeal is thanks not only to the dizzying array of breezy beaches at travelers' disposal along both the Pacific and Caribbean coasts—nor the famous canal that links the two. Instead, many Americans are opting to relocate to Panama because of its affordable retirement visa. Established in 1987, Panama’s indefinite Pensionado Visa grants permanent residency to foreign nationals who can prove a lifetime monthly income or pension of at least $1,000 a month. However, this income cannot come from personal savings. Accepted sources include government or corporate pension plans, or Social Security payments of at least 1,000 Panamanian balboa (directly equivalent to $1,000, according to Panama’s public security ministry). That threshold could be lowered to $750 per month if you purchase a local home that costs at least $100,000. But if you want to bring a dependent—such as a spouse or a child—you’ll have to pay an additional $250 per month and dependent. It’s a great pick for those seeking a lower-cost alternative to post-career life in the US. Retirees can live comfortably in Panama’s largest metropolis, Panama City, for between $1,700 and $3,000 per month. Beyond a lower cost of living, Pensionado visa holders also qualify for a list of discounts, including 25% off local utilities, 50% off entertainment tickets (such as movies and sports), and 15% off personal loans, according to the Panamanian embassy in Washington, DC. The cuts apply to healthcare, too: 10% off medication, 15% off dental and eye exams, 20% off doctor’s bills, and 15% off hospital treatment (if not covered by insurance)—great perks if you plan to live near the Johns Hopkins Medicine International-affiliated Hospital Punta Pacifica. Visa recipients also receive an exemption from the import tax on certain household goods—a benefit that also extends to new imported cars for personal use every two years. Discounts aside, the financial prerequisite for Panama’s retirement visa is relatively affordable compared to other countries. The exception: Portugal’s D7 visa, which has a comparable monthly passive income requirement of 920 euros (about $1,055). However, next door, Spain’s Non-Lucrative Visa requires a minimum yearly passive income of 28,800 euros (about $32,860), while Italy’s Elective Residence Visa dictates an annual private income stream of about €31,000 (about $35,250). To apply, Americans must authenticate the required documents through a Consulate of Panama in the US and hire a Panamanian lawyer to submit their application and required documents (such as health certificates and proof of lifetime funds) locally. According to the Panamanian embassy in Washington DC, applicants must be physically be in Panama when the visa is issued.

item.title: Björk, an Eclipse, and 40 Years of Icelandic Underground Music
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.02
I was warned that the light change right before totality would feel the strangest. As I looked up at the cloud-strewn Icelandic sky, the crowd pulsing around me, it was as if the world had transformed into a film noir—our upturned faces suddenly cast in washed-out shades of grey. Then, for a minute, everything slipped into pitch-black darkness. In those few moments, strangers hugged; I cried and laughed simultaneously; and one person yelled “You’re doing great, moon!” When the moon crossed between the Earth and the sun on August 12, we couldn’t see the total solar eclipse—but we could feel it. We were standing in the moon’s shadow. There were no groans, complaints, or frowns, in part because our anticipation was two-fold. The dark green weather forecast (indicating the heaviest level of cloud coverage) had sent many of the more devoted eclipse chasers north, chasing clear skies. But thousands of us chose to remain in Víðistaðatún, a sculpture park strewn with massive lava rocks in Hafnarfjörður about six miles from Downtown Reykjavik, for Echolalia, a one-day rave headlined by Björk, arguably Iceland’s most famous musician. Yes, the party was, in part, organized to mark the 2026 total solar eclipse, which drew thousands of travelers from all over the world to remote corners of Iceland, Greenland, and Spain. But whether attendees knew it or not, there was something else to celebrate, too: Echolalia was organized by Reykjavik-based record label Smekkleysa to commemorate its 40th anniversary. Smekkleysa, which translates to “Bad Taste," was founded in 1986 by members of Icelandic alternative rock band The Sugarcubes (Björk, Bragi Ólafsson, Einar Örn Benediktsson, and Sigtryggur “Siggi” Baldursson), along with Ásmundur Jónsson, the host of the underground radio show Áfangar and co-founder of Gramm Records. It's a name that feels fitting for a label that has spent decades being an incubator for the experimental and the offbeat. As Smekkleysa's original 1986 manifesto declares: “good taste and financial restraint are the main enemies of creativity and well-being.” Echolalia promised to live up to the name. In addition to the rave itself, Björk was presenting a multi-sensory exhibition at The National Gallery of Iceland—also called Echolalia—featuring three of her songs played in immersive, theatrical soundscapes. To better understand how Smekkleysa's anti-establishment spirit still resonates today, I sat down with Bragi, Siggi, and Ásmundur at the record label’s Reykjavík headquarters, where we took over a picnic table alongside dozens of locals soaking up the rare sunny afternoon. The topic was the local music scene, of course, and how it’s changed in the decades that the label has existed. For an hour, I listened to the three friends trade stories about the earlier days, describing periods of time as the bands they were playing with instead of actual years. Smekkleysa was born as a fledgling incubator, giving experimental musicians a space to, well, explore. “It was very DIY, you know,” Siggi told me. “We ended up coming together with this group—the musician side and the writer side—to form an umbrella organization, which was supposed to bring together different strands of the Reykjavik counterculture at the time.” Right then, a young woman floated by, all smiles, and gave Siggi a hug as she greeted the others at the table. It was Björk’s daughter, Ísadóra Bjarkardóttir Barney, who was helping bring Echolalia together. This is an island of friends-turned-family, after all. And while 40 years may have passed, this crew agreed that the Icelandic music community still had its edge. “There are new generations coming up that are doing things on their own terms and with their own tools,” Siggi said. “The tools change, but the sentiment doesn't change very much.” Part of the reason? The lack of a big music business on the island, especially when compared to the rest of Europe. “This is a rather sort of closed-off community—but we still have a huge number of artists from Iceland that are internationally known,” Siggi added. Iceland’s close-knit creative community has something that’s shaped my own experience here after 22 visits, and is one of the main reasons why I continue to return. There has always been a sense of harmony among its artists—and no matter how big someone like Björk gets, there’s always a ready excitement to collaborate with new artists and mediums to try something new. For instance, Smekkleysa teamed up with Plata, a newly formed Icelandic record label that launched just this July, to release a nine-track compilation album that takes listeners through Reykjavik’s club, art pop, and experimental scenes. Two days after the eclipse, they threw a launch party at Smekkleysa's record store in downtown Reykjavík. Despite always sensing this collective support, this is the first trip where I learned a phrase that encapsulates the feeling: DIT, or “Do It Together.” “People tend to naturally come together here, not unlike a collective,” says Siggi. At Echolalia, DIT underpinned everything from the textile weaving workshop that asked attendees to make a giant piece of art together to the openness of the attendees themselves. I met groups of people traveling together who had met on event-specific Reddit forums just weeks before. There were nine DJs total—all pegged as friends of Björk’s. Icelanders Gummi Arnalds, Ronja, Knackered, sideproject, and Los Caballos played alongside Barcelona-based Arca, US-based Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith, and Shanghai-based 33EMYBW. DJs greeted each other mid-set as one would set up to follow the other’s act, there was an epic hug between Arca and Björk, and friends were brought on stage to hype the crowd (Ronja, looking at you). Björk is a walking testament to the idea of “doing it together.” In recent years, she has been far more involved in uplifting both established and up-and-coming artists, making relatively surprise cameos (Rosalia, “Berghain”), collaborating with Venezuelan producer Arca as a co-producer on the Vulnicara and Utopia albums, and working with musicians like Shygirl and Sega Bodega for Fossora. By building upon her own legacy, she’s actively nurturing a future generation of music-makers, one held together by collaboration and boundary-less experimentation. Given the ethos of this event, it makes sense that the crowd could have doubled as an international departures terminal at an airport. I made friends with a lovely mother-daughter duo from Quebec I deeply hope to cross paths with again; met a fellow New Yorker; recognized at least three people I had seen wandering the sister Echolalia exhibit at The National Gallery of Iceland days earlier, chatted with plenty of new stateside buddies, and had a quick conversation with a model from Lithuania. But there were just as many locals bridging everything together. Even though it was a one-day event, this 10-hour rave was a culmination of the lifetime of Smekkleysa’s work, which, at the end of the day, is all about bringing people together for the love of music. And while the eclipse brought international attention to the event, it's far from the only gathering like this that they’ve hosted. “From 1987 to 1990, maybe 1992, we would do regular variety shows called Smekkleysukvöld, or Bad Taste Evenings,” Siggi says. “People would create all sorts of stuff for that—everything from writing little plays that would be performed on stage to creating spoof bands.” In 2000, the crew put on The Word Music, a four-day festival that gathered experimental poets, musicians, and more. “We probably didn't imagine still doing these things at our age today,” Bragi slipped in. But they’re still doing these things well. If you’ve been to a live show, you’ve felt the camaraderie that comes with feeling so in tune with whatever is coming out of the speakers. There are few feelings more human than locking eyes with a stranger for a second, massive smiles on your faces, as you catch yourselves grooving to the same song transition. Now, imagine an entire crowd in the middle of a lava rock park that doubles as a disc golf course doing the same thing, actively becoming a singular dance move. This was Echolalia for the eight hours I was there, and likely for the last two that I missed because my feet just couldn’t dance anymore. If I was somewhere else—or alone—for a cloud-covered solar eclipse, the moment the world went dark in the rain might have felt almost apocalyptic. But here, dancing shoulder-to-shoulder with hundreds of strangers who decided to embrace the cosmic and earthly elements alike, it felt more like being a kid again. We looked at one another for reassurance that, yes, this was happening—and that everything was okay. My local friends watching it back in Reykjavik told me their toddler immediately asked “Hvað er að gerast?” as everything plunged into darkness. It translates to “What’s going on?” and I couldn’t have related more. When confronted with the deep time of the cosmos, we're really all the same age. It reminded me of No. 6 of the Bad Taste Manifesto: “Members shall always be clear about their importance to the future, and pledge to think in centuries as well as seconds.” There was no better person, then, to close out the second half of the eclipse, when the moon broke apart from the sun. Björk welcomed daylight's return with an hour-long soundtrack of high-energy beats, which would sound equally at home in outer space as down here on Earth. Taking breaks to bang a pair of drumsticks and bounce around in her Robert Wun-designed balloon couture, Björk was the nucleus of the outfit expanding around her, much like the dance floor that sprawled around the DJ booth on stage. Sometimes you travel all the way to Iceland to see a total solar eclipse… and you don’t get to see it. Not really, at least. The world doesn’t end, the planet keeps on spinning, and we all continue on, doing it together.

item.title: Where was 'Lady' filmed? A look inside the real-life home of the eccentric Lady Isabella
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.16
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Lady filmed? “I’m Lady Isabella, welcome to Ravenhyde Hall. Come on in, come and see where the magic happens…” These are some of the first words we hear from the leading lady of, well, Lady – director Samuel Abrahams’ new dark comedy centred around the life of a narcissistic, bizarre aristocrat. Sian Clifford (Fleabag, Ludwig) plays in the titular role in the film, which premiered at the BFI London Film Festival in October 2025, with Juliet Cowan, Laurie Kynaston and Olisa Odele claiming the supporting roles. The opening shots of Lady Isabella set the tone of the eccentricity to come. First, legs draped in vivid purple trousers lead down to shiny black loafers are shown to belong to a figure… lying face down on a grand staircase. Next, Lady Isabella is face down in a bush, her hands by her side, dressed in gardening gloves. Then, face down at a dining table. The life of an aristocrat must be hard, hey? As the crew Lady Isabella’s hired to film her life around the home wander around, the lead character’s idiosyncrasies unravel among dressed dining tables that stretch into the distance, kitchens fit for rustling up banquets and a jumble of taxidermy creations. Among the outrageous asides and outlandish happenings, there’s another star that steals the spotlight – the gorgeous country estate in which everything takes place. To film the hilarious mockumentary-style flick, Lady’s production team descended on Somerleyton Hall, a Grade II listed country house and estate in Suffolk, a 20-minute drive south of the popular seaside town of Great Yarmouth. Somerleyton Hall’s history stretches all the way back to the age of the Vikings, with records of a homestead on the land as the Nordic warriors settled along England’s east coasts. The first property to resemble what would eventually become a fantastical manor arrived in the Tudor era as the Lords of Somerleyton (who later moved to America fearing prosecution for their Catholicism following the accession of Elizabeth I). The land has seen myriad comings and goings since, as the Jacobeans, Victorians and Edwardians built on the foundations left by the generations that preceded them. The Somerleyton Hall visited by countless curious families and history buffs today is a Jacobean Manor house surrounded by thousands of acres of resplendent gardens. The property and garden is open on select days between spring and autumn, typically opening around the beginning of April and closing at the end of October.

item.title: 11 best places to see bioluminescence for awe-inspiring adventures
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.48
The best places to see bioluminescence around the world sit atop many travellers’ bucket lists. Whether it's through the pages of glossy magazines like ours, glittering on social media feeds or told through the tales our jet-setting loved ones share on their return from their latest adventure, this natural phenomenon is undeniably captivating. Perhaps it's jellyfish that twinkle at the harbour’s edge or plankton that creates scenes akin to starry skies as toes paddle in the ocean – either way, bioluminescence is a fascinating natural phenomenon that, once witnessed, is impossible to forget. However, it’s unlikely that you’ll see glittering, rippling waters by chance. Here, from the shores of Oaxaca in Mexico to Maldivian atolls via our very own British Isles, we reveal the best places to see bioluminescence in all its dazzling forms. Where can I see bioluminescence in the UK? Cornwall is one of the most famous places to spot sparkling seas during the summer months, particularly Grebe Beach and Pedn Vounder. Starry seas can also be seen in Wales, with frequent spots in locations including Dunraven Bay (Vale of Glamorgan) and Rhossili Bay (Gower). Is it safe to touch bioluminescent water? It is generally safe to touch and swim in bioluminescent waters, especially in destinations where the sparkling waters are featured as tourist attractions with boat trips and excursions. However, some bioluminescence results from harmful algal blooms that can cause skin rashes and severe illness if ingested. If in doubt, research the area you’re visiting thoroughly and speak to guides on organised trips. 1. The Maldives The picture-perfect islands of the Maldives are some of the best places to see bioluminescence around the world thanks to an abundance of plankton that illuminates the waves after sunset. While it’s possible to see the phenomenon on islands across the archipelago, one of the most famous spots of them all is on the quietest side of Vaadhoo Island, a minuscule island of the Raa Atoll known for its beachy corner nicknamed ‘Sea of Stars’. When to go: Between June and October How to get there: Domestic flight and boat transfer from Velana International Airport in Malé Where to stay: Vaadhoo Island lacks the honeymoon-esque stays you may associate with the Maldives – check into InterContinental Maldives Maamunagau Resort and appreciate the glowing waters meters from your beachside abode. 2. Mosquito Bay, Vieques, Puerto Rico You may not have heard of the picturesque island of Vieques. However, you’ve likely seen the nighttime spectacle that occurs on glossy pages and social media feeds. After sundown, Mosquito Bay becomes a glossy blue portal thanks to the bioluminescent dinoflagellate Pyrodinium bahamense, which glows blue when agitated. Glide through the waters on a clear-bottomed kayak with a local tour operator for a truly mesmerising experience. When to go: December to April (dry season) How to get there: Direct flight from San Juan (SJU) followed by a ferry to Vieques Where to stay: Go back to nature – albeit with the luxury trimmings – at the cosy Finca Victoria. 3. Luminous Lagoon, Jamaica Home to dinoflagellates aplenty, Jamaica’s Luminous Lagoon is one of the most incredible excursions on the island, and a memorable way to shake up the evening itinerary. Hop on a tour boat at sunset and, soon enough, the water’s epipelagic zone comes alive with a vibrant blue light. Watch as sealife darts under the boat’s hull, leaving phantasmagoric lines of light in their wake. Should you choose, some tours allow you to hop into the (surprisingly shallow) water and watch as splashes create incredible displays of light. When to go: December to April (dry season) How to get there: Drive from Sangster International Airport (MBJ) Where to stay: Kick back a 30-minute drive away from the spectacle with an indulgent all-inclusive stay at Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay. 4. Jervis Bay, New South Wales, Australia Considering the length of its coastline and the abundance of wildlife that lies offshore, there are surprisingly few places to spot notable displays of bioluminescence around Australia. That said, places do exist, with Jervis Bay in New South Wales being one of the most famous. As the noctiluca scintillans dinoflagellate species washes ashore, settle into the powdery sand and watch the water’s ripples create an effect akin to the Northern Lights on the shore. When to go: Summer; September to February How to get there: About a 2.5-hour drive south of Sydney Airport Where to stay: Escape the hustle and bustle of everyday life with a glamping trip like no other at Paperbark Camp. 5. Krabi, Thailand There are a few bays and coves in this popular region of Thailand that promise a watery light display on clear nights. Ao Nang Beach is one of the most famous and most accessible, with beachside hostels, restaurants and bars a stone’s throw from the shoreline offering places to hide out in ahead of nightfall. While no less famous, perhaps, Phra Nang Beach is another spot a little further along the coast for a peaceful, intimate bioluminescent session reachable by boat transfers from Ao Nang Beach. When to go: November to May How to get there: 20-minute drive from Krabi International Airport Where to stay: Phulay Bay, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve, is just a 40-minute drive from the glistening waters. Expect dazzling villas and pavilions, sprawling pools and access to dazzling beaches through the lush landscape. 6. Toyama Bay, Japan While many of the best places to see bioluminescence around the world are so due to an abundance of glowing plankton and algae, the story is a little quirkier in Japan’s Toyama Bay come spring. Here, the bioluminescent performance atop the otherwise pitch-black Japanese waters is caused by a considerably larger creature – the firefly squid. Join a fishing trip and watch as the organisms emit blue light from photophores, creating a wet and wild firework display as they are pulled from the icy depths. When to go: April - May How to get there: Hokuriku Shinkansen bullet train from Tokyo Where to stay: The DoubleTree by Hilton Toyama is a perfectly plush spot to rest in between city exploration and bay visits. 7. Oaxaca, Mexico One of the most popular places to visit for bioluminescence in Mexico is the Laguna de Manialtepec, a coastal lagoon about west of Puerto Escondido. As fish (and people braving the water for a dip) dart through the waters, the twinkling algae that call the lagoon home make the water turn fantastically phosphorescent. A little farther on, similar experiences are available at Lagunas de Chacahua. When to go: July to October (rainy season) How to get there: Fly to Oaxaca Xoxocotlan International Airport (OAX), typically via Mexico City from the UK Where to stay: You’re spoilt for choice along this stretch of Mexican coastline – see our guide to the best hotels in Oaxaca for all the inspiration you need. 8. Koh Rong, Cambodia By day, the Cambodian island of Koh Rong is a natural playground for families and couples who take to the water armed with snorkelling gear, looking down at the vibrant sea life below. By night, the waters beyond the powder-soft sands take on a life of their own, akin to a starry sky beyond the resorts and lush vegetation. While the bioluminescent plankton isn’t unique to Koh Rong – you can spot it on other Cambodian isles – the lack of light pollution around these shores makes nighttime beach strolls and boat excursions under the new moon unforgettable. When to go: November to May How to get there: Fly to Phnom Penh, then catch a bus to Sihanoukville port and catch a boat transfer to the island Where to stay: The Royal Sands Koh Rong is the plushest address on this gorgeous island. 9. Cornwall, UK (Grebe Beach and Pedn Vounder) The waters that surround the British Isles aren’t the first that come to mind when you think of the best places to see bioluminescence. However, come summer, the English Channel throws a few surprises upon Cornwall’s shores. Some of the most notable places to spot starry shores in this corner of the world include Grebe Beach, a hidden gem at the end of the Helford River. On balmy nights, the water can turn a luminescent blue with a splash. Elsewhere, in Penzance, the bioluminescent action is best observed at Pedn Vounder, where, a few times a year, the Channel puts on a display under the constellations. When to go: July and August How to get there: 5 - 6 hour drive from London; direct trains to Penzance or connecting trains onto Falmouth Where to stay: In Falmouth, The Greenbank Hotel, a charming waterside retreat, gets our vote. In Penzance, hang out with the cool crowd at Artist Residence Cornwall, where unique bedrooms are set within a storied 17th-century property. 10. Cat Ba Island, Vietnam The region around Vietnam’s Halong Bay has long been a hotspot for those seeking glowing waters. However, being one of the stops on most travellers’ bucket lists, crowds and light pollution from boats and cruise ships mean the starry displays are notably more striking in the quieter coves and bays. Enter Cat Ba Island’s Beaches, where splashes at sea equate to dazzling scenes. The natural wonder is best experienced on an overnight boat tour, as captains typically anchor in quiet spots under sparkling skies. When to go: June to October How to get there: Bus transfers from Noi Bai International Airport (HAN) in Hanoi Where to stay: Why not take over your own incredible villa while soaking up the island’s tranquil vibe from Valía Villa Cat Ba. 11. Waitomo Glowworm Caves, New Zealand Instead of a swimsuit, pair of flippers or a kayak, the bioluminescence hiding in one of New Zealand’s most recognisable natural wonders requires visitors to wear comfortable shoes and a warm jacket. The Waitomo Glowworm Caves have been a tourist attraction for more than 130 years, with travellers passing through the awe-inspiring caves in silence, watching as the Arachnocampa luminosa glowworm species – only found in this part of the world – show off their captivating colours. When to go: Year-round How to get there: About 120 miles south of Auckland Airport (AKL) Where to stay: Assuming you’re based in Hamilton, about an hour’s drive north of the caves, for a few days, check into The Narrows Landing Hotel.

item.title: Virgin Trains' cross-channel services have been given the green light – here's the latest
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.24
It's been more than 30 years since the first Eurostar whizzed through the Channel Tunnel, transporting travellers metres under the seabed between London, Paris and beyond into the continent. While there has been word on the rails that rivals have sought to end Eurostar’s monopoly over the tracks for many years, plans were yet to be given the green light – until now. On 13 August 2026, the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) rail regulator announced the approval of a new framework track access agreement between HS1 Limited (trading as London St. Pancras Highspeed) and VTE OPCO Limited (Virgin Trains). The agreement means Virgin Trains are permitted to run up to 20 new daily return services between London and Paris, Brussels or Amsterdam. Furthermore, the head-turning approval grants access to cross-border rail services between 1 October 2030 and 31 December 2040. Following the ORR's announcement, Martin Jones, deputy director, access and international, said, “This is an important next step in bringing competition and growth to the market for international rail services, and we welcome the progress Virgin Trains and London St Pancras High Speed have made. While there is still more work to do, we are supporting Virgin and the wider industry to grow international services.” However, with many years before passengers can consider an alternative to Eurostar, there are still several steps to take. Virgin Trains must procure rolling stock, secure access to other rail networks, and obtain safety approvals from ORR and the relevant EU authorities. Following the announcement of Virgin Trains’ bid to run competitor services last year and the ORR’s approval for the group to use Temple Mills International rail depot in East London, founder Sir Richard Branson said, “The ORR’s decision is the right one for consumers – it’s time to end this 30-year monopoly and bring some Virgin magic to the cross-Channel route. Virgin is no stranger to delivering award-winning rail services, and just as we have successfully challenged incumbents in air, cruise and rail, we’re ready to do it again. We’re going to shake up the cross-Channel route for good and give consumers the choice they deserve.”

item.title: 3 new Italian train journeys for history buffs, design lovers, and foodie travellers
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.93
October is one of the most magical months to visit Italy. In addition to pleasant temperatures and fewer crowds, this is the magical time of year when Italy’s harvest seasons briefly overlap – with olives, wine grapes, and truffles all peaking throughout the month. For travellers, an autumn getaway to Italy is an opportunity to experience seasonal foodie festivals, rare menu items at restaurants, and have better access to popular destinations throughout the country. Starting in October 2026, travellers can experience all this and more via three new rail journeys. These special itineraries range from international routes aboard ultra-luxe sleeper trains to glamorous coastal excursions and retro-chic day trips through the country’s winemaking regions. Whether you're interested in Italian history, architecture, or cuisine, there's a train trip for you. Here’s a look at three new Italian rail journeys that are scheduled to debut in autumn 2026. Rome to Istanbul on Orient Express La Dolce Vita The newest autumn route from Accor’s Orient Express La Dolce Vita calls upon some of Italy’s most romantic cities, traverses the Romanian countryside, and visits the palaces of Budapest. The five-day, four-night sojourn begins in Rome, where the luxe train departs in the early evening. Passengers can sip an Italian aperitivo in the lounge car as the sun sets over Tuscany’s hills. In the morning, travellers will awake among the graceful canals and bridges of Venice, with a private water taxi to ferry them into the heart of the Venetian lagoon to explore the city’s many islands. A stop in Budapest is next on the itinerary, and passengers will have the chance to wander the historic squares and sample Hungarian wines. After a scenic journey across Europe’s Carpathian Mountains, the train crosses into Romania, where guests will tour Transylvania’s castles, including the Neo-Renaissance Peles Castle and Bran Castle (where Dracula was filmed) before arriving in Istanbul. Along the way, travellers can expect haute cuisine from Michelin-recognised chef Heinz Beck in the sleek restaurant car, festive nights with live music from a singer and pianist, and elegant cabins with a room service menu of Italian specialties like fennel taralli, olives, and cheese platters. The first journey departs on 22 October, 2026, and fares start at £17,000. Paris to Portofino on Belmond Venice-Simplon Orient Express It’s hard to imagine a more iconic Italian journey than this special itinerary from Belmond that combines a night on the Venice-Simplon Orient Express with a two-night stay at Splendido, A Belmond Hotel, Portofino. The train departs Paris in the afternoon and passes by charming cities in Burgundy before winding its way along the French Riviera past dazzling resort towns like Cannes and Nice. The route then dips down into Italy, through the port town of Genoa, and along the blue shores of the Ligurian coast to its terminus in Portofino. Aboard the VSOE, crew will pull out all the stops, including Champagne and afternoon tea service after boarding, a multi-course dinner and sommelier-selected wines in the historic restaurant cars, live music and artisanal cocktails in the Art Deco Bar Car 3674, and the Midnight Brunch with lobster rolls and truffled club sandwiches. Travellers then check in to the newly refreshed Splendido, overlooking the Gulf of Tigullio. Here, guests can enjoy the redesigned pool club, take a tennis clinic, or hike to a local lighthouse. The journey ends on a high note: cocktails and a private gala dinner at Splendido’s terrace restaurant overlooking the gulf. Because the journey takes place from October 15-18, 2026, travellers can expect comfortable temperatures and fewer crowds in Portofino. Fares start at about £17,400. Milan to Alba on FS Treini Touristi With FS Treini Touristi’s new “Truffle and Wine” route, travellers can hop aboard a stylish vintage train car and learn about authentic Italian cuisine while the green hills of Piedmont roll by the windows. The route glides through Italy’s Langhe region from Milan to Alba, known for its white truffles and well-balanced Barberas. Passengers board meticulously restored Gran Confort carriages, which date back to the 1970s and are emblems of Modern Italian design, with velvet-upholstered seats and panoramic windows. Travellers will see hillside vineyards and medieval villages trundle by, but there’s more than just scenic views to enjoy on board. During the 3.5-hour ride, passengers can sample the region’s flavours with tastings of local products, learn about Alba’s traditions, culture, and landscapes. Once in Alba, travellers are free to explore on their own, and there are plenty of culinary adventures to embark upon, from browsing seasonal markets, to sipping local wine in historic bars, and visiting artisanal chocolate shops. Best of all, the route is timed to coincide with the International Alba White Truffle Fair, which runs from October 10 to December 6, 2026. Here, visitors can celebrate all forms of this beloved regional ingredient, including cooking demonstrations, sampling local delicacies, and purchasing white truffles directly from the trifulao, or truffle hunters, themselves. The roundtrip route operates every Sunday from 11 October through 6 December, 2026. One-way fares are about £60.

item.title: 15 of the best hotels in Seville for a taste of southern Spain
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.90
Seville carries the heart and soul of southern Spain and some of the best hotels in Seville are a reflection of this. Its historic splendour has inspired countless works of music, art and poetry but it’s also full of contemporary style and flavour for modern holidaymakers. As the capital of Andalucía, its heritage ranges from colonial influences brought by merchants trading across the Spanish Empire to the enchanting, ornamental Islamic traditions of Al-Andalus. The city’s hotels range from charmingly historic to stylishly modern: age-old buildings have been carefully converted into characterful new places to stay, while contemporary hoteliers, designers and chefs are giving Seville the extra touches that appeal to the savvy traveller of today. Whether you're in search of gastronomy, cocktails and rooftop pools or majestic architecture and traditional Andalusian decoration, this is your guide to Seville’s best hotels. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Seville: - For an Old Town location: Cristine Bedfor - With a pool: Casa Palacio Don Ramón - For couples: Cavalta Boutique Hotel - For first-time visitors: Hotel Colón, a Gran Meliá, What are the best hotels in Seville with a view? In the Santa Cruz District, some of the rooms at EME Catedral Mercer have beautiful views of Seville’s cathedral – although the best vantage point is from the rooftop bar. For a grand stay, some of the rooms at Alfonso XIII have views from their private balconies. How we choose the best hotels in Seville Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

item.title: Best Middle Eastern restaurants in London to try now: from buzzy new openings like Kismet to neighbourhood favourites like Cafe Palestina
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.54
Given the cultural diversity of London, a city shaped by a sprawling patchwork of overlapping and interlocking communities, it’s no surprise that Middle Eastern restaurants in London offer an impressive array of flavours and regional specialities to explore. A short stroll down Edgware Road to the west will take you past delis brimming with heaps of pickles and fragrant toum, each spot known by locals for serving some of the best shawarma or shish tawook. In other hotspots, like Green Lanes in North London, visitors can find fresh savoury gözleme a stone’s throw from a café specialising in sweet baklava and knafeh. Many of these establishments have been stalwarts of London’s food scene for decades, but over the past year alone, the city has seen a wave of new Middle Eastern openings. For those looking to explore this ever-evolving food scene, here is our guide to the best Middle Eastern restaurants in London. Kismet Hidden above The Globe Tavern in the heart of Borough Market, visitors to Kismet have to walk through a traditional London pub, climb a narrow staircase and slip behind a velvet curtain to enter its dining room. Here the atmosphere changes entirely. Inspired by the meyhanes of Istanbul and Northern Cyprus – traditional taverns in which live music accompanies leisurely shared meals – Kismet offers the kind of warmth and familiarity that's often difficult to find in a city as large as London. The windows covered with delicate crochet curtains cast patterned shadows upon white linen tablecloths, and family photographs sit alongside dark mahogany furniture. Turkish music fills the space, with the waiters humming along as they weave back and forth to the open kitchen. The set menu, which embraces the meyhane tradition of sharing, is recommended. Begin with mezze such as hibeş, a whipped tahini with citrus, cacık made with strained yoghurt and cucumber, alongside the rich “atom”, featuring buffalo milk yoghurt topped with chilli butter. Continue with mangal-grilled specialities, including tavuk şiş, a wonderfully smoky chicken thigh and red pepper mix. Be sure to save room for dessert; the waiters arrive carrying silver trays laden with Turkish tea and slices of pistachio baklava served directly to the table. Address: Kismet, Above the Globe Tavern, 8 Bedale St, SE1 9AL Website: kismet.london Kinz At home inside a former Lloyds Bank building in Notting Hill, Kinz makes the most of the property’s 1930s generous architecture. The Lebanese restaurant boasts a triple-height dining room framed by three large windows, a tasteful nod to the traditional three-way arches of the Ottoman era. Other details honour Lebanese design, with striped linen seating and backgammon boards featured alongside photographs of the country by local artists. The menu focuses on Lebanese home cooking, moving from mezze to larger sharing plates. Start with smoky moutabel, or spinach fatayer, delicate triangular pastries filled with greens. The meat kibbeh, filled with spiced lamb, beef, pine nuts and onions, is another highlight, while the fattoush is served with an extra drizzle of gloriously tart pomegranate molasses. For larger plates, opt for the chicken taouk mashawi skewers served with plenty of toum, or the warak enab, which pairs vine leaves with spiced lamb in a lemon sauce. Be sure to finish with a traditional cup of Lebanese coffee or a “Beirut Pistachio”, featuring a sweet espresso shot laced with pistachio cream. Address: Kinz, 50 Notting Hill Gate, W11 3JD Website: kinzrestaurant.com Logma Named after the Persian, Arabic and Turkish word loghmeh, meaning perfect bite, Logma brings together Iranian and Iraqi home cooking inspired by founders Ziad Halub and Farsin Rabiee’s family recipes. Despite having only recently opened in Hackney, the cafe-bistro has quickly become known for the queues that snake along the pavement outside. Luckily, the line moves quickly, thanks to Logma’s focus on generously filled sandwiches served at speed. Signature combinations include slow-cooked aubergine, kofta, pickles and house sauce, while weekly specials might feature dishes such as fesenjan with walnuts and pomegranate molasses, or fennel stew served with saffron rice. Seating is limited, with most diners opting to take their order away. Pick up a “Dirty Logma” – coffee with date syrup, oat milk and cardamom – to tide you over for the 15-minute stroll along the canal towards nearby Victoria Park, where you can enjoy your sandwich picnic-style. Address: Logma, 81 Goldsmiths Row, E2 8QR Website: @logmaldn Patogh Tucked away on a side street just off Edgware Road, Patogh is an old-school Persian eatery serving succulent kebabs and freshly baked bread. In the homely downstairs seating area, visitors often find themselves brushing elbows with other diners, conversation spilling between groups as the chefs hurriedly work away in the open kitchen at the back. Lamb is tumbled in richly spiced marinade, grilled until moist and served alongside buttery saffron rice. Wash your meal down with a glass of steaming green tea or doogh, a refreshing Persian drink made from yoghurt and milk. Address: Patogh, 8 Crawford Place, W1H 5NE Website: patoghlondon.com Akub Located in the heart of Notting Hill, Akub is a small Palestinian restaurant combining traditional flavours with modern influences. Dishes are surprising yet familiar; the buket mousakhan consists of succulent chicken, onion and sumac served in one large bread parcel; wild sea bass is cured in arak, olive oil and sumac to honour the region’s fish dishes; zaatar and tahina ice cream are served alongside the more traditional flavours of pistachio and vanilla. Be sure to pay attention to the drinks on offer, too, with regional specialities incorporated in Akub’s Zaatar Martini, Shattarita and Lemon Ashta cocktails. Address: 27 Uxbridge Street, W8 7TQ Website: akub-restaurant.com Diwan Dimas Found towards the end of Edgware Road, Diwan Dimas is a humble deli serving Damascene sweets and other Arab dessert dishes. Here, visitors can order syrup-laden baklava, ashta-filled beinnaren and pistachio-stuffed burma. While I would encourage trying each of these buttery desserts separately, the real star of the show at Diwan Dimas is the knefeh. Known among locals as the best knefeh in London, the dish is made the traditional way – soft goat’s cheese, lightly sweetened, is topped with finely-shredded filo pastry and generous spoonfuls of syrup. Address: Diwan Dimas, 21 Edgware Road, Tyburnia, W2 2HX Website: ubereats.com Imad’s Syrian Kitchen Owner and head chef Imad Alarnab started a series of supper clubs and takeaway lunch pop-ups when he moved to London after fleeing the war in Syria. These modest events quickly gained notoriety, particularly Imad’s famous “falafel lunch boxes”, and the chef was able to open his own restaurant in the city. Now located in Kingly Court, Imad’s Syrian Kitchen serves a range of traditional dishes. Mezzes include saroja (delicately cooked aubergine layered with feta, halloumi, sour cherries and date molasses) and mtuma bitinjan (crispy fried aubergine served with tahini and tart barberries). More widely known main dishes, such as shishtawook and tahini kofta, are on offer, but I would suggest trying the makmour jaj, which marries yoghurt-marinated chicken with bulgar, pomegranate and fried vermicelli. Address: Imad’s Syrian Kitchen, Top Floor, Kingly Court, Carnaby Street, W1B 5PW Website: imadssyriankitchen.co.uk Nandine This restaurant has come far from its humble beginnings in Elephant and Castle, where head chef, Pary Baban, began serving Kurdish food to local workers who visited her family-run newsagent in the 1990s. Due to growing demand over the years, Pary relocated her restaurant to a larger space in Camberwell and quickly became a local celebrity chef; during the daytime, families with young children gather around large tables for brunch and sweet Kurdish desserts, before a younger crowd slowly dribbles in for the evening service. Must-tries include the slow-cooked lamb shank, patatau ron (battered aubergine topped with roasted onion, tomato and amba tirshyat) and kubba (Kurdish rice dumplings stuffed with spiced beef). Address: Nandine, 45 Camberwell Church Street, SE5 8TR Website: @nandineuk Cafe Palestina This quaint cafe in sleepy northwest London acts as both a popular restaurant and community hub, with Arabic lessons and events for children on offer. If you can bag one of the sought-after tickets, you can gain an insight into this sense of community at one of the cafe’s occasional supper club events. If not, make your way down for a weekend brunch, sampling the classic hummus, smoky aubergine mutabbal, fresh tabbouleh salad and fragrant olives served in their breakfast platter. I would recommend first-time visitors try the vine leaves and spinach pastry too, savouring some sweet cardamom coffee on the side. Be sure to make your way to the back of the cafe, where Palestinian goods, such as ceramics and speciality foods, can be found. Address: Cafe Palestina, 53 Fortess Road, NW5 1AD Website: cafepalestina.co.uk Berenjak Designed with the classic neighbourhood eateries of Tehran in mind, Berenjak brings authentic Persian flavours to the London food scene. Whilst better known and therefore slightly busier than our other spots, the authentic, home-style food at Berenjak makes it well worth the visit; mezze dishes include walnut-flavoured hummus e khanegi, smoky aubergine mirza ghasemi and coal-cooked kashk e bademjoon. I would recommend one of the shared dishes for the main, with zereshk polow ba morgh – delicate rotisserie chicken bathed in saffron sauce and served with crispy tahdig – a personal favourite. Address: Berenjak Soho, 27 Romilly Street, W1D 5AL; Berenjak Borough, 1 Bedale Street, SE1 9AL Website: berenjak.com Yeni Inspired by traditional open-fire cooking and regional dishes, chef Civan Er adds a modern twist to his otherwise quintessentially Turkish menu. Guests are able to watch the chef cooking at the grill located towards the back of the restaurant, with the exposed brick decor and simple tableware evoking the outdoor garden dining that is popular in Turkey. Dishes include fried kelle cheese coated in thyme honey, and lamb served with walnuts, ksir and sour cherries. The nature of the sharing plates means you are able to try a little bit of everything, but make sure to order at least one yeni manti for the table – the beef-stuffed manti dumplings with fermented yoghurt are a twist on the classic. Address: Yeni, 55 Beak Street, Carnaby, W1F 9SH Website: yeni.london Take a stroll up Green Lanes Green Lanes, which has become known for its diversity, is now a thriving home for Turkish, Kurdish and Greek restaurants in London. A stroll towards Turnpike Lane will leave you spoilt for choice as kebab shops, traditional Turkish restaurants and baklava-filled delis vie for your attention. If you have enough time on your hands, try the Turkish lamb stews at Gökyüzü, spinach and cheese stuffed fried bread at Gözleme House and sweet pastries at Antepliler Kunefe. If you feel like trying your hand at some cooking, Gözleme House also sells frozen manti by the kilo (small dumplings filled with mincemeat). Simply boil these at home, serving with garlic yoghurt and chilli butter, for an authentic Turkish meal. Address: Green Lanes, Hornsey, N8 0RE Bab al-Yemen Located in Fulham, Bab al-Yemen stays true to its roots, serving Yemeni food with traditional-style floor seating. The casual decor of the restaurant, coupled with the friendliness of the waiters, puts visitors right at home, sinking into the plush floor seating as they wait for their food. Lamb fahsah, a stew made with fenugreek and spices, or Mofa, a lightly spiced sea bass dish, are favourites amongst regulars. It is worth noting that the restaurant tends to fill up in the evening, so be sure to call ahead or opt for their takeaway option. Address: 236 North End Rd, W14 9NU Website: babalyemen.co This article was first published by Condé Nast Traveller Middle East.

item.title: This iconic European city is officially the world’s best city for a ‘workation’ in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.47
If, like many of us at Condé Nast Traveller, you touch down in a new city and exhale something along the lines of “I could live here!” within a day or two, then the prospect of an official ‘workation’ may be an especially attractive proposition. With millions of us completing our daily tasks on laptops, taking international calls on Zoom and enjoying greater office flexibility, the workation has quickly become one of travel’s biggest trends. However, as much as working on the move may appeal, it can feel a little overwhelming choosing the ‘perfect destination’. Thankfully for curious digital nomads, travel eSIM provider Holafly has highlighted the best workation destinations for 2026. To uncover where we should be whipping out our laptops, Holafly compiled a list of the 20 most-visited cities in the world and measured them by key metrics that affect travellers’ ability to work in a new destination. The metrics include the average summer temperature, air quality, elevation, access to local water and nature amenities, median one-night hotel price, walkability, broadband speed, and whether the city has a WeWork co-working location. With more than 17 million global visitors passing through each year, it’s unsurprising that the French capital is named the best workation destination in the world for 2026. Thanks to a much more bearable summer temperature than many other destinations in the top 25, an average broadband speed of 240.67 megabits per second and a walkability score of 9.7, Paris has emerged as a hotspot for digital nomads right now. In second place is Bangkok. The Thai capital has become an extremely popular destination for flexible workers – largely due to lower prices. The median price of a hotel is around £24 a night, while the city’s access-to-nature score is 15/15 and broadband speed is the highest of the top three cities at 317.03 megabits per second. London comes in third with a considerably high walkability score and plenty of coworking spaces, although it is among the most expensive cities on the list for hotel stays. item.title: 15 best children's sun creams: our parent editors recommend for heat waves and holidays
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.46
Testing sun cream on children isn't like testing it on yourself: it has to survive being licked, rubbed into eyes and applied in the ninety seconds before someone bolts for the paddling pool. So the best children's sun creams are the ones that hold up to that chaos, all while still doing the actual job of protecting skin that burns easily. There are some basic guidelines to follow. Always choose a minimum of SPF 50+ with four- or five-star UVA ratings or an equivalent "very high" broad-spectrum claim and pick a formula suited to your child's age and skin type. Beyond that, it’s crucial to reapply constantly – especially after swimming, sweating, towelling or a determined bout of face-rubbing. Sun cream is just one part of a sun protection system that also includes shade, protective clothing and a hat. A safety note before anything else: sun cream is not a licence to stay out in the sun for longer. It reduces the risk of burning, but it doesn't remove it. As the NHS states: babies under six months should be kept out of direct sunlight altogether rather than relying on sun cream. And it’s worth remembering that the sun’s strongest hours (11am-3pm in the UK) need shade and protective clothing to stay safe. Disclaimer: this is general information, not medical advice for an individual child. If you have specific concerns about sunscreen use for your baby, speak to a GP, health visitor or pharmacist. The best children’s sun creams at a glance - Best overall: La Roche-Posay Anthelios UVMune 400 Dermo-Pediatrics Hydrating Lotion SPF50+ - Best for sports: Ultrasun Kids SPF50+ - Best for strong sun: Altruist Kids Cream SPF50 - Best for water resistance/swimming: P20 Kids SPF50+ - Best for sensitive skin: Bioderma Photoderm Pediatrics SPF 50+ - Best for eczema-prone skin: Heliocare 360 Pediatric Atopic Lotion Spray SPF50 - Best for babies: Eucerin Sun Kids Dry Touch SPF50 - Best coloured SPF: Nivea Sun Kids Suncream Spray SPF 50 Coloured - Best vegan sun cream for kids: Childs Farm SPF50+ Sun Cream (Fragrance-Free) - Best roll-on sun cream for kids: Garnier Ambre Solaire Sensitive Advanced Kids Coloured Roll-On SPF50+ - Best spray sun cream for kids: E45 Kids & Baby SPF 50 Sensitive Spray - Best fragrance-free formula: Avène Kids Sun Protection Spray SPF50+ - Best combination of chemical and mineral formula: Green People Children's Organic Sun Cream SPF50 - Best 100% mineral formula: Sunly Kids Mineral Sunscreen Stick, SPF 50 - Best budget sun cream for kids: Soltan Baby SPF50 The best sun creams for children How we tested and selected the products - Reliable UVA and UVB protection 2. Ease of application 3. How well products perform during swimming and play 4. Suitability for sensitive or eczema-prone skin 5. Value, texture and likelihood of children tolerating regular application FAQs What SPF should children use? SPF50 or 50+ with a four- or five-star UVA rating is a sensible choice for children, even though the official minimum set out by the NHS, Cancer Research UK, the UK Health Security Agency and the British Association of Dermatologists is SPF30. Children's skin is thinner and burns more easily than adult skin, which is why most parents reach for the higher factor in practice and it's what every product on this list uses. But understanding what that number actually protects against matters as much as the figure itself. SPF and UVA protection aren't the same thing and sun cream needs to be checked for both. SPF (Sun Protection Factor) measures protection specifically against UVB rays – the ones chiefly responsible for sunburn – and is rated on a scale of 2 to 50+ on UK products, with 50+ giving the strongest UVB protection. On its own, the SPF number says nothing about UVA protection. UVA rays penetrate more deeply into the skin, are the main driver of premature skin ageing and still contribute to skin cancer risk even though they cause less sunburn than UVB. That's precisely why UVA protection is shown separately, using the UK's star rating system: a 0-to-5-star scale found on most UK sunscreen packaging, where more stars means stronger UVA protection. So you’re looking for four or five stars, or the alternative "UVA" letters inside a circle, which confirms a product meets the EU's minimum UVA standard. A sunscreen that genuinely protects a child needs both a high SPF and a high UVA star rating – one without the other leaves a real gap in protection. It’s worth noting that sunscreen can rub, sweat or wash off even when it's described as waterproof, which is why it needs reapplying after swimming, sweating or towelling dry – regardless of how the product is marketed, including once a day and water resistant formulas. A high SPF is never a reason to stay out in the sun for longer. Putting on more sun cream doesn't mean more time can be spent outdoors and NHS advice says don't spend any longer in the sun than you would without sun cream at all. Sun cream should never be relied on alone. Instead, it is one part of a wider approach that also needs shade and clothing, whatever the number on the bottle says. What to look for in childrens' sun cream - SPF 50+ - 4 or 5 star UVA protection or UVA letters inside a circle - Broad-spectrum protection - Age-appropriate formulation - Fragrance-free option for sensitive skin - Water-resistant formula for swimming and sport - Easy-to-spread texture - Packaging that makes it possible to apply enough product - In-date product, checked against the "period after opening" (PAO) symbol Mineral versus chemical sun cream for children Sun creams sold in the UK work in one of two ways: they’re chemical or mineral. According to the British Association of Dermatologists, most sunscreens actually contain a mix of both: organic (chemical) filters, which work by absorbing UV radiation and turning it into harmless warmth and inorganic (mineral) filters, which both absorb and scatter UV rays away from the skin. In practical terms, chemical sun creams tend to disappear into the skin without a trace, while mineral formulas – usually built on zinc oxide or titanium oxide – sit visibly on the surface and reflect the rays back. None of the UK's main health bodies singles out mineral filters as the inherently safer choice for children, in the way some online advice suggests. The British Association of Dermatologists' own sun protection fact sheet states that expert reviews have concluded the ingredients used in sunscreens don't pose a concern for human health and its guidance, along with that from Cancer Research UK and the UK Health Security Agency, centres on SPF and UVA star rating rather than filter type. The advice is to use a minimum of SPF30 with four or five UVA stars, whichever type of sun cream it is. Where mineral formulas do have a slight practical edge is that they can be easier to see (and therefore easier to check for gaps) once applied. Is sun cream safe for babies and young children? Sun cream is considered safe when used as directed. The British Association of Dermatologists states that expert reviews have found the ingredients used in sun creams don't pose a concern for human health, though occasional irritation or allergy is possible. For babies and very young children specifically, though, sun cream isn't the first line of defence and shouldn't be the only one used. Babies and young children should be kept out of direct sunlight as much as possible, particularly during the strongest part of the day, which is 11am to 3pm in the UK between March and October, per NHS guidance. This also helps reduce a baby's heat load, since babies can overheat more easily than older children. In practice, this means leaning on shade rather than sun cream: a wide-brimmed hat, lightweight clothing that covers the skin and a pram parasol or canopy suited to the pushchair, combined with time spent under trees, umbrellas or indoors during peak hours. For babies under six months, the British Association of Dermatologists advises avoiding sun cream altogether unless there's genuinely no other way to protect them, applying it only to small exposed areas such as the cheeks and the backs of the hands as a last resort. This is the point at which it's worth asking a GP, health visitor or pharmacist for guidance suited to your own baby, particularly if they have a skin condition or you're unsure what's appropriate. If a child has sensitive skin, it's worth patch-testing a new sunscreen first: apply a small amount to a small area, such as the inside of the arm, and wait two to three days to check for a reaction before using it more widely, following advice from a health professional first if the child has a diagnosed skin condition such as eczema. If irritation, redness, stinging or any sign of an allergic reaction does develop, stop using the product and seek advice from a pharmacist or GP, especially if it doesn't settle quickly or appears to be getting worse. How to apply sun cream to children correctly - Apply generously before going outside, following the product's own instructions - Cover all exposed areas, including ears, neck, shoulders, hands, feet and the backs of knees - Take care around the eyes and mouth where skin is thinner, but don’t forget these areas - Reapply frequently, especially after swimming, sweating, towelling or rubbing - Do not rely on a single morning application - Check the label for specific instructions on water resistance - Always use clothing, shade and hats alongside sunscreen What SPF is best for children? At least SPF30, with a UVA star rating of four or five stars (or the "UVA" letters in a circle, which shows a product meets the EU standard). Because children's skin burns more easily than adult skin, SPF50 or 50+ is the standard on every product in this list, because it gives extra margin above that minimum. How often should you reapply children's sunscreen? Every two hours as a baseline and immediately after swimming, sweating or towelling dry, regardless of whether the product claims to be water-resistant or once a day. Cancer Research UK is explicit that all sunscreens need reapplying throughout the day, whatever the label says. Apply sun cream 15-30 minutes before going out, then again 15-30 minutes after stepping into the sun, since the second application catches anywhere missed the first time round. Can babies wear sun cream? Not under six months old. Instead, keeping infants that age out of direct sun and relying on shade and lightweight, covering clothing instead. If there's genuinely no way to keep a young baby out of the sun, it’s ok to apply small amounts of high-SPF sun cream to exposed areas such as the cheeks and the backs of the hands. From six months, a sun cream with at least SPF30 and strong UVA protection like the baby-specific formulas on this list, can be used on any skin not already covered by clothing, a hat or shade. Is mineral or chemical sunscreen better for eczema-prone skin? None of the UK's main sun-safety bodies makes a blanket recommendation either way, and the right answer varies child to child. NHS clinical guidance on managing childhood eczema does offer some practical, eczema-specific pointers, though: choose a fragrance-free sun cream, as fragrance is a common cause of stinging and irritation in eczema-prone skin. Products labelled for sensitive skin or toddlers tend to contain fewer of these irritants and if a child still reacts to those then a mineral sun cream built purely on zinc oxide or titanium dioxide with no chemical filters at all, is worth trying instead. Can children use adult sun cream? The official guidance is built around SPF and UVA star rating rather than whether a product is marketed for adults or kids. In principle, an adult sun cream with at least SPF30 (SPF50 for extra margin), four or five UVA stars and broad-spectrum cover meets the same official standard as anything labelled "for children." In practice, formulas marketed for children are often fragrance-free or designed with fewer common irritants, which can matter more for a child prone to reactions than the “kids" label itself so it's the ingredients and the SPF/UVA figures worth checking, rather than the marketing on the front of the bottle. Always follow the specific product's minimum-age guidance, since some adult formulas aren't tested or recommended for very young skin. What is the best sun cream for children with eczema or sensitive skin? What suits one child won't necessarily suit another. NHS clinical guidance on managing childhood eczema does offer practical pointers, though: choose a fragrance-free sunscreen since fragrance and certain sunscreen chemicals are common causes of stinging and irritation on eczema-prone skin. Products labelled for sensitive skin or toddlers tend to contain fewer of these irritants. And if a child still reacts, a mineral sun cream built purely on zinc oxide or titanium dioxide, with no chemical filters at all, is worth trying instead. The same guidance suggests applying the morning emollient at least 30 minutes before sunscreen and patch-testing any new product on a small area of skin for two to three days before using it more widely. Children's sun cream FAQs What is the safest SPF for children? The official minimum is SPF30, but a higher SPF50 or 50+ with four or five UVA stars gives children's skin extra margin. Mineral or chemical sunscreens are both effective and what you choose is down to preference. Is SPF 30 enough for children? Yes, provided it also has a four- or five-star UVA rating and is applied generously and reapplied regularly. SPF30 is the baseline, though many parents opt for SPF50. Is SPF 50 better than SPF 30? SPF 50 offers a modest increase in UVB protection over SPF 30. But SPF alone isn't the full picture – the UVA star rating, generous application and regular reapplication matter just as much as the SPF you choose. What is the best sun cream for a baby? You should avoid sun cream under six months where possible and stay out of the sun. And from six months avoid the sun but use an SPF with at least SPF30 with strong UVA protection and a minimum-age suitable for your baby. Is mineral sun cream better for children? NHS guidance simply notes mineral formulas are often easier to see once applied, which some parents may find helpful. That ‘white cast’ is typical of zinc-based or zinc blend formulas is something adults hate but can be useful for ensuring your child is fully covered in SPF. Is fragrance-free sun cream better for eczema? Often, yes. The NHS clinical guidance on managing childhood eczema recommends fragrance-free sun cream, since fragrance can be a common cause of irritation for eczema-prone skin. Look for products designed for atopic skin, which is another word for very dry, itchy skin that’s prone to eczema and easily inflamed. How often should you reapply sun cream to children? At least every two hours and immediately after swimming, sweating or towelling dry. Cancer Research UK is really clear this applies even to "water-resistant" and "once a day" products, too. Can children use adult sun cream? Yes, provided it meets the same SPF30 and above and four-to-five-star UVA standard. You don't need to use a children's-specific formula, though it's worth checking the product's own minimum-age guidance. Is spray sun cream safe for children? Yes. As a general precaution though, avoid spraying directly onto a child's face. Spray into your hands first, then apply it to them. Does sun cream expire? Yes it does. Check the "period after opening" symbol on the packaging, as out-of-date sunscreen may no longer give the protection stated on the label. You could always pop a sticky label on your SPF and write the date of purchase on it if you’re concerned.

item.title: 6 beautiful hotels in Fethiye from which to experience the Turkish Riviera's most sparkling ocean views and sensational food scene, 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.91
There's no shortage of beautiful hotels in Turkey, and the sparkling Turkish Riviera is becoming an increasingly popular holiday hotspot for good reason. Narrowing down our top picks of where to stay is not easy, but booking one of the best hotels in Fethiye is a recipe for success if extended summer climes, picture-perfect coastlines and top-tier hospitality are what you favour. From buzzy boutique spots only reachable by boat to sprawling resorts that somehow never feel crowded, Fethiye's hotels are designed to suit all manner of traveller. Here, we list six of our tried and tested favourites, and the ones we'd revisit time and time again. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Fethiye: Best for couples: Yazz Collective Best for families: Cape Arna XO Best for wellness: Ahãma Best affordable: D-Resort Gocek How we choose the best hotels in Fethiye, Turkey Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. For more information on how we review hotels and restaurants, please look at our About Us page. This is our edit of the best hotels in Fethiye, Turkey. What is the best time of year to visit Turkey? The season on the Turkish Coast runs from May to October. September and October are heavenly – it’s quieter, the sea is still warm, the days warm and evenings cooler. July and August can be crazy hot. Istanbul is a blast year-round, though it’s no winter-sun destination – sometimes it snows in January. For more information, visit the best time to visit Turkey.

item.title: Who really owns the Caspian Sea?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 7.57
For decades, debate in Iran over the Caspian Sea has often centered on a deceptively simple question: What percentage belongs to the country? Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan all border the body of water. But the Caspian is treated neither as a conventional sea nor simply as an international lake. Instead, the five countries have developed a special legal regime governing navigation, territorial waters, fishing, security and seabed resources. The most important step came in 2018, when the five presidents signed the Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea in Aktau, Kazakhstan. It established territorial waters of up to 15 nautical miles and an additional 10-nautical-mile exclusive fishing zone for each country. But it did not divide the entire Caspian into five fixed national shares. Why doesn't Iran own half the Caspian Sea Before the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Iran and the Soviet Union were the only two countries bordering the Caspian. The 1921 Russo-Persian Treaty of Friendship restored Iranian navigation rights restricted under Imperial Russia. A 1940 treaty further regulated trade and navigation. None of the agreements, however, awarded Iran 50% of the Caspian. Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, says that this distinction is central to understanding the dispute. "None of these treaties specified a percentage for either Iran or the Soviet Union," he told DW. "They emphasized common use rather than dividing the sea into ownership shares." After the Soviet collapse, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan emerged as independent states, turning a bilateral legal arrangement into a five-country negotiation. Some Iranian politicians argued for a 50% share since it had previously shared the sea with the Soviet Union alone; others called for 20%. So far, neither claim has gained international recognition. What the 2018 Caspian Sea agreement settled "The Caspian is neither completely a sea nor completely a lake," Vakhshiteh said.
