The Framework Laptop 12 starts at $699 for a pre-built Linux configuration in green or $549 for a DIY version in black, gray, light purple, pink, or green. Framework is collecting pre-orders now and plans to start shipping the new laptop in October.

item.title: Apple has new in-app transaction commission rates for EU devs
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.15
Apple has new in-app transaction commission rates for EU devs It’s the latest change based on legal challenges under the Digital Markets Act. Apple has laid out its new business terms for apps that will be distributed in the European Union. The new policies, which take effect starting October 1, will see the company's heavily debated Core Technology Fee replaced with a new Core Technology Commission that will be applied to in-app purchases. There are several different permutations of commission rates based on how the app accepts a transaction. Devs that participate in the App Store Small Business Program, the Mini Apps Partner Program and the Video Partner Program will be offered discounted rates under each branch of the terms. "The majority of developers" using Apple In-App Purchase tech on apps distributed on the App Store apps will be charged a 15 percent fee, the company wrote. For devs outside those programs, the commission will be 26 percent. App Store apps using alternative tools for payment processing will be charged a 20 percent fee, while for App Store apps that link out of the app to complete purchases, the fee will be 15 percent. Program members using either of those paths will have commission rates of 10 percent. Any apps that are distributed outside Apple's App Store will have a flat fee of 5 percent as their commission. Apple has been involved in a convoluted, years-long legal battles over how it will conform to Europe's Digital Markets Act (DMA). Most recently, the company took a loss in its fight to avoid the more tightly policed "gatekeeper" status under the DMA. It may also be hauled into court on country-specific charges around potentially anti-competitive practices, most recently in Germany. There has been some movement in the US to loosen sideloading and alternative payment systems restrictions. Apple is also looking for US court support for taking a cut of 5 to 15 percent for transactions on third-party payments.

item.title: Warren Spector, founding father of immersive sims, has retired from game development
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 4.96
Warren Spector, founding father of immersive sims, has retired from game development Spector was the creator behind Deus Ex. The creator of Deus Ex, the action role-playing game franchise originally developed by Ion Storm, has announced his retirement. In a LinkedIn post, Warren Spector said he was a month away from his 44th year as a developer and had worked on tabletop games, 17 digital games, ran small and large teams and helped people with their careers. Now, his age and health are catching up with him, and it was time to "write some books, do a lot of reading, do some lecturing, maybe do some consulting." Spector also said that there are still three games he would like to make, but that the business has changed and it's not as fun for him anymore. While he admitted that he tried to retire in the past but changed his tune, he said he thinks he means it this time. He is typically regarded as a founding father of immersive sim games, characterized by giving players the freedom to solve problems in a variety of ways. On Deus Ex, wherein you play an anti-terrorism agent in a dystopian cyberpunk setting, Spector also served as director and producer. He worked on several Ultima titles as producer and writer, as well as on Disney's Epic Mickey for the Wii as director. His latest game was Thick As Thieves, a stealth-action heist game, released just a few months ago. He also worked on System Shock 3, but Tencent took over that project and its status remains unclear.

item.title: What's the difference between Android's Qi2 And Qi2.2 wireless charging?
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 4.72
What's the difference between Android's Qi2 And Qi2.2 wireless charging? There are some key distinctions that make a big difference. We live in a wireless world, so understanding the different standards at play can help you to maximize the performance of your gadgets and your chargers. For most devices, the wireless charging standard you'll be using is Qi2. The latest iteration of this is Qi2 25W, also commonly called Qi2.2. It was announced last summer that the new speed would be supported by both iPhones and select Android smartphones. Although Google was slow to adopt Qi2, we're now starting to see Qi2 25W listed as a feature for the next generation of Android phones, including the Pixel 11 lineup announced recently. So does it matter which version your device supports? There are a couple key distinctions that make Qi2.2 a worthwhile upgrade. More power, more speed The difference between Qi2 and Qi2.2 charging comes down to power. Qi2 25W offers 25 watts of power delivery when it's charging a compatible device. Qi2 is capped at 15 watts, so the new standard offers a substantial boost to power. In practice, that means your device will charge faster if it's using Qi2 25W. With Qi2, your gadgets could take between 50 and 80 minutes to reach 50 percent battery from zero. Qi2 25W, on the other hand, will get you to half battery in about half an hour. Considering wireless charging has traditionally been less efficient than wired, that's a welcome improvement. An additional benefit to Qi2.2 is improved thermal protection. So if you've ever noticed your phone getting pretty toasty while it's on a wireless pad, the upgrade will be a good one. Even if you can't feel the difference, it might subtly help to extend your phone's lifespan, because the lower peak temperature while charging can help your battery last longer. All told, Qi2 25W offers a solid improvement over its predecessor, so reap the rewards if your hardware supports this latest power option.

item.title: Things I learned about the rumored HomePod display from macOS beta code
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 2.75
Things I learned about the rumored HomePod display from macOS beta code Apple's latest software references customizable faces for the rumored "HomePad." Apple's HomePod isn't exactly a hit, and it has never really caught up to its competitors such as Amazon Echo devices. Yet, Apple insists on having its own lineup of smart speakers, and it looks like there are new HomePods on the way – at least that's what Apple's own code tells us. The company seems to have leaked a bunch of references to unreleased products in a recent beta of macOS 26.7. It's a massive leak, the kind that doesn't happen very often. And for the small group of HomePod fans, the good news is that major upgrades are coming soon. A HomePod with watch-like faces is on the way The current HomePods are essentially speakers with Siri. Aside from a touch-sensitive surface for media controls, they don't really have an interactive display. But here's the thing: that's likely about to change. The beta code from Apple makes clear references to a new "HomeAccessory" that is likely a HomePod (or maybe a HomePad?) with a screen. If it seems like you've heard about this before, that's because there's a good chance you have. There have been rumors about a HomePod with a display the size of an iPad for years, but it looks like it's almost ready to be launched. So what exactly does the code leaked this week reveal? Perhaps the most interesting part is about the interface – or at least what to expect from it. Like other HomePods, this new model with a display is likely to run a variant of tvOS. The interface will be quite different, though. The code reveals that its home screen will feature "Faces" and a "Face Gallery." Think of them like Apple Watch faces, but bigger. These faces appear to be customizable with different widgets and even Smart Stacks, so you'll see different widgets throughout the day. The code also suggests that the new HomePod can detect when the user's iPhone is nearby to decide whether or not to display personal information in the widgets. That's a really nice touch for keeping sensitive data private. iPhone widgets can also be added to this HomePod. It should work much like placing iPhone app widgets on your Mac using Handoff. Support for Siri AI and App Intents is also expected based on what the code tells us. Previous rumors suggest that this HomePod with a display will have a more square shape. Although the exact design remains unclear, the leaked code confirms one detail about it: a wall-mountable version. There are references to "HomeAccessory" and "HomeAccessory_wall" in the beta released yesterday. Apple has other home devices in the works There's another intriguing product that's been rumored recently: a tabletop robot. According to Bloomberg, it's expected to feature a display attached to a robotic arm that can rotate in any direction. While product specs are still quite vague, the product is reported to be codenamed J595. References to that codename can be found in HomeKit-related frameworks in this macOS beta, seemingly confirming that the product is indeed in development. Don't expect to see the tabletop robot anytime soon, though. It probably won't be unveiled before 2027. These aren't the only HomePod-related details revealed by the leaked code. It looks like Apple is also set to release a new generation of the HomePod mini, codenamed B525. But you should probably keep your expectations low since this will likely be a minor upgrade without any big changes. At least you can expect a few new colors, according to MacRumors. This macOS 26.7 beta, which came as an easter egg full of surprises, also references new iPhones, AirPods, iPads and even Macs.

item.title: What Makes Someone A ‘Touron’? Travel Experts Share 11 National Park Mistakes To Avoid
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 6.79
A "touron" may sound like just another internet insult, but the term is now used for travelers who ignore rules, take unnecessary risks or damage the places they came to see. Social media now makes these mistakes especially visible, yet this behavior is not new. Nor are the consequences, which range from fines and serious injuries to damaged ecosystems, endangered wildlife and extra pressure on park rangers and rescue teams. What Is A 'Touron’? A “touron” is a blend of tourist and moron, generally used for a visitor whose careless, disrespectful or dangerous behavior puts themselves, other people, wildlife or a destination at risk. One of the earliest articles that used the term appeared in The Washington Post on Sept. 20, 1987, which defined a “touron” as “a tourist, usually an annoying one.” Social media has since given the term a much larger audience, such as Tourons of National Parks, an Instagram account dedicated to collecting videos of questionable visitor behavior. The Biggest Mistakes That Turn Visitors Into Tourons Visitors could earn the “touron” label by ignoring the basic rules that protect people and parks. Recent cases show how quickly seemingly thoughtless decisions can escalate. In 2026, a Yellowstone visitor received five days in jail after walking across fragile hydrothermal features at Mammoth Hot Springs, leaving damaging footprints behind. San Francisco Gate also reported that Yosemite visitors are leaving fresh graffiti and stickers around popular trails. A case from Pictured Rocks this year involved four visitors who carved into sandstone cliffs and collected more than 100 pounds of rocks. So, I interviewed 10 experts on the biggest mistakes visitors make in U.S. national parks. I also asked about their consequences and how travelers can explore these protected spaces more responsibly. 1. Getting Too Close To Wildlife Wild animals in national parks may appear calm, but approaching them can quickly become dangerous. Getting too close can provoke an attack, disrupt natural behavior and put both the visitor and the animal at risk. "Wildlife is one of the many reasons people visit national parks, but they are best appreciated from a safe distance," says Mike Reynolds, chief program officer at the National Park Foundation and a former acting director of the National Park Service (NPS), in an email interview. "Wildlife reacts to human behavior as well and the more we respect their natural habitat, the more we help parks manage them for the future," he adds. 2. Feeding Wildlife Feeding wildlife or allowing animals access to human food can teach them to associate people with an easy meal. That can change their natural behavior, increase the risk of dangerous encounters and, in some cases, ultimately result in an animal being relocated or euthanized. "Visitors also need to understand that interfering with wildlife can be detrimental to the animal. There have been quite a few stories recently about bears becoming too used to people and it causes parks to relocate them, or even euthanize them," says John Bowers, director of marketing and sales at Visit Jackson Hole, in an email interview. 3. Leaving Marked Trails And Boardwalks Stepping off a designated trail or boardwalk can damage vegetation, accelerate erosion and create unofficial paths that other visitors begin following. In places such as Yellowstone, leaving a boardwalk can also expose visitors to unstable ground and dangerously hot geothermal features. Jason Frye, author of Moon Great Smoky Mountains National Park, says shortcuts and "pirate" trails can affect an ecosystem for years, disturbing nesting wildlife, destroying habitat or even interfering with scientific research. "Once they’re established, they seem to draw unknowing hikers like a beacon," he adds in an email interview. At Yellowstone, Todd Walton, director of sales and marketing at Yellowstone National Park Lodges, is even more direct in his email to me: “We see people getting off established trails and boardwalks — which is a very bad idea, especially in thermal areas where the ground is very fragile and unstable. Not to mention potentially over 180 degrees, so it would cause massive burns and likely kill someone if they fell in.” 4. Ignoring Signs, Barriers And Closures Signs, railings and closures are not suggestions. They warn visitors about hazards that may not be obvious and, in some cases, protect fragile park resources. Ignoring them can result in serious injury or death while also putting rangers and rescuers at risk. Bill Wade, executive director of the Association of National Park Rangers, says one of the biggest mistakes visitors make is that they "either don’t read or they ignore flyers, signs and barriers warning them of risks and hazards.” He points to incidents such as visitors entering swift currents near the top of Nevada Fall in Yosemite and being swept over the edge, or crossing railings at Grand Canyon overlooks for a better photo and losing their balance. 5. Risking Safety For The Perfect Photo A photo is not worth crossing a barrier, approaching wildlife or stepping into a restricted area. While social media can encourage visitors to prioritize getting the shot, their behavior increases the risk of accidents and could damage the places they came to photograph. "There is often an illusion of control, a false sense of familiarity created by television and social media, and an increasing desire to capture the perfect photograph rather than fully experience the place," says Jesús Parrilla, founder of Experiential Hospitality Group, in an email interview. Those choices can also force rescue teams into unnecessary danger and divert park resources from conservation and maintenance. 6. Arriving Unprepared Visitors can get into trouble without breaking a single park rule if they underestimate the weather, terrain, distance or their own physical ability. Setting out without enough water, appropriate clothing or a map can turn an ordinary hike into an emergency. "Before heading out, research your park destination, check current advisories, and plan for the activities you want to enjoy. Because conditions vary dramatically by elevation, location, and season, always check the weather forecast, pack appropriate gear, carry more water than you think you need, and know your physical limits," Reynolds says. Walton also warns against relying solely on phones because cell service in national parks can be unreliable. Preventable rescues consume staff time and park resources that could otherwise support visitors, conservation and maintenance. 7. Leaving Trash Behind One discarded wrapper may seem insignificant, but millions of visitors making similarly small choices can create a much larger problem. Trash can harm wildlife, diminish the experience for other visitors and leave park staff dealing with damage that could easily have been prevented. Kevin Jackson, co-founder and CEO of EXP Journeys, says visitors sometimes behave as though they are the only person in the park: leaving trash because it is "just one wrapper,” without recognizing how often other people make the same decision. "Even something as simple as tossing away an apple core or banana peel isn’t as harmless as it looks,” says Leigh Barnes, president of North America at Intrepid Travel, in an email interview. “Food scraps can attract wildlife, spread pests or disease, and disrupt the natural balance of an ecosystem," he explains. 8. Taking Rocks, Flowers Or Other “Souvenirs” Pocketing one rock or picking one wildflower can feel inconsequential. But when thousands of visitors do the same thing year after year, the cumulative effect can physically change the landscape people traveled there to experience. Frye warns, “If there are 1,000 visitors on that trail that day and every one of them picks one bloom, then you don't have a meadow of wildflowers to enjoy tomorrow.” "The same goes for taking home a shell or an interesting-looking rock," says Barnes. "One souvenir might not seem like much, but when thousands of visitors do the same thing year after year, it starts to change the landscape people came to experience in the first place." 9. Driving As If Park Roads Are Ordinary Roads Speeding, driving off designated roads or simply treating park roads like ordinary highways can endanger wildlife, damage protected landscapes and leave visitors stranded in remote terrain. National park roads often pass directly through wildlife habitat, where conditions demand more caution than a typical road trip. Walton also lists "driving too fast" among the common mistakes visitors make. The consequences can extend well beyond a speeding ticket. In Death Valley National Park, a driver who went off the legal roadway and became stuck in mud apparently used a historic salt-tram tower as a winch anchor, as reported by the National Park Service. The attempt toppled the 113-year-old structure and pulled its concrete footings from the ground. 10. Hiking A Trail When It Is Too Wet Using a wet trail can cause more damage than many hikers realize. Footsteps create ruts. Visitors walk around puddles and the trail gradually widens, increasing erosion and potentially forcing park crews to undertake extensive repairs or close the route. "When soil is saturated, every footprint becomes a rut that channels water. That is how a 24-inch trail becomes 6 feet wide," says Ryan McLaughlin, founder of trail-condition platform Loam, in an email interview. He warns that beyond forecasts, checking existing conditions is equally important. "Rain three days ago matters more than sun today," he explains. He encourages everyone to do a simple test first: “If you sink in, or the ground sticks to your boots, turn around and pick something else.” 11. Geotagging Fragile Locations Sharing the precise location of a fragile viewpoint, trail or natural feature can suddenly send large numbers of visitors somewhere that may not be equipped for them. The resulting crowds can damage landscapes, disturb wildlife and strain park infrastructure and nearby communities. "A single post can encourage thousands of people to seek out the same viewpoint, placing pressure on fragile landscapes, park infrastructure, wildlife and nearby communities," says Clare Tobin, CEO of Wild Frontiers, in an email interview. She suggests considering whether a location can handle increased visitation before tagging it precisely. "Not every discovery needs to be pinpointed online," she adds. How To Be A Better National Park Visitor Being a good national park visitor means arriving prepared, following park-specific rules, giving wildlife space and leaving the landscape as you found it. Small choices such as staying on trail, carrying trash and knowing when to turn around help protect both visitors and the places they came to experience. "The best visitors arrive prepared, curious and humble," says Parrilla. “Rather than asking, 'What can I do here?' ask, 'How does this place work?'” In short, here are a few ways to be a good park visitor: - Plan before you go. Research the park, current advisories, weather, trail conditions and the activities you plan to do. - Bring enough food and water. Pack appropriate clothing, map and supplies. - Know your physical limits. Choose a trail that fits your capabilities. - Stay on designated trails and boardwalks. Respect closures, barriers and signs even when a shortcut or photo opportunity looks tempting. - Give wildlife plenty of space. Never feed, touch or deliberately approach wild animals. - Pack out what you bring in. Food scraps count as trash, too. - Leave rocks, flowers and other natural or cultural features where you find them. - Be prepared to change your plans. Weather, trail conditions, wildlife activity or your own limits may mean choosing another route or activity. - Ask a ranger. Visitor centers are valuable sources of current information about trails, hazards and changing conditions. Some of these guidelines can also apply to other nature settings. For example, if you’re visiting California state parks or Colorado state parks also plan ahead and respect nature. Why Responsible Tourism Matters Now More Than Ever Responsible tourism means recognizing that visiting a national park comes with a responsibility to protect its wildlife, landscapes and communities. How one visitor behaves may seem inconsequential, but repeated across millions of visits, those decisions will have a wider impact and not only on the ecosystems, but on park staff and infrastructure. "Because the parks belong to all of us, and that means we each bear a responsibility to ensure the next visitors enjoy it to its fullest," says Frye. Responsible behavior also matters because protecting parks requires significant resources. The National Park Service’s FY2025 operating budget was about $3.1 billion, while recreation fees were expected to bring in roughly $366 million. Preventable rescues, damaged trails and vandalized resources require staff time and money. "Sometimes stewardship is simply knowing when to stop, step back and give a place room to be wild," said Bowers. National parks are wild places, not backdrops. Prepare before you arrive, follow signs, stay on trails, keep your distance from wildlife and leave what you find. Responsible travel protects visitors, animals, park resources and the opportunity for future generations to experience these places on their own terms. Frye frames it as a shared responsibility: "If the national parks are 'America's best idea,' then shouldn't we, as Americans, do everything we can to ensure the parks live up to this ideal?"

item.title: 4 Manila Spas Where Heritage Meets High-Tech
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 5.36
Wellness in Manila is becoming more layered. Across the city’s spas, treatments are moving beyond the familiar massages toward a broader approach to restoration, one that can encompass traditional healing practices, personalized skincare, digital wellness tools and holistic programs designed around physical and mental well-being. Rather than following a single formula, established properties are driving this evolution in different ways. At some, centuries-old Filipino healing traditions remain central. At others, customization, technology and wellness resources allow guests to shape their experience around individual needs. The Retreat Spa at Okada Manila At Forbes Travel Guide Five-Star Retreat Spa at Okada Manila, Filipino healing customs also remain part of the spa experience. Indayog ng Duyan is a hilot-inspired therapy using warmed banana leaves soaked in virgin coconut oil. The leaves help the therapist identify areas of concern while the treatment focuses on restoring balance and encouraging the body to heal naturally. Okada Manila’s foot spa and reflexology center, Sole Retreat, provides an array of services that use deep pressure, rubbing techniques and acupressure. Areas of pain are treated as signs of nerve-ending sensitivity, which is expected to diminish over a series of treatments. Nüwa Spa At Five-Star Nüwa Spa, personalization has long been part of the philosophy. The first Five-Star spa in the Philippines, Nüwa Spa has held the distinction since 2020, while Nüwa Manila at City of Dreams has received Five-Star recognition since 2018. Its treatments take inspiration from Nüwa, the goddess in ancient Chinese mythology who restored the sky using five-colored stones. The story reflects a principle of Chinese medicine centered on achieving equilibrium through nature, which the spa incorporates into treatments designed around a guest’s constitution, emotions, the changing seasons and the flow of chi. Therapies also draw from Ayurveda, reiki and other Asian healing practices. That emphasis on personalization extends to skincare. Nüwa Spa offers facial and body treatments using products from French luxury skincare brand Biologique Recherche, whose methodology begins with an individual skin analysis. The guest’s condition informs a tailored regimen. The approximately 7,000-square-foot spa includes twin-bed suites for couples and comfortable single treatment rooms, along with a serene lounge, vitality pool, steam room, sauna and relaxation area. Even its massage beds reflect a more considered tack to comfort, with heated surfaces and an ergonomic design.
The Fairmont Spa Time-honored Filipino healing takes a more prominent role at Four-Star Fairmont Makati’s spa, where the signature Traditional Hilot Foot and Body Massage interprets local wellness heritage for a contemporary urban setting. The 90-minute ritual combines therapeutic massage with antioxidant banana leaf strips infused with warm coconut oil. Traditional acupressure and a dagdagay wooden stick are used on the soles of the feet to help release tension, encourage relaxation and support a deeper mind-body connection. The treatment is designed to harmonize the body’s natural energies, providing a distinctly Filipino approach to restoration and recovery. Fairmont Makati’s Mango Passion Fruit Tropical Saltmousse Scrub and Massage takes a more sensory route. A saltmousse scrub exfoliates and protects the skin before a hydration-focused massage using essential oils infused with geranium and orange. Together, the treatments reflect the spa’s emphasis on combining local traditions and holistic rituals to support relaxation, recovery and overall well-being. The Peninsula Spa Five-Star Peninsula Manila expands wellness beyond the treatment room through Life Lived Best, The Peninsula Hotels’ global wellness and sustainability platform. Built around three pillars (physical fitness, mental health and nutrition), the program guides the hotel’s spa and wellness initiatives, including yoga classes, spa treatments, personal training sessions and the Naturally Peninsula plant-based dining program. Technology plays a practical role through Peninsula’s Wellness Portal, which allows hotel guests to access wellness resources from their personal devices. They can request in-room fitness accessories, follow guided workout videos, listen to audio meditation sessions, explore spa recommendations and view Naturally Peninsula menu selections throughout their stay. The experience can be tailored further through PenChat, The Peninsula Manila’s 24-hour digital concierge service. Patrons can use their preferred messaging app to connect with hotel staff and access wellness concierge support from chefs, spa managers and fitness professionals. MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: The New €1 House Program In Naro, Sicily
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.95
A new town in Sicily has launched a one-euro house program. The town of Naro, in the province of Agrigento in southwestern Sicily, is now accepting applications from potential buyers and sellers interested in joining the program to buy or sell a house for one euro. For buyers, the homes must be used either as a main residence, a second home, a guest house or for a commercial activity or headquarters. It is open to foreign nationals, such as Americans, as well as commercial companies and foundations. Naro Joins Many Other One Euro House Programs The one-euro house scheme is an urban regeneration program that makes headlines every time another municipality comes online. Most are in Italy, but there are some in France and Spain. One of the first programs can be traced back to England. In 2015, a project was launched in Liverpool to offer dilapidated and derelict houses for just £1, provided that they were converted into proper homes. In many cases, it took tens of thousands of pounds to renovate the properties. It is an increasingly successful attempt to arrest the decline of aging, dwindling populations, particularly as houses have emptied while people have headed to larger cities in search of work. Buyers are obviously attracted to living in authentic villages and towns. Think stone buildings, cobbled streets, small arches and medieval courtyards. The price tag, which is real, albeit symbolic, represents just the first step in a promise you are giving the municipality to invest your time and money. In return, local regions can revitalize and move into the twenty-first century with new residents. The town of Mussomeli, in Sicily, about a one-hour drive from Naro, was nearly abandoned a decade ago. According to The Times, its one-euro program has turned the provincial town around—even former residents are returning. Issues around poor quality of life (garbage, access, and culture) have been transformed by new EU funding, improved public transport connections to Sicily’s capital, Palermo, and the recruitment of new healthcare professionals from Argentina. To-date, 600 houses have been sold to foreigners, with 180 of those for €1. The town is now home to 18 different nationalities. New life has brought cafes, guesthouses, and visitors. In Italy, the U.K.’s Independent newspaper found that renovation costs are still comparatively low, ranging from €20,000–50,000 ($23,000 to $58,000), depending on the property's size and condition. Realtors say potential applicants should consider spending €1,000 per square meter (roughly €100 per square foot) on renovations. In France, the French National Housing Association (ANAH) estimated that the cost of many of these €1 homes would be about €80,000 ($93,000) for a house of around 100 square meters (1,076 square feet). In addition to the one euro, there are legal fees, registration and land registry taxes, and buyers would have to prove they have the financial means and detailed renovation plans for the buildings in question. According to Idealista, the work must be insured or backed by a bank, and a clause requires it to be completed within a specified time frame. This latter point makes sense, as the goal is to renovate the villages and towns, not to pass empty, dilapidated homes into new hands, only to have them remain empty. Naro is a twenty-minute drive to the nearest beach and about an hour to the main southern coastline. It is a wine-growing area and has a strong agricultural community and heritage. How Americans Can Live In Italy For Americans who want to live in Italy, buying property does not, by itself, grant the right to reside there. U.S. citizens may visit Italy and the wider Schengen area for up to 90 days in any rolling 180-day period without a visa, but they need an appropriate long-stay visa and residence permit to remain longer. Until March 2025, Americans with Italian ancestry could potentially claim Italian citizenship by descent through a great-grandparent or more distant ancestor, provided they met the other legal requirements and could prove an unbroken line of citizenship. Italy’s Decree-Law 36/2025 substantially restricted this route. For most new applicants born abroad, eligibility now generally requires an Italian parent or grandparent who holds—or held at the time of death—only Italian citizenship. An alternative route may apply where an Italian parent lived in Italy for at least two consecutive years after acquiring citizenship and before the applicant’s birth or adoption. Otherwise, retirees or the financially independent can choose the Elective Residence visa if you have an annual income stream of around $35,250. This must come from rental earnings, a pension or some other private income. It cannot come from a salary or a job. Alternatively, workers can choose Italy’s digital nomad visa. It is valid for one year, provided you’ve worked remotely for at least six months and have an annual income of about $32,000. You can apply for both visas at your local Italian consulate and, once in the country, you’d apply for a residence permit. If you’re looking for other regions offering a similar one-euro program, Idealista has an updated map and details for many regions, such as Cammarata, Mussomeli and Troina. The Abruzzo region also provides grants. Applicants can apply to Naro via https://case1euronaro.it/, which is available in English and several other languages. The site is very helpful and takes buyers through the process, step by step. MORE FROM FORBES

item.title: George Lucas Museum Of Narrative Art Ready For Launch
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.77
Launch is still more than a month away, but excitement is building. No, it’s not a spaceship launch, but the futuristic building holding the upcoming Lucas Museum of Narrative Art. The eagerly anticipated new Los Angeles museum will welcome earthly visitors on September 22. Tickets are available now. Few people have seen it yet, but the museum named for Star Wars and Indiana Jones creator George Lucas is already generating major buzz . It won’t be a “Star Wars Museum,” but the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art will be dedicated to the emotional power of visual storytelling across art, film, illustration, photography and popular culture. Many believe the new museum will become one of Los Angeles' most significant cultural attractions. George Lucas and his wife Mellody Hobson co-founded the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art to honor the universal tradition of telling stories through images. The museum includes creative work from prehistoric cave paintings to today’s on-screen art. Built in Los Angeles’s Exposition Park, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is housed in a 300,000-square-foot building designed by Ma Yansong of MAD Architects with Stantec. The building includes a 1.5-acre rooftop garden that will also house the upcoming restaurant, Skywalker Grill. While George Lucas is known for creating such art and images in the Star Wars and Indiana Jones universes, he has also been collecting narrative art for more than 50 years. So, what is “narrative art?” According to the museum, “Narrative art is created to tell stories through images. Much of the world’s artistic expression has been motivated by storytelling, transmitting narratives rooted in religion, myth, history, literature, or notable events.” Narrative art that tells a story has appeared in many forms, from cave drawings and hieroglyphics to paintings, murals, illustrations, comics, and sculpture. Over the last two centuries, narrative art has expanded to photography, magazine and book illustration, film, and digital media. The museum will explore how artists depict the essential myths that help us make sense of the world and give us shared values and common beliefs. As it is said, a picture is worth a thousand words. The striking new museum resembles a spaceship, a land speeder or other futuristic structures. It has also been called a transcendent entity floating above the city like a cloud hovering over the ground, a lakeside sand dune and a giant park canopy blending with the surrounding gardens. The building is integrated into a new 11-acre campus including a park designed by Mia Lehrer of Studio-MLA as a green, multilayered gathering place. The Museum’s founding collection includes more than 40,000 works of art. The inaugural exhibits exhibitions include more than 1,200 objects representing narrative art from across time and around the world. Installed across more than 30 galleries, they occupy approximately 100,000 square feet of gallery space. The first exhibitions will trace the evolution of human culture through storytelling, from ancient sculptures of gods and goddesses to Renaissance paintings to photographs, comics, and modern cinema. Many exhibitions are organized by themes, focusing on myths about love, family, community, and adventure that connect to every generation. Other exhibitions are devoted to individual artists of the 20th century, whose images connect modern imaginations with ancient emotions and beliefs. Contemporary vehicles of visual storytelling such as illustration, comics, and graphic stories have not always received the respect they deserve. The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art creates a home for what George Lucas has called “the people’s art.” The exhibitions will include: - Architecture, the innovative designs that inspired the architectural vision of the museum. - Selected works of Thomas Hart Benton’s depiction of American life. - Illustrations of children’s literature by Beatrix Potter, Leo Politi, E.H. Shepard, Jacob Lawrence, and others. - Everyday life will be explored with a series of galleries dedicated to visual stories about Childhood, Community, Family, Love, Motherhood, Play, School, Sports, and Work. - Civic Life, showing artists’ portrayals of experience in the courthouse, the polling place, the political headquarters, and elsewhere. - Comics and Graphic Stories, showing off the museum’s deep holdings of American and European comics, including works by Mœbius, Marie Severin, Jack Kirby, Alison Bechdel, Jim Lee, Frank Miller, R. Crumb and Rafael Navarro. The museum will also show Manga and Anime. - History, with paintings, prints, and illustrations telling (or re-interpreting) the stories of major historical events. - Murals, with large-scale, public works of narrative art by Judith F. Baca, Diego Rivera, and JR. - The Narrative Forms gallery will highlight narrative art across genres of Adventure, Fantasy, Romance, and Science Fiction by artists including Julie Bell, Boris Vallejo, Ken Kelly, Georges Méliès, John C. Berkey, and Jeffrey Catherine Jones. - Photography galleries will show powerful documentary images by Robert Capa, Gordon Parks, Alfred Eisenstaedt, and Dorothea Lange. - The dreamy visions illustrator Maxfield Parrish created in the early 20th century will be shown, as will a selection of the Museum’s holdings of works by premier American illustrator Norman Rockwell. - Western Stories illustrating the myths of the American West, including wagon trains, shoot-outs, and frontier towns will have a gallery. - And although it’s not the “Star Wars Museum,” the museum will show props, movie posters and costumes from the Lucas Archives, as well as documentaries featuring artists and filmmakers. Tickets for the museum’s opening went on sale in July, two months before the scheduled September 22 opening. There was huge demand, with thousands of people waiting up to six hours to get tickets. While opening day is sold out, a quick check of the web site revealed some availability in late September and plenty of tickets for October, November, and December. You can get tickets here. All tickets are timed entry. Tickets are $25 for adults and $21 for those 65 and older. Children, members, and active-duty military are free. Each buyer is limited to 9 tickets.

item.title: Disney’s Josh D’Amaro Shares Insight Into Growth At The Company
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 4.60
“It’s still strange to me to hear Josh and CEO because I’ve been here for 30 years,” says Josh D’Amaro, CEO of The Walt Disney Company during a small group media panel at Disney’s big fan expo, D23: The Ultimate Disney Fan Event. But over the past five months as the leader at The Walt Disney Company, D’Amaro has made one thing very clear: he wants to grow the company with a fans-first mindset. Having the fans-first mentality is something that D’Amaro has carried with him since the beginning of his career. During the panel, he shared that one of his first meetings after being hired at Disney was about construction on Main Street, U.S.A. at Disneyland Park and where to move a trash can so it didn’t impact guests. Additionally, he shared that as he grew with the company’s parks business, if he wasn’t in a meeting, he was in the parks talking with guests and cast members (what Disney calls employees), often without a large entourage. “For any leader, quite frankly, there’s nothing more important than staying in direct touch with who your consumer is, who your fan is, and what they want,” he says. Through these conversations, D’Amaro says fans and employees told him about their Disney story, hopes for the company, and even concerns about various projects. Even now as CEO, while on a much larger scale than a Disneyland trash can, D’Amaro shares that the same level of detail, excellence and fan experience is what drives him and his teams, from Walt Disney Imagineering to the studios Disney owns. “It has to be perfect. It’s got to be right for our fans, and we take that very, very seriously,” he shares. Disney’s Three Pillars Besides hearing fans and making sure they feel seen, D’Amaro says three things are really important to him as CEO. The first is that Disney continues to tell the world’s best stories, whether that’s through movies, park attractions, or even Broadway shows. The second is celebrating the intersection of technology and media. “I don’t think it’s ever been more relevant and more powerful. I want to push into the technology that’s available to us, marry it with beautiful story-making, and push the company forward," he explains. The third pillar D’Amaro revealed is showing up as one company, regardless of the various businesses within the larger Disney ecosystem. “We’re not ESPN and streaming and theme parks and movies. We're the Walt Disney Company, and for anyone that's looking around contextually at the entertainment landscape right now, it kind of looks like people are trying to look like Disney,” D’Amaro says. So what does “One Disney” really mean? D’Amaro explains that each of the company’s businesses, whether it’s streaming, sports, consumer products, theme parks or movies, can stand on its own, but they are better when they work together. “Each of the businesses alone is great, but together, when we deliver to our fans a seamless, comprehensive experience with us, it’s great for them as a fan, and it's great for us as a business,” he says. This idea seems comparable to D’Amaro’s previous statements about a potentially massive Disney super app that would allow fans to interact with the company’s various businesses and experiences on one platform. Disney’s Biggest Global Opportunities Some of Disney’s biggest opportunities lie outside of the United States. In fact, D’Amaro credits Disney’s global expansion to his predecessor, Bob Iger. “One of his top priorities was to expand internationally; you saw a big opportunity for Disney to show up in other parts of the world outside of the U.S., and that’s come to fruition,” D’Amaro says. One of the biggest areas for growth that D’Amaro sees is Disney Cruise Line. “These cruise ships are kind of like the best ambassador for our brand you can possibly have,” he tells the media group. “We can float them out to new markets and invite people into our stories and into our Disney family.” Disney Cruise Line recently launched its first Asia-based cruise ship, Disney Adventure, which homeports in Singapore. In 2029, a new ship in partnership with Oriental Land Co., Ltd. will be based in Japan. Additionally, Disney Cruise Line has announced it is building a new class of smaller ships, sized between the Magic- and the Wish-Class ships. The upcoming mid-sized ships will be able to visit more unique destinations around the world due to their size. D’Amaro also mentions streaming as a massive global opportunity for Disney. He says that because Disney’s streaming services exist in many parts of the world, Disney can introduce people to its other businesses as well. “The footprint is large today, and it’s only going to expand over time,” he says. Where is Disney Going in the Future After the events and showcases of D23, from screening movie trailers and clips to pulling back the curtain on what’s coming to Disney Parks around the world, D’Amaro says he hopes Disney continues to be a place where everybody is welcome, and where fans can escape from everything else that’s going on in the world. “At the same time, I think that we need to take that same core feeling and make sure that we’re bringing it to new fans and new parts of the world,” D’Amaro continues. “We want to make sure that these stories carry into new generations where they're discovering characters and storytelling in ways that make complete sense to them.” That’s part of the reason Disney is getting into the gaming space and bringing TikTok and Disney+ together. Disney knows that’s where younger fans are taking in stories, and the snowball effect of interacting with the brand through digital media can entice the same fans to go to a theater or to a theme park. “Walt was exceptional about being willing to take a next step into something that the world had never seen before. And I think the possibility of holding onto who you are and what you are, but still stepping into the unknown—that’s what Disney is,” says D’Amaro.

item.title: How Regional Travelers Are Rethinking Air Travel Via Private Aviation
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 3.83
Private aviation is more popular than ever, reaching record highs with over 3.5 million global private jet flights and a worldwide fleet of roughly 24,000 business aircraft, according to Aircraft Performance Group. Driven by a growing global wealthy class and a shift toward flexible fractional ownership, the industry treats private flight as a time-saving business tool rather than a pure luxury. Industry Scale and Usage - Global Activity: Surpassed 3.5 million business jet flights globally, averaging about 11,500 flights daily. - U.S. Dominance: The United States holds roughly 62.5% of the total global private jet fleet. - Geographic Reach: Private planes can access over 5,000 U.S. airports, compared to fewer than 500 served by commercial airlines. Flyte is a private aviation company with a fleet solely comprised of Cirrus Vision Jets, specializing in short-haul trips around 500 miles. With no membership fees, customers can easily book a jet in under two minutes with the help of the platform’s AI systems. Private aviation was built for access, but too often it became expensive, opaque, and overcomplicated. Flyte’s model is changing that with modern Vision Jets, upfront pricing, smaller airport access and booking that takes minutes. Marc Sellouk, CEO of Flyte, recently discussed Flyte’s impact on the ever-growing private aviation industry: Describe the clientele who are using Flyte. Our current clientele is regional business travelers and people looking for a premium flying experience. When we talk about regional business travelers, these are executives, founders, and legal or finance teams who need to make tight, high-stakes trips along key business corridors like New York to D.C., Boston, or Philadelphia. These are professionals who can't afford to burn an entire day sitting in traffic at commercial hubs or suffering through predictable airline delays. For them, Flyte is a productivity engine that lets them do a full day of meetings and still make it home for dinner. In addition to business people, we also serve premium leisure and lifestyle travelers. These are families, weekenders, and golf enthusiasts heading to places like the Hamptons, Nantucket, or Martha’s Vineyard. Through our recent strategic partnerships, like Blade and LDV at The Maidstone, we’re seeing a tech-savvy traveler who wants the privacy, speed, and convenience of private aviation without the legacy price tag or heavy commitment of traditional jet cards. What unites all Flyte passengers is that they aren't flying private to show off. They're flying private because it makes practical, economic, and operational sense for how they live and work. Why are larger airlines abandoning regional routes? Major carriers are built around a hub model that relies on massive 150- to 200-seat mainline aircraft like Boeing 737s or Airbus A320s. They are phasing out smaller 50-seater regional jets mainly because of the operating costs. Between fuel, maintenance, and elevated pilot wages, those smaller planes are unprofitable to fly unless every single seat is full. When an airline’s smallest plane holds 150 people, shorter 300-mile routes between secondary cities simply don't make financial sense anymore. At the same time, the pilot shortage forced major airlines to pull flight crews out of regional partners to fill cockpits on their high-margin international and transcontinental routes. Now, hundreds of regional airports across the country have lost commercial service entirely or seen their flight schedules slashed. While legacy airlines are focusing where they make the most money, millions of regional business and leisure travelers are now struggling to find an alternative to get to their destinations. Describe the latest private aviation trends, such as travelers choosing private to avoid long TSA lines and lengthy delays. The biggest trend we’re seeing right now is that private travel has shifted from a status symbol to a utility tool driven by necessity. Travelers are exhausted by the friction of commercial travel. Every day could be a roulette of problems, whether it’s TSA staffing bottlenecks or air traffic control outages; getting through a major hub airport can take longer than the actual flight itself. People realize that spending three hours at an airport to take a 45-minute flight doesn't make sense anymore. By flying privately out of regional FBOs, you literally drive up to the aircraft, step on, and take off in minutes. The second major shift is a move away from traditional, capital-intensive private aviation models like jet cards or full aircraft ownership. Business and regional commuters are looking for tactical flexibility. They want point-to-point, on-demand mobility using right-sized aircraft like Very Light Jets that deliver the exact same time savings and privacy, but at a price point that actually makes financial sense for short-haul trips. What is your forward growth strategy? Our growth strategy is focused on scaling in a smart and strategic way, and building a disciplined platform that captures the massive demand left behind by commercial airlines cutting regional flights. We’re actively expanding our fleet of Cirrus VisionJets operated by our FAA-certified carrier, Ponderosa Air. As we grow aircraft capacity, we’re strengthening our core regional corridors in the Northeast and Florida while expanding to new cities where speed and frequency are critical. A big part of our model is leveraging strategic distribution partnerships. Rather than relying solely on traditional charter brokers, we integrate with popular platforms like Blade to feature our VisionJets directly on their network, alongside key lifestyle and sports partnerships that maximize aircraft utilization and introduce Flyte to new travelers. At the same time, we are dynamically deploying fleet capacity around high-demand seasonal corridors like Nantucket, Martha's Vineyard, and the Hamptons, and key business hubs during peak travel windows. Combined with investments in tech-enabled scheduling and AI-driven logistics, our ultimate goal is to build a seamless national network where booking a 300-mile regional flight is as frictionless and reliable as ordering an Uber.

item.title: Luxury Travel Is A $1.7 Trillion Business. Hotels Want More Of It.
item.description:
Source: Forbes - Travel Score: 3.38
Luxury hospitality has spent the past decade expanding beyond lavish suites and Michelin-worthy dining into something less tangible: the promise of access. The global luxury travel market is projected to reach $1.7 trillion in 2026, according to Grand View Research. Today’s top luxury hotel brands are aiming to sell much more than a place to sleep. Increasingly, they are positioning themselves as curators of a destination, using their local relationships and cultural credibility to create journeys that would be difficult for even well-connected travelers to assemble on their own. “The biggest shift I'm seeing is that luxury is no longer defined by what a hotel has, but by what it can unlock,” said luxury hospitality expert David Carofano, Strategy and Commercial Director at Crown Creative. “Beautiful design, exceptional architecture and great service have become the baseline. Today's luxury traveler is looking for exclusive access to experiences they couldn't create on their own, whether that's playing one of the UK's iconic golf courses, harvesting grapes alongside a winemaker, or dining with one of the Caribbean's most celebrated chefs. “The strongest hotels are evolving into lifestyle brands that guests want to belong to, using food, partnerships, culture and highly curated experiences to become part of their guests' identity. Ultimately, luxury travelers are collecting stories, not amenities.” Rosewood Hotels & Resorts' newest Guided by Rosewood itinerary in Mexico is perhaps the clearest expression yet of that evolution. Rather than encouraging guests to settle into a single resort for a week, the eight-day itinerary moves travelers through four dramatically different regions of the country, stitching together stays at Rosewood Mayakoba in Riviera Maya, Rosewood Mandarina in Riviera Nayarit, Rosewood San Miguel de Allende and Las Ventanas al Paraíso in Los Cabos. The result is a privately choreographed grand tour that raises the bar on the standard vacation “package.” Guided By Rosewood’s Mexico Luxury Hotel Vacation Package The journey begins amid the mangroves and lagoons of the Yucatán Peninsula, where guests explore sacred cenotes and underground rivers before visiting the seaside ruins of Tulum. From there, the experience shifts west to the Pacific Coast, where Rosewood Mandarina blends adventure with wellness through ocean excursions and the Mara'kame Journey, an Indigenous-inspired cleansing ritual at the resort's Asaya Spa. The itinerary then trades beaches for cobblestone streets in San Miguel de Allende, introducing travelers to artisan Ricardo Marquez's traditional brass workshop and a hands-on session creating colorful mojigangas with local artist Hermes Arroyo before concluding in Baja California Sur. There, horseback rides along the Sea of Cortez, a traditional underground barbacoa feast and immersive desert experiences at Las Ventanas al Paraíso provide a finale that feels worlds away from where the trip began. It’s a smart way to leverage Rosewood’s national footprint and showcase the beauty of four of its properties: the Rosewood Mayakoba, Rosewood Mandarina, Rosewood San Miguel de Allende, and Las Ventanas al Paraíso, A Rosewood Resort. “Travelers are increasingly discovering that Mexico offers far more than beautiful beaches, with destinations like Mexico City, Oaxaca, Mérida and San Miguel de Allende drawing visitors through their rich culture, exceptional cuisine, craftsmanship and vibrant local communities,” Carofano said. None of the Guided by Rosewood experiences are impossible to book independently. Having them orchestrated in concert are key part — not a side benefit — of the sticker price. A spokesperson for the brand declined to provide a baseline price, or a price range, because “each package is individually crafted for the guest by the Rosewood concierge team.” Per the Rosewood website, interested travelers can email the properties directly for estimates for their curated itinerary. Guided By Rosewood: The Evolution Of The Luxury Travel Package Luxury travelers value time as much as money. Rather than spending months researching guides, securing reservations and coordinating domestic flights, affluent guests are increasingly happy to pay for seamless execution and insider access. Rosewood might catch first-time visitors with its curated itinerary, but its attention to detail will appeal even to repeat travelers who have already checked off Cabo or the Riviera Maya, and now want to understand how those destinations fit into Mexico’s broader cultural landscape. “U.S. travelers are moving beyond the traditional Cancun-only vacation, increasingly combining multiple destinations across Mexico,” said Daria Guristrimba, Founder and CEO of Globe7, a London-based invitation-only travel atelier serving ultra-high-net-worth individuals worldwide. The itinerary reflects this trend. The price reflects Rosewood’s expert positioning. While each booking is customized, the journey combines stays at four of Mexico's most exclusive resorts — properties where nightly rates frequently range from roughly $1,000 to well above $2,000, depending on season and room category — before private experiences, transfers and domestic travel are factored into the equation. The result is an itinerary likely to cost well into the five figures for two travelers, placing it squarely in the ultra-luxury category. Guided by Rosewood: A Unique Hotel Chain For Luxury Travel Rosewood is also unusually well positioned to execute this strategy. Unlike global giants such as Marriott International, Hilton or Hyatt (which feature multiple hotel brands across hundreds of properties) Rosewood's footprint is intentionally selective. Its brand identity is forged around distinctive properties rather than scale. Rosewood lists only 20 properties in the Americas in its portfolio, including the four in Mexico. “As a luxury travel advisor, I love working with boutique properties,” Whytney Rawls, a travel advisor and expert, former flight attendant, and founder of The Amara Escapes. “They're incredibly thoughtful, attentive, and intentional with every detail. There's always someone available to help, you don't get bounced between departments, and the response time is almost always immediate.” That smaller collection makes it easier to present each destination as part of a coherent brand philosophy rather than simply another pin on a map. The Mexico itinerary follows the first Guided by Rosewood itinerary — a six-day journey through Austria and Bavaria — with Southeast Asia slated to join the series next. Together, these itineraries hint at where luxury travel and hospitality is heading next: away from selling individual hotels and toward selling complete narratives.

item.title: How Alliances Survive
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.86
In 1984, months after the Reagan administration’s decision to deploy Pershing II intermediate-range nuclear missiles to Western Europe brought hundreds of thousands of protesters into the streets of Europe’s major cities, a clutch of senior French, German, and Italian officials cornered NATO Secretary-General Peter Carrington outside his Brussels office. Tensions were still running high, and the Americans, they complained, were rude, reckless, and dismissive of allied counsel. Carrington heard them out. Then he shrugged and offered his usual verdict on why American indispensability demanded allied forbearance: “Alas, they are the only Americans we have.” Today, that forbearance is being severely tested. In less than two years, the second Trump administration has threatened to seize Greenland and leave NATO, withdrawn troops from Germany, meddled in allies’ elections, and levied tariffs on friends—all while lavishing summitry and flattery on Beijing and Moscow. Allies have responded with understandable alarm. “The old relationship we had with the United States,” declared Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, “is over.” A “deep rift” was forming, warned German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. “The West as we knew it no longer exists,” declared European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Ng Eng Hen, Singapore’s defense minister, lamented that the United States had gone from a partner to a “landlord seeking rent.” In the United States, a growing consensus holds that the alliances are unlikely to recover. Former House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Greg Meeks has questioned “whether or not our friends and allies will ever trust the United States again.” The scholar Robert Kagan, in a eulogy for an era in which U.S. allies stuck with Washington, declared that “those days are now over and will not soon return.” This pessimism is understandable—but significantly overstated. The grievance in allied capitals, while heartfelt, is not a lasting guide to what comes next. Dire as the moment appears, the United States’ alliances will survive the Trump shock for reasons the headlines miss. First, the alliance system has weathered now forgotten shocks at least as serious as these, and the present ones owe more to presidential personality than to durable new politics. Second, the threats that gave rise to the alliances have not faded but intensified and converged, as allied perceptions of China and Russia align as never before. Third, powerful gravitational forces continue to pull allies together economically, technologically, and militarily, overcoming efforts to “de-risk” from Washington, while professional bureaucracies quietly advance cooperation far from the glare of politics. Allowed to harden into conventional wisdom, pessimism risks becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy, as policymakers, convinced the alliances cannot be saved, stop doing the work to ensure they endure. But together, these uniting forces will carry the alliances through the Trump moment and set them up—should allied capitals seize the opportunity—for the transformation required to meet the challenge of a China, backed by a newly aggressive Russia, that can outscale every other country on the metrics of power that matter most. The current anxieties, however inadvertently, may even strengthen the alliance system: as they have in the past, tensions can spur reforms that create tomorrow’s capability. Allies could be transformed from dependents into co-creators of power, pooling capacity into what we have previously called “allied scale.” The Trump administration has called on allies to do more so that the United States can do less; in fact, in the future, both the allies and the United States will need to do more, creating two-way flows of capacity and interdependence that make the whole greater than the sum of its parts. It is true that as French President Emmanuel Macron and other allied leaders have argued, “there is no going back.” That does not, however, mean the end of the alliance system. It means reforging the alliance system for a new era. THE NEW FATALISM The damage that U.S. President Donald Trump has done to U.S. alliances so far in his second term exceeds that done in the entire four years of his first term. That is in part because the internationalist staff that imposed guardrails the last time is gone. But the growing concern over the future of American alliances is not just about Trump. It is driven by a belief that longer-standing corrosive forces compounded by Trumpian attacks on trust are eroding the system to the point that it will be beyond salvation. The first set of corrosive forces is within the United States. As senior Biden administration officials Phil Gordon and Mara Karlin observed in these pages, a generation of failed interventions, economic challenges, and inward-looking politics have left Americans more reluctant to underwrite global order than at any time since before World War II. Trump, the argument goes, is as much a symptom as a cause. The first Trump term might have seemed an aberration, but the second marks a pattern—suggesting that the pendulum might not swing back. The second set of corrosive forces is within allied capitals. Gutted American credibility, in this account, is prompting allies to adjust their strategic orientation in ways that will prove irreversible. Trump’s treatment of alliance commitments in Europe and Asia as conditional and transactional changes their essential character even without major troop withdrawals or the use of force against allies. Already, European governments are elevating “strategic autonomy” and pursuing defense independence from the United States, with France and the United Kingdom even proposing a new nuclear umbrella for Europe. Asian allies, too, are revisiting a founding bargain of the U.S. alliance system—extended nuclear deterrence—and considering acquiring their own nuclear capabilities. And both sets of allies are forming new middle-power coalitions to reduce reliance on Washington, from recent European arrangements with India to the trade agreements Japan is pursuing with Latin America. All are searching for ways to de-risk from the United States. The skeptics worry that no matter how pro-alliance the next American leader might be, such hedging will persist: Why would allies stake decades of military planning—bases, procurement, force structure—or pursue economic and industrial integration with Washington if the alliance is itself called into question every four to eight years? The answer to that question is more complex than it seems and should lead away from despair. Allied collapse remains far less likely than allied endurance and evolution for reasons observers often miss. Because alliances surprised strategists by surviving the Soviet collapse, they came to be seen as products of the softer elements of international politics: sentiment, institutions, trust, shared values, nostalgia—precisely the elements the Trump administration has battered most. But they were forged and have always been sustained by hard material realities. Far from vanishing, those material realities are pulling harder than before. THE GOLDEN AGE THAT WASN’T The current pessimism juxtaposes today’s challenges against an alliance golden age that never existed. The real history of U.S. alliances is one of recurring crises: allies expelling American troops, presidents blindsiding partners, capitals erupting in protest, and in every era, confident predictions of a coming collapse. Although many foreign policy elites think this time is different, American and European publics do not agree. According to Chicago Council on Global Affairs polling data, which runs as far back as 1974, the share of Americans who believe Washington should make major decisions together with allies rather than go it alone now stands at a 50-year high. Throughout the Trump era, from 2016 to today, the belief that maintaining existing alliances is “very effective” for advancing U.S. aims increased from 32 percent to 55 percent, reaching ten-year highs among both Democrats and Republicans. Across the Atlantic, polling from the European Council on Foreign Relations has shown alarming dissatisfaction with the United States. But what is most striking is that a clear majority of citizens in 13 of the 15 European countries polled, and a plurality in the remaining two, believe that the relationship will “get better again” once Trump leaves office. Fewer than a third believe the damage will last after he leaves office. European publics, it would seem, think that Trump is an aberration and not a true representative of the United States. Their faith that “this too shall pass” carries some significant historical weight. In the security domain, today’s challenges are real—threats to seize Greenland, to abandon Ukraine, to quit NATO, to pull forces from Germany, to tie Taiwanese arms sales to Beijing’s preferences. But the alliances have weathered worse. Even under Trump, the United States has not credibly threatened financial calamity against an ally, as it did to the United Kingdom, in the 1950s, to halt its intervention in Suez. Nor has an ally expelled American troops or seriously undermined an alliance structure, as France did, in the 1960s, after withdrawing from NATO’s unified command. The United States has not withdrawn large numbers of troops from allies, as the Senate nearly forced it to do, in the 1970s, when it only barely beat back the Mansfield Amendment, which would have cut U.S. forces in Europe by roughly half. In Asia, there is no present analog to the major shocks of the 1970s, which drove Seoul and Taipei to pursue covert nuclear programs. U.S. President Richard Nixon’s 1969 Guam Doctrine instructed allies to furnish the manpower for their own defense, an imperative underscored by the withdrawal of 20,000 U.S. troops from South Korea. His 1972 opening to Beijing blindsided Taipei and Tokyo. A few years later, the fall of Saigon raised alarms about American resolve and led Singaporean leader Lee Kuan Yew to declare that U.S. influence in the region would “never be the same.” Despite serious dissatisfaction with the United States, there have been no mass protests in allied capitals, such as those against the Pershing II deployments. Nor has the shared threat perception of the alliance system evaporated, as it did in the 1990s, following the Soviet dissolution. The main exception is the threat of U.S. force against Greenland, which could indeed collapse the alliance system if Washington followed through. But this threat is so peculiar and personalistic and so extreme that no serious figure in either party has endorsed it. Democrats have vocally opposed it, and so have Republican leaders: House Speaker Mike Johnson said that U.S. military intervention in Greenland “would not be appropriate,” and Senate Majority Leader John Thune said, “I don’t see military action being an option here.” Trump walked it back. The economic record looks similar to the security record. The “Liberation Day” tariffs have hurt the perception of the United States as a credible economic partner—but this is not the first time Washington has turned its economic heft against its own allies, including through the use of tariffs. In August 1971, the “Nixon shock” did both at once: it unilaterally ended the dollar’s convertibility into gold, blindsiding allies whose economies were anchored to it, and imposed a ten percent across-the-board import surcharge. In 1985, the Plaza Accord forced allies to make a major currency adjustment under the shadow of protectionist pressure, straining the German and Japanese economies more severely than the tariffs allies confront today; within three years, the yen doubled against the dollar, an adjustment far larger than the 15 percent tariff on Japanese exports. The current tensions are the most significant since the end of the Cold War. And yet the lesson of history is that alliance systems often prove more resilient in retrospect than contemporary observers expect at the time. Crises repeatedly generate predictions of collapse, but alliances adapt precisely because the underlying incentives remain compelling. The first Trump administration’s browbeating over burden sharing was bitterly received in allied capitals and did real damage—but it also pushed European defense budgets toward the NATO two-percent target, drove Japan to double its defense spending, and prompted coordination on China’s technology challenge. Under the Biden administration, many of those same allies joined a dense web of initiatives that would once have been inconceivable: the AUKUS agreement between Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States; the Quad security partnership focused on the Indo-Pacific; rapprochement between Seoul and Tokyo; joint export controls on semiconductors; a coordinated European and Asian response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. None of this was Trump’s design, but it shows how the tensions of one era can produce capability in the next, handing subsequent leaders the opportunity to strengthen alliances in ways previously beyond reach. CONVERGENCE AT LAST Today, that dynamic is especially powerful given that threat perceptions are increasingly converging and intensifying around a shared challenge from Beijing and Moscow, even with allies facing a short-term challenge from Washington. This is notable because, since the end of the Cold War, allied threat perceptions have often diverged. Europe, for example, gradually grew more anxious about Russia’s military challenge but generally treated China as a market and manufacturer. Asian allies often saw it in reverse: they were wary of China’s growing military strength but less concerned about Russia, seeing its energy as an economic opportunity. That divergence worked to Beijing’s and Moscow’s advantage. For decades, Washington strove to align perceptions across theaters, to little avail. That convergence is at last arriving. Chinese and Russian conduct has, more than any Western initiative, forged links between Europe and Asia. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine shattered Europe’s remaining illusions not just about Moscow but also about Beijing. China has become Russia’s most important patron, providing dual-use technological and even lethal military support on the battlefield as well as critical financial, industrial, and diplomatic reinforcement. It is China that is building the Russian defense industrial base and military capability that now menaces Europe. Reflecting that realization, NATO’s communiqués now brand China a “decisive enabler” of Russia’s war, and its secretary-general argues that the Indo-Pacific and European theaters must be viewed “as one.” Asian states, for their part, see Russia’s shocking use of force as a sign of the risks that face them if the military balance with China erodes further. Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and even Singapore have rallied behind Ukraine, seeing a Russian defeat as essential for restraining Chinese ambition. The leaders of NATO’s four Indo-Pacific partners—Australia, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea—now regularly attend its summits. Meanwhile, Beijing and Moscow are also binding themselves more tightly together in Asia, staging exercises and strategic bomber patrols around U.S. allies, including during major multilateral gatherings. Allied threat perceptions have shifted not only in the security dimension but also, perhaps most strikingly, in the economic and technology dimensions. Asian and European governments alike are coming to see China as the United States long has: a mercantilist power targeting the foundations of their industrial strength. European leaders now speak of a second “China shock,” a flood of subsidized manufactured goods that, as Macron has put it, are “literally killing a large part of European industry.” Von der Leyen has warned of Chinese “overcapacities that erode our own manufacturing base” and calls the situation “simply not sustainable.” Merz has floated a new Plaza Accord to force an appreciation of China’s currency. None of this yet amounts to a single allied policy. Convergence on the nature of the threat does not mean full alignment on the response in either the security or economic dimensions; there are divisions, too, over how far to de-risk from China, how to balance economic and security interests, and how to manage Taiwan and Ukraine policy. But a shared diagnosis is the precondition for common action, and for the first time in a generation, the diagnosis is beginning to align. This convergence is a remarkable geopolitical fact. Even during the Cold War, allies differed on threat perception, with West Germany pursuing Ostpolitik and détente even as frontline states pressed for deterrence, and the Euromissile deployments split publics and governments alike. By some measures, there is today comparably more unity even against a less urgent threat. What is particularly transformative is that the Atlantic and the Pacific are ceasing to function as entirely separate strategic spaces—setting the stage for truly global alliance efforts, even if the Trump administration is unlikely to take advantage of this convergence over the next two and a half years. TIES THAT BIND There is little question that allies are seeking to de-risk from the United States in key domains through new middle-power coalitions. But the shift toward de-risking is being offset and ultimately outweighed by larger megatrends: surging Chinese exports in the economic realm, the AI revolution in the technology realm, and increases in defense spending in the military realm. These are creating new linkages with Washington faster than the old ones can be broken. In the economic domain, the United States now absorbs around 20 to 30 percent of all allied exports, a much higher share than even five years ago, as China buys less. Last year, even amid the trade war, Europe, Japan, and India all exported significantly more to the United States than to China; over the last five years, exports to China fell roughly 15 percent for Europe, 20 percent for Japan, 20 percent for South Korea, and 20 percent for India—while exports to the United States rose roughly 30 percent each for Europe, South Korea, and India. That dependence on the U.S. market will only grow: the second China shock will make the U.S. market an even more critical lifeline. And American reindustrialization efforts are increasingly dependent on allied investment and technology sharing, from shipbuilding to semiconductors to batteries, reinforcing interdependence. Technology is increasingly sticky in both directions, too, partly because of the AI revolution. Reports abound of European governments instructing officials to abandon Microsoft Teams and Zoom, migrate off American operating systems, and stand up “sovereign” alternatives in the cloud and AI. But the new wave of technology innovation is re-creating allied dependence. Yesterday’s dependence on American mobile and desktop operating systems has not abated, and now U.S. allies also depend on American cloud infrastructure, advanced chips, and AI models. Three U.S. “hyperscalers”—Amazon, Google, and Microsoft—account for about two-thirds of the global cloud market, while European providers hold barely 15 percent of their own domestic market. U.S. hyperscalers are expected to spend more than $700 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026, against European sovereign spending of roughly $13 billion. And the gap is growing. Europe’s efforts are for now too modest, too regulated, too fragmented, and too focused on alleviating government restrictions rather than promoting commercial use to fundamentally change dependencies that have accumulated over decades.
