Have Lunch at Colibri Mexican Bistro Colibri Mexican Bistro is located at the historic Presidio Officers' Club, a short walk from the Inn at the Presidio. Lunch started with a La Doña tequila cocktail for me and a Cactus Bloom (no alcohol) for Kel. We shared guacamole, chips, and a lineup of salsas. The yellow mango salsa was my favorite. We kept going: butternut squash soup, grilled corn the way you find it on the streets in Mexico, rich mole poblano, and a mango cheesecake crème brûlée to finish. Colibri's location makes it a convenient lunch stop when exploring Lovers' Lane, the Main Post, or the Walt Disney Family Museum. 11. Plan Dinner at Dalida Dalida ended up being one of the meals I still think about from our San Francisco trip. The restaurant serves Eastern Mediterranean food from a historic building facing the Main Parade Lawn. Its menu is designed for sharing, making it easy to sample several dishes. We started with the Breaking Bread appetizer (warm pita, bright spreads, olives, and pickles) then moved on to arayes kebab, lamb-filled manti, and saffron tahdig rice. Dessert was a chocolate hazelnut tart and roasted barley ice cream, both worth saving room for. Dalida is popular, so making a dinner reservation in advance is a good idea. 12. Stay Inside the Presidio You can always visit the Presidio as a day trip, but staying overnight inside the park changes the pace. We spent two nights at the Inn at the Presidio, which occupies a restored Georgian Revival building originally constructed in 1903 for unmarried Army officers. From the inn, we could walk to Lovers' Lane, Colibri, Dalida, the Main Parade Lawn, and the Walt Disney Family Museum. Presidio Tunnel Tops and Lucasfilm were also within walking distance. Having a room in the park meant we could wander at our own speed, duck back for a break, and never feel rushed. If you're curious, I've written a full review of our hosted stay at the Inn at the Presidio on Feastio. 13. Play the Presidio Golf Course We did not play golf during our stay, but golfers may want to reserve a tee time at the Presidio Golf Course. The public 18-hole course, dating back to 1895, runs through groves of eucalyptus and Monterey pine in the park's southern hills. There's also a driving range, pro shop, clubhouse restaurant, and lessons if you want to work on your swing. Advance tee times are recommended. Planning Your Presidio Visit The Presidio is bigger than it looks, and the hills can make a short walk feel longer than you'd expect. I like exploring on foot, but if you're trying to see Baker Beach, Fort Point, and the Main Post in one day, you might want to use a car, rideshare, bike, or the shuttle to save time. The free Presidio GO Shuttle connects the park with downtown San Francisco and operates routes within the Presidio. Several Muni bus routes also serve the area. If you've only got a day, I'd focus on Presidio Tunnel Tops, the Walt Disney Family Museum, Lovers' Lane, Lucasfilm, and at least one spot to see the Golden Gate Bridge. Grab lunch at Colibri or from the food trucks, and end the day with dinner at Dalida. With two days, you can explore at a slower pace and include Baker Beach, Fort Point, Inspiration Point, and the Palace of Fine Arts. The Presidio rewards a little extra time. What I first thought of as just the land around the Golden Gate Bridge turned out to be one of San Francisco's most surprising and varied corners. Where else can you walk a wooded trail, visit a cartoon museum, explore a historic fort, sit down to a memorable meal, and take in a world-famous view-all in a single day? Disclosure: Our stay at the Inn at the Presidio was provided as part of a hosted visit to San Francisco. As always, all opinions and recommendations are my own.

item.title: Can an AI-Powered Scribe Curb Physician Burnout?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 6.15
Share Podcast Can an AI-Powered Scribe Curb Physician Burnout? The use of automated note-taking tools during patient visits holds promise in reducing physicans’ administrative load–but the tradeoffs are complicated. In 2024, Mass General Brigham, the largest health system in Massachusetts, piloted an AI-powered ambient note-taking program among a subset of clinicians to address increasing rates of staff burnout and turnover–largely driven by the administrative burden of clinical documentation in the electronic health records (EHR). The pilot program aimed to test AI tools which used natural language processing to record, transcribe, and summarize physician-patient encounters, reducing time spent on documentation and allowing physicians to focus more on patient care. Early results showed promising reductions in clinician burnout, intention to leave, and increased physician efficiency. But concerns about the technology, including the generation of inaccurate notes with errors or hallucinations, made physicians resistant to learn and adopt it into their workflows. Harvard Business School Associate Professor Susanna Gallani and host Brian Kenny discuss the challenges leadership at the health care organization anticipated as they considered scaling the AI technology responsibly in the case: The AI Scribe: Enhancing Physician Presence and Curbing Burnout at Mass General Brigham. BRIAN KENNY: Welcome to Cold Call, the podcast where we dive deep into the groundbreaking ideas in Harvard Business School case studies with the faculty who wrote them. In healthcare, some of the most important innovations aren’t new drugs or breakthrough devices. They’re new ways of giving clinicians back the one resource they can never make more of, time. As artificial intelligence rapidly finds its way into hospitals and medical practices, leaders face a difficult balancing act. Can technology reduce administrative burdens without creating new risks? Will it strengthen the relationship between physicians and patients or subtly change it? And how should organizations measure success when the benefits extend beyond efficiency to include trust, wellbeing and the quality of care? Today’s case explores a real-world effort to answer those questions inside one of the nation’s leading academic health systems. We’ll examine the organizational challenges that accompany technological change and the difficult trade-offs involved in evaluating investments whose returns are both financial and deeply human. My guest today is Professor Susanna Gallani, and we’ll discuss her case, “The AI Scribe: Enhancing Physician Presence and Curbing Burnout at Mass General Brigham.” I’m your host, Brian Kenny, and you’re listening to Cold Call on the HBR Podcast Network. Susanna Gallani studies performance management systems and explores the interplay between monetary and non-monetary incentives, and you probably study much more than that too, Susanna. Welcome back to Cold Call. SUSANNA GALLANI: Thank you. Thank you for having me. It’s good to be back. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah, it’s been a little while, so we’re happy to have you back on the show, and we were just chatting before we rolled tape here, and every conversation these days seems to turn to AI. It’s just top of mind for everybody, to the point maybe of AI fatigue, but there are some real-world implications for the case that you wrote and for how Mass General is trying to use AI to help physicians. So, thanks for writing it. Thanks for being here to talk about it. SUSANNA GALLANI: Sure. My pleasure. BRIAN KENNY: Maybe we just get started by asking you, how did you hear about this? Why did you think this would be an interesting case to write? SUSANNA GALLANI: So there’s a combination of things that are happening in this space. First of all, the case is written with Rob Huckman and Suraj Srinivasan and also an external co-author, Asaf Bitton, who is at Ariadne Labs, and of course the conversation about AI in healthcare is everywhere. Everybody talks about AI in healthcare and what we can do or cannot do with that, and we were looking for our course, “Transforming Healthcare Delivery,” which is a second-year course here in the MBA program. We were looking to introduce more of this AI content in our course, because as you can imagine, the evolution of AI in healthcare is a big transformational drive, and we still don’t know exactly what it’s going to do, but we want to be up with it as it evolves, and so Rob had heard about this implementation, and I had known about that system. MGB, which is the organization that we study in the case, is not the only one that is implementing this technique and this technology. It’s pretty much everywhere right now, but MGB was doing it at a large scale, and of course, it’s a leading academic medical center. So it was interesting for us from a number of perspectives, because it layers up, in addition to the delivery of healthcare, there’s also the training and the research part, and so all of these aspects kind of converge into the problems that we address in the case. BRIAN KENNY: MGB being Mass General Brigham, just for our listeners who aren’t from the Boston area, it’s an enormous enterprise. I don’t know how many physicians they have on there. SUSANNA GALLANI: About 12,000. BRIAN KENNY: Okay. So just enormous. So this is an effort to scale something up in a very significant way, and I think oftentimes, when we think about AI in healthcare, we’re thinking about how it could accelerate cures or treatments of some kind. This, I found to be very interesting, because it was really about how they’re doing their work and how they can do their work more efficiently. Can you talk maybe a little bit about some of the challenges that clinicians face? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. So in a way, I have heard this described as the first innovation in healthcare that is improving care without asking the physicians to do more, and I want to extend this. This is not just physicians, it’s clinicians in general, because there’s nurses and there’s advanced practice providers as well. So this is not just a solution for physicians, narrowly defined, but this is the first time that we’re trying to do more and better in healthcare while taking work off the physician’s plate, the clinician’s plate, which is important, because we know we have a burnout problem. We have a wellbeing problem in healthcare. We have a turnover problem. If you listen to the first Friday of the month job report, healthcare jobs are always at the top of the list in terms of job creation, because there’s so much churn, and in addition, the needs for healthcare are increasing. Populations are aging. During COVID, we’re still experiencing the tail end of the COVID effect where people didn’t take as good care of themselves as they should have or they would have in other times. So there’s a lot of demand of physician’s time. In addition to that, we see that physicians don’t want to be physicians anymore, because it’s becoming a job that is away from their calling and it doesn’t let them really engage with the patients in the way that they would want, which is where this technology comes in, because it’s a way for them to really free themselves up from the monitor or the computer while they are sitting with the patient and really focus on the conversation like you and I are doing with each other. Imagine that as I’m saying these things, you were typing up things on your computer. It would feel very unnatural to me to be talking to you, and the same thing is in the office visit, and think about the experience of a patient. I always say healthcare is one of the most human experience we can have, and having the physician look into your eyes or listening, actively listening to what you’re saying and engaging in your conversation instead of doing a lot of what we do in the classroom, which is absorb what you just said and just transfer it to another medium helps a lot in the relationship with the patient. BRIAN KENNY: I hadn’t really thought about it until I read the case, but it occurred to me that my doctor does take a lot of notes while we’re having meetings, and that seems to me like a fairly recent thing, and I think it’s part of the administrative tasks of doctors have increased exponentially. We’ve got all these systems, the information needs to be in there. They’re trying to get better at sharing information across platforms so that your dermatologist can see what your primary care physician is doing and so on, but it reminds me a little bit of education. In elementary education, my wife is a teacher and the amount of administrative work that she has to do has increased quite a bit over the years. So it just sort of sparked that for me. Maybe you can describe what AI Scribe is and how it works. SUSANNA GALLANI: Yeah. It’s actually very simple as a concept. Obviously very complicated to implement it or to develop it, but basically this is how it works. When you see the doctor, they will probably ask for your permission to record your conversation with them, and it will be through an app on their phone. There’s nothing magical. There’s no invasive technology of any kind. BRIAN KENNY: They just put the phone on the table. SUSANNA GALLANI: Just put the phone on the table, and if you agree to that, that conversation will be recorded, and the recording will be decoded by an AI engine behind the scenes, and it will automatically populate the notes that the doctor would otherwise take during the visit. That’s all it is in a nutshell. Now, this unlocks a number of other things. First of all, there’s billing attached to that. So as the AI decodes what was said in the interaction, they also understand that the AI understands or identifies services that are being provided and can attach a billing code to it. So there’s a revenue generation aspect to it, which, by the way, the doctor would have to do anyway. So it’s not that we’re increasing the billing, not necessarily at least, and this is still a task that the doctor would have to do, and oftentimes, they end up doing after hours, the so-called “pajama time,” which is so dreadful, and it takes physicians away from their family time. BRIAN KENNY: So is it agentic in the sense that it just does it automatically? It takes agency? SUSANNA GALLANI: So the agentic part is what happens after with the data. At the moment, the core of this technology is just simply recording, transcribing, and interpreting in a way, in a way that you can create billing codes. The other thing is prescriptions. So if there is a drug that is being discussed in the interaction, the AI identifies that drug and puts it as a possibility for the prescription that the doctor might want to sign off. Now importantly, none of this is set in stone until the doctor actually signs the notes. So there’s still a requirement for the physician to go through the note and make sure that everything has been done correctly and approve it, otherwise the process is not complete. Shortly after, one of the main safety measures of this technology is that the recording is completely deleted. BRIAN KENNY: Okay, but the notes exist. The notes remain. SUSANNA GALLANI: The notes remain in the EHR of the organization that implements… BRIAN KENNY: Who was it at Mass General Brigham that decided they should try to do this? Were they trying to solve a particular problem or were they just aware? Was it the burnout that you mentioned? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. Predominantly that was the driving force. In fact, they actually stated very clearly in one of our interviews that that was exactly the reason. The main reason why they wanted to try this technology was to reduce the burnout among their clinicians. BRIAN KENNY: What were the sort of organizational challenges that they had as they tried to implement this? How was it received by the physicians? SUSANNA GALLANI: Variation as you can imagine. So initially they piloted with about 800 people that were self-selected, and so that went quite well. Although it did spark some controversy and some concerns. There are concerns on all sides. The physician, for example, sometimes is uncomfortable because they have to actually say more things out loud. BRIAN KENNY: Interesting. SUSANNA GALLANI: Because the AI will not transcribe something that it doesn’t hear. So it’s important that the physician kind of verbalizes their thinking, the drugs that we just mentioned. So if I don’t say, “I’m thinking about prescribing you whatever milligrams of this particular drug,” the AI has no idea that you’re thinking that. So in order for it to do the work for you, you have to actually verbalize actively during the visit, which is very different. BRIAN KENNY: Could be better for the patient, though, because you’re hearing a lot more than you might otherwise hear. SUSANNA GALLANI: It could, to the extent that the physician uses accessible language, and that’s one of the barriers that now the patient might actually be sitting next to somebody who’s speaking gibberish from what they can understand, because they are using technical terms and classification of stages of disease and things that might be obscure or maybe somewhat terrifying for the patient that doesn’t understand what’s being said. The other pushback was, “Well, when I read this note, this is not how I would write the note.” So there’s a level of comfort and acceptance and identity that is kind of missing when the note is automatically generated by a machine, and these notes are there to be read later on, and so if the physician doesn’t recognize their code, for lack of a better term, they resist to that. Say, “Well, this is not the information I would want to have in the note. Of course, you can imagine some physicians said there’s too much information, because the fact that Mrs. Jones recently lost her husband and feels lonely might be very significant for the primary care physician or for somebody in behavioral health, but maybe for the surgeon that is doing their appendectomy, is not important. So how do we tailor the amount of additional information that is non-clinical in nature? There’s variation in how much people desire to have in the note. So there’s a number of those additional challenges, and plus there’s change. There’s change and there’s trust that needs to happen. So the physician also doesn’t know what this information is going to do, and so there’s a little bit of resistance upfront. From the patient’s perspective, the most prominent type of challenge is accepting that that conversation is being recorded. So where is my data going? What is this data going to be used for? Is it still my data? Do I feel comfortable speaking to you naturally when I know it’s being recorded? BRIAN KENNY: Yeah, yeah, and I could see, with all the rules and regulations that we have in place to protect people’s information and identity, I could certainly understand that being a concern. There also might be the cynics out there who say that the hospitals are only doing this because it’s in their best self-interest from a legal perspective or a productivity perspective. Were there certain things that Mass General was sort of measuring as they went through this process? Sort of key metrics that they had in mind? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. They measured productivity for sure. That was one, but mostly what they were most interested in was their burnout measures, and during this pilot program, they actually noticed a significant drop in burnout. BRIAN KENNY: Really? SUSANNA GALLANI: People that had embraced this technology felt that they had more time for themselves, that they didn’t feel they had to be on their electronic medical records the whole time during the visit, that they could engage with the patient, but also their family time was freer and more under their control. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. SUSANNA GALLANI: So they definitely noticed an improvement there. BRIAN KENNY: Okay, and are they also using it…? A lot of people are doing telehealth visits now. That’s a way that people are seeing their doctors without having to go in person. Do they still use the technology even in a telehealth type? SUSANNA GALLANI: That was not in the case, but it would be very difficult for me to imagine that that doesn’t happen, because it’s even easier. We have recordings of our Zoom meetings, so why wouldn’t we use this in a telehealth situation? BRIAN KENNY: Were the physicians at all… And this may not have come up in the case either, but it makes me wonder if physicians were concerned that it would be used for review purposes or my performance is being gauged by what’s coming out in these notes. SUSANNA GALLANI: So the notes are not technically part of the performance evaluations. They are for the trainees, which is another important piece of the case, but the concern that the physicians voiced with us was, “You are now giving me back time. What are you going to ask me to do with that time?” BRIAN KENNY: Right. There’s the cynical piece I was trying to get out before. SUSANNA GALLANI: That was the cynical piece, exactly, and that is a valid concern, because in the case, we describe one physician remembered when they were given human scribes, but this human scribe had a cost, and so they had to produce more, so see more patients, in order to pay for the human scribe to be assigned to them, and so the same type of concern was underlying this implementation saying, “Yeah, that’s great. Now you’re giving me back time, but how are you going to take that time back in other ways?”, and so if we end up doing this, obviously the purpose of reducing burnout will just go out the window. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. You want to try and create some more life balance for these people who are working crazy hours all the time. You mentioned there were some early adopters, the people who sort of signed up for it voluntarily. What happened when they tried to do a more general rollout of it? Were there people who were refusing to use it? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. First of all, it was voluntary. So nobody is compelled to use it, but there is some sort of an expectation, because the second order effect, one of the second order effects of this technology is that it generates better data, and so imagine anything you want to do with clinical data, whether it’s research, whether it’s improving care, you want to have enough adoption, enough mass, to have that mass of data so that it’s consistent across an organization. That would make sense. Well, when they open it up for a larger group, which they still haven’t rolled it out to everyone, but they’re progressively getting there, one of the largest groups, which is the group that historically has the highest level of burnout is primary care. Once they opened it up to that group, it was opt-in, but for those people that chose to use the license, many of them, a significant amount did not pursue it. So they had the license, they just didn’t do it, and in fact, there was a rule that if you didn’t use it for three months, they would ask you why and potentially take it away, because it has a cost. There is a monthly fee for this license, which is person by person. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. I mean, we’re finding that the human side of AI, the getting people to adopt the tools and to use them, is highly variable. Some people are comfortable doing it. They think, “Oh, this is great. This is going to make my life easier.” Other people are thinking, “This is something new I have to do. I have to learn how to use this and what if it breaks or what if I don’t do it right?” What would you say to people who are listening, who are maybe going through the same kind of a process in their own organization? What are the sorts of things that you have to be thoughtful about as you’re trying to scale up this kind of platform? SUSANNA GALLANI: The first thing is trust. We talked about it. It’s really difficult for people to just embrace this. When this technology changes daily, it is, from a user’s perspective, an enormous black box. You put things into it, and you don’t really know what happens to those things. Things being information, sometimes sensitive, sometimes personal, and so having this expectation that everybody will jump at the opportunity to use it is probably misguided. BRIAN KENNY: Yes. SUSANNA GALLANI: So understanding what do you need to do to make it so that people trust what you’re going to do with that technology. Generally speaking, security of that technology, it is a black box for the leadership too. It’s not that we understand this infinitely well. BRIAN KENNY: We’re all learning. Yeah. SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes, and it’s changing so much that we tend to understand less and less instead of more and more in certain ways of what it does and what it’s capable of doing. So the first thing would be trust. The second thing would be use it to bring up the humanity of the workers and not to replace them, because there’s a huge fear. Now, this is less prominent in healthcare, I will say, than other industries, but we all are thinking about, “Is this thing going to take my job?”. So understanding that that is a concern that people have, even if it is buried in the back of your psychology, but especially if you’re bringing this technology in to help people—make it help people instead of making them afraid of it. BRIAN KENNY: We’ve done a couple of other cases that are similar in nature to this one. One was Pernod, the spirit company, and they were rolling out a platform, an AI platform, to their sales organization, and the benefit that they touted was essentially the same thing, which is, “You don’t need to worry about what’s going on underneath the hood with your customers. We’re giving you an opportunity to really develop a relationship with your customer. We’re giving you information that’s going to be helpful to them and help your relationship with them,” and this is reminding me of that, but even at that, there were a lot of salespeople who felt like it was going to cramp their style and people were going to be understanding their customers better than they were and then they wouldn’t need the salesperson anymore. It sounds like Mass General is really just trying to help these clinicians free them up of some of the tasks that they’ve had to do that are not patient focused, and really give them an opportunity to focus on the patient, which sounds like a win-win. SUSANNA GALLANI: Yes. It’s exactly that. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. As we think about this particular case, which is sort of at the intersection of technology operations and management control, are there lessons that you can think of that this could offer more broadly outside of a healthcare setting, let’s say, like we were just talking about, who are considering AI for sort of thought intensive work, knowledge intensive work? SUSANNA GALLANI: Yeah, for sure. The fact that this is happening in healthcare is just the context. It is, as you were mentioning, happening in many other industries. So it’s not specific to healthcare. Obviously in healthcare, there is maybe a specific type of risk because we’re talking about healthcare data or healthcare information, which is a little bit different than maybe your purchasing information, which it still has to be treated with respect and the appropriate safety precautions, but I think healthcare is one level deeper than that. So in terms of generalizable lessons, well, one thing that is clear to me is that we don’t have to jump into this all at once, and especially when we’re not ready. This technology is changing way too fast to make it profitable or valuable if we jump in when we’re not ready, because by the time we get the organization to be ready, then that technology will be obsolete. So one of the things that they are pondering at Mass General Brigham, but I’m sure in other organizations too, is when is the right time to introduce this technology, and for whom? I mentioned the trainees before. So this, again, it’s a problem that we see in other industries as well. I actually had a recent conversation with a legal firm in England that is thinking about introducing AI for their work, but the problem they share with Mass General Brigham is, what are you going to do with the trainees? When you have a junior partner or an associate in a law firm, as well as a resident at Mass General, are you going to teach them to use AI or are you going to be AI independent, should that technology go away or not work? Or what are the opportunities that we’re missing in not training our trainees to use AI, but at the same time, what opportunities are we missing if we train them just to use AI? So either way, you have to consider the pros and cons of either choice. BRIAN KENNY: Right, and we know that one of the ways that AI learns is by consuming mass amounts of information. So it almost seems like when you scale this up, you really do need to get a high percentage of adoption, or you’re not going to get the full benefit of what the AI is capable of doing. It’s not going to learn as much as it could, and not as fast. So it’s pretty complicated to think about all the implications of that. This has been a great conversation, always is when you’re on the show. So thank you for being here. Just one last question would be, if you think about maybe one thing that our listeners should take away from this case, what would it be? SUSANNA GALLANI: I go back to the point I made earlier, which is think about the human that is using the technology, and use the technology to solve a problem that the human has before thinking that it’s just going to be great. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah. SUSANNA GALLANI: We have to really be specific of what problem we’re trying to solve, and I think that Mass General Brigham did a great job in really pinpointing what was the purpose of that implementation. It was not just about… Certainly, they’re not unhappy to improve productivity, but the purpose, the driver of the decision was we have to reduce burnout, and that was their priority. BRIAN KENNY: Yeah, that’s great. Susanna, thank you for joining me on Cold Call. SUSANNA GALLANI: Thank you. Thank you for having me. BRIAN KENNY: If you enjoy Cold Call, you might like our other podcasts: Climate Rising, Coaching Real Leaders, IdeaCast, Managing the Future of Work, Skydeck, and Think Big, Buy Small. Find them wherever you get your podcasts. If you have any suggestions or just want to say hello, we want to hear from you. Email us at coldcall@hbs.edu. Thanks again for joining us. I’m your host BRIAN KENNY, and you’ve been listening to Cold Call, an official podcast of Harvard Business School and part of the HBR Podcast Network.

item.title: Research: How AI Agents Broaden the Scope of Knowledge Work
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.52
Summary. AI agents don’t just speed up knowledge work; they change its nature. In a field study of Perplexity’s conversational assistant and autonomous agent, researchers found that not only You ask two different AI tools the same question—say, to pull together a comprehensive competitive landscape for a new product line. The first comes back in seconds with a tidy summary and a list of links. You read it, open a dozen tabs, copy numbers into a spreadsheet, build the chart, and write the memo yourself. The second comes back twenty-some minutes later with the spreadsheet built, the chart drawn, and a draft memo attached. One handed you information to act on. The other handed you completed work.

item.title: Research: What Physical Retail Stores Deliver in a Digital Economy
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.32
Research: What Physical Retail Stores Deliver in a Digital Economy Summary. As shopping becomes increasingly digital, the role of physical stores is shifting from simply completing transactions to solving customer problems that online channels cannot. Research on One could be forgiven for concluding that the physical store is in terminal decline. Vacant storefronts remaining a common sight on many high streets, and e-commerce continues to capture a growing share of consumer spending. Yet some of retail’s fastest-growing companies are not retreating from physical stores. They are opening them at an accelerating pace.

item.title: Living and Working in the Age of Longevity
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.04
Share Podcast Living and Working in the Age of Longevity A conversation with London Business School professor Lynda Gratton on the new rules for long-term career planning. People are living longer, healthier lives than ever before. But many of our assumptions about executive careers—from climbing the corporate ladder to retiring at 65—haven’t caught up. London Business School professor Lynda Gratton says we need a new way of thinking about work and life, and argues that traditional career paths are giving way to more flexible, multi-stage journeys that require greater personal agency, continuous learning, and a long-term perspective. She explains why leaders should think of their lives less as a ladder and more as a fabric they actively weave over time, and offers up practical advice for balancing productivity and personal well-being, preparing for career pivots before they’re necessary, and developing the skills that will matter most in an AI-powered future. Gratton is the author of the upcoming book Living the 100-Year Life: How to build a career that lasts and a life you love. ADI IGNATIUS: I’m Adi Ignatius. ALISON BEARD: I’m Alison Beard, and this is the HBR IdeaCast. ADI IGNATIUS: So, Alison, as you know, my father passed away recently at the age of 104. He stayed sharp pretty much up to the end and that is relevant to our conversation today. ALISON BEARD: Yes, I am so sorry about his passing. He was such an amazing man. Not only a father to you and several highly accomplished siblings, but secretary of the Navy in the 1960s and then a successful businessman. ADI IGNATIUS: Well, thank you, I appreciate that. But my point in mentioning that is that a lifespan like his is becoming less and less rare. We’re living longer, we’re living healthier, there are many more centenarians, and that has profound implications for work and for our careers. ALISON BEARD: Yeah. I don’t know if I personally want to work until I’m 100, but I do think that old notions about retiring at the age of 60 or 65 don’t really make sense anymore. Many of us can be very productive and lead valuable work lives for much longer. ADI IGNATIUS: Yeah, exactly. And I think management has to adapt to this, individuals do, too. And our guest today, Lynda Gratton, has excellent advice on how people should think about their career options over a relatively long time span. Gratton is a professor of management practice at London Business School and is author of the new book Living the 100-Year Life, which builds on her earlier book co-written with Andrew Scott called The 100-Year Life. She has a lot to share about how we can plan our careers differently in light of our longevity and what organizations need to do to keep up. Here’s our conversation. LYNDA GRATTON: Thank you very much for having me. ADI IGNATIUS: So for our audience, I want to talk mostly about the implications of this on work and career. But before that, at a high altitude, how should we think about all of our very possibly centenarian lives, about the pace, the expectations, about the pursuit of happiness? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, I would say that we’ve always wanted to have more years. Anyone, if you ask anyone, “What would you like, would you like more years?” Everybody’s going to say, “Yes, of course I’d love more years.” And actually, right now we have that opportunity. We have the opportunity to do what our parents and grandparents didn’t do, which is to live a great deal longer. But of course, that’s complex for us in many ways because some of the ways that our institutions are formed, the assumptions we have about our lives, all of those are based on the idea of a three-stage life. You are educated, you work and you retire at 60 or 65, and then you live maybe for 10 years. But now I’m saying you could live to 100, everything else has to be remade. And this generation of people, whatever age you are right now, all of us are learning how to do that, whether we’re 70, 50 or 30. We’re actually learning what does it take when you live a 100-year life? I’m incredibly optimistic about it. I think it’s a wonderful thing. But it does mean that we have to change the way we think about our lives. ADI IGNATIUS: So I tend to be somebody who lives to work as opposed to works to live. How should somebody like me think about my working identity in this era, in this new world? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, the economics of a 100-year life is that you need to make money in some form or another probably into your 70s or even your 80s unless you’ve saved 20% of your income from the time that you started work, or maybe 15%, and very few of us have done that. And so- ADI IGNATIUS: I have not. LYNDA GRATTON: You haven’t. No, neither did I. So it’s a sort of a financial reality, but I don’t think it’s really that that makes it important. I think what really makes it important is the idea that work can be such a wonderful thing for humans. It brings so much things. It develops our skills, it allows us to meet new people. Especially of different generations, which I think is really important as you age. It allows us to have new experiences. So I am all for working into our 70s and even possibly our 80s. But then of course, to do that, you’ve got to think about, well, how are you going to do that and what sort of work do I do? And that I think is the question that lots of people are asking right now. ADI IGNATIUS: Well, and is the career ladder - I mean, the blueprint of the working life now for younger people is very different from when I entered the workforce, where you worked for one company or maybe a couple for long stretches. Is the career ladder obsolete? Is that not the way to think about work and career now? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, if you think about a ladder, you can imagine yourself climbing up that ladder. And what does it require? Well, it requires a lot of energy, but not really a lot of agency because all you have to do is put one hand on the next rung. What I think is happening now is that we have to use our personal agency and that’s something that’s entirely different from what we’ve had to do in the past. And there’s lots of ways of thinking about, lots of metaphors to think about your life. The one that I use is the idea of weaving your life, where you’re the weaver and you’re weaving your life. And every day, you’re weaving a life that creates both productivity for you, but also nurture. And those two elements to your life are so important because you need both of them, but the reality is that they’re hard to deliver at every point in our time. ADI IGNATIUS: So I think many of us are relatively passive, have exercised relatively little agency in our careers because we’ve been headhunted, somebody has come out. Or we need a job and we apply to 10 places and one says yeah. There’s a passivity to that. You’re really urging us to have that kind of agency and that’s important if you’re going to live until you’re 70 or live until you’re 100. But why are we so bad at that and how do we get better at that? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, I think fundamental to the career ladder was this idea that the transaction between you and the organization is that you were a child and the organization was an adult. It was sort of an adult-child thing where the organization said, “Don’t worry, I’ll look after you,” and you as a child said, “Okay, I’ll do the best I can. I’ll put one hand above the other on the ladder.” We’ve actually moved to something which is much more adult to adult. The adult in the sense of what organizations require of you and what they say they want in the deal they describe, but also adult in terms of how we as individuals make commitments, understand ourselves, decide in a reflective way what we want. And I think we’ve been moving … I wrote a book years ago called The Democratic Enterprise, which described the beginnings of that shift and I think that shift is now really, really on its way. And being an adult means you have to be proactive and that’s something that I talk about a lot in the book. How do you gather your proactivity? ADI IGNATIUS: So you write that we should all try to weave our 100-year life into our 20s, into our 30s, into our 40s and 50s. What do you mean exactly by that? LYNDA GRATTON: What I love about the metaphor of weaving a life is that when you think about your life as a loom, there’s a past, all the stuff you’ve woven already. There’s where you are right now with the choices you and I are making right this moment in our lives. And then we have the future, which of course is hard for us to imagine, but we do have a sense of what our future self is. And I think that’s a really profoundly human idea. And across that loom, there are threads that help us to be productive. Threads like mastery or knowing, cooperating or amplifying, which is the way we work with AI. And they’re really important, but if you just have that then you burn out. So the threads of nurture are also really important. Threads which are about our relationships, intimacy, friendship. But also, how we manage energy, both in terms of calming ourselves and indeed, in terms of creating adventure. And those eight threads are there in our lives at all times and it’s we who choose which to strengthen and which to leave fragile. Now often, we don’t make that choice consciously and sometimes we’ll regret those choices, but each one of us has got to that stage at any point in time in our life. ADI IGNATIUS: So we’ve been talking mostly about how individuals should think about their lives and their careers. But I want to move it into the institutional level now because I don’t think our laws, or our protocols or our practices are in step with everything you’re writing about. That we, our institutions do basically shuffle people off when they’re 60 or 65 because they’re too old, or they’re too highly paid or don’t know the new technologies. That, it seems to me that needs to be resolved, that that’s a fundamental conflict in this era where we are living, not only living longer, but we’re healthy and we can be productive. We need to be productive. And workplace laws that are probably 100-years-old. LYNDA GRATTON: Yeah, absolutely. We just haven’t yet designed institutions for longevity, we really haven’t. We’re beginning to design them for technology, but we still haven’t designed them for longevity. And that’s going to be difficult because it means letting go of a whole lot of assumptions that came with a career ladder about promotion being the only way up, about people staying a long period of time and never coming back again, or not coming in at the age of 30, but every step, every step is a step that you take. You can’t take sabbaticals, you can’t work flexibly. So there’s a whole bunch of stuff that has to change. And when you see change happening at the level of a society, individuals are always the first thing to change and then institutions eventually catch up. And I think we’re in that stage right now. I have colleagues who are working into their 80s, other companies have. I’ve got friends who are taking sabbaticals at different times in their life. There’s fathers who are doing parental leave in a way that they never did before. So the world of freelancers. You remember the HBR article that Diane Gherson and I wrote about the huge increase in freelancers. So we’re already seeing a lot of those early signs that actually organizations, perhaps not realizing that that’s what they’re doing, they are becoming more flexible about the way they employ people. And that really helps anyone who wants a portfolio life or a multi-stage life. ADI IGNATIUS: Can many of us afford the portfolio life or is that … The portfolio life sounds great to me at my stage, at this stage in my career. A portfolio life, my kids, young people I know, there’s no health insurance, there’s no … The portfolio life is a constant hustle. Is that what we need to adapt to? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, it could be. There’s lots of different ways of running a life and my thinking is that there might be times when you just want to stay with a company. There might be times when you want multi-stages and a multi-stage means that you stay with a company and then perhaps you start your own business, perhaps you do something else. So the variety is in the sequence, but the variety can also be horizontal, like in a portfolio, where you try and do all these things at the same time. And as you rightly say, Adi, that’s hard to pull off. And we think about people in their 60s and 70s being able to pull it off. But interestingly, when I asked my MBA students, “How many of you anticipate having some sort of portfolio life,” a load of them put up their hands. And then I said, “Well, what age do you think this is going to happen?” And they said, “Right now.” I thought, “Wow, that’s really interesting. They’re seeing it as a life choice from the beginning, not something that you build up.” Now, why are they thinking that? Well, I think that that HBR article that Diane and I wrote about freelancers gives you a little bit of an understanding of that. Because actually, if you build skills, if you work as a freelancer, if you start your own business, you actually can begin to build a portfolio much earlier than we had imagined would be possible. Now, that’s not to say that lots of people are going to build portfolios, or it’ll be the majority, but I think what we are going to see is a lot more variety about the fabric of our life. When you say it’s a ladder that everybody’s climbing, everybody’s climbing the ladder together and they’re all going up in the same way. When you say it’s a fabric that we’re weaving, actually your pattern could be so different from my pattern. And that’s what I think we’re going to see, a lot more choice, a lot more variety. But of course, that brings the question of personal agency right to the center again. ADI IGNATIUS: So that, that sounds great in terms of personal development. Why should managers care about this? Why, as we as individuals weave our lives and our work lives, do leaders need to change their mindset to appreciate that and absorb that? Or how should leaders respond to this and in what way is this in the interest of managers who are trying to run a business? LYNDA GRATTON: Yeah. Well, I just ran a pilot program this year with three very large companies, with the executives from three large companies. It was a 10-week program and the question was how do we think about supporting longer lives? And actually, the results of that program were really fascinating because what it showed … Well, the first thing it showed is that there is real burnout going out in 40-year-olds. In fact, I wrote an hbr.org piece about this, the pivotal 40s. So if you’re a manager and you’re worried about burnout in your 40s, you need to be worried about longevity. Because what’s happening is people are getting to their 40s and going, “Really, is this it? Is this another 20 years of this? I’m out.” Either physically or metaphorically out. And you don’t want that. So I think that it’s in your best interest. The second reason why managers should care about this is that in a time of AI where AI knows so much, wisdom, networks, judgment are really important and that develops with experience, with age. And I think thirdly, we know there’s so many advantages for multi-generational teams to work together. So there’s all sorts of good reasons why you should think about, openly about employing people at whatever age they’re at and not really thinking too much or worrying too much about are they over 50, are they over 60, are they over 70. And if you’ve got a really good performance management system, you can do that. So at London Business School, for example, we have a couple of faculty who teach into their 80s. Why are they there? Well, in part because we have a feedback system with our students where every student has to rate every professor at the end of the semester and that’s made public to all of the other professors. And let me tell you, if you’re not really on your game, you don’t need anyone to tell you that. And so as long as you have really good performance management, people know whether they’re still performing. You don’t need to use age as a proxy. ADI IGNATIUS: Right. You probably also have tenure though, that is part of the explanation. LYNDA GRATTON: Yeah, we do have tenure and that is part of the explanation. But actually, I think that pride is even, well, not always in every case, but often pride beats tenure. ADI IGNATIUS: So you mentioned AI. And I’m sure a lot of listeners are thinking about, “Wait, wait, wait, wait, wait. Maybe this all makes sense, but AI changes everything.” Our assumption has been AI wipes out entry level work. It wipes out a lot of other work. And the conversation shifts to, instead of this work ethic that you’ve talked about, that maybe we redefine the definition of happiness in life, which is not necessarily I derive happiness and satisfaction from work, but maybe there’s another measurement. And maybe I work less and have hobbies more because AI is doing all the work. How do you think about how AI changes, accelerates, decelerates the phenomenon you’re writing about? LYNDA GRATTON: When I was naming the eight threads, and certainly the four threads of productivity, I created the thread called amplification, which I certainly wouldn’t have had 10 years ago. And the amplification is the thread that connects us to AI, that actually brings us together. And what we know about AI right now, but of course this will change, is that if you’re experienced and have good judgment, it will increase your productivity by six-times. So one of the questions we have to ask, as you are saying now is, well, if I’m going to be six-times more productive, what do I do with all that time and how do I spend it? Do I just do more of the same or do I do different things? And the threads in a way, particularly the nurture threads like adventure and calm, are a real invitation to do things differently. I think the second thing about AI is that we can anticipate that a proportion of our jobs will be taken by AI every year. And so weaving the fabric is a lot better than running up a career ladder because when you’re weaving a fabric, you’re already transitioning, pivoting. You’ve already got self-awareness. You’re already thinking about, “What do I need? Who am I? Where am I? What are the promises I want to make to my future self?” So it’s a much more robust way of thinking about a life than thinking it simply as a career ladder. ADI IGNATIUS: So I want to ask you for really practical advice because we are HBR after all. Starting with individuals, what are some first steps people can take to start thinking about all of this in a healthy way? And when I say all of this, it is you are likely to live longer than you have imagined, you’re likely to be productive maybe longer than you had anticipated, and your future happiness and self-worth depends on getting this right. What are some of the first things people can do right now? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, I think the first thing they can do, as you suggest, is actually acknowledge that they could live to 100. That’s a big first step. Secondly, you can really ask yourself, “Where am I now?” One of the things that I did with the book is to build a diagnostic to help people work that out. You can go to the website, it’s freely available, and you can download your report. Because I do think knowing where you are now is really important. So for example, in my case when I started working on this, I realized that my thread of friendship was pretty fragile. I’d spent so much time working, building mastery and it really made me think, “Okay, if I want to live to 100 and have a great life, I know friendship’s really important.” And that leads to the third point, which is to say small actions and experiments. I don’t think anyone pivots … I couldn’t say today, “Okay, I’m going to have a great friend by tomorrow.” But what I could do is to say, “You know, I could talk to one of my friends this evening for eight minutes,” it turns out it’s only eight minutes you need, and I’ll promise myself to do that. Or else I could say, “I’m not feeling very calm at the moment, I’m going to go for a walk tomorrow morning.” So what I’m saying is that you actually commit to things that are going to be useful for you in the future. And those are things like friendship, calm, having an adventure, building a skill, these are all relatively small things that you can start. So I would say start now and choose something that’s going to help you, that lasts into the future. ADI IGNATIUS: Are you positing that there’s a trade-off maybe between working all out when you’re earlier in your career versus pacing yourself and planning for the long haul? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, I think one thing that I feel and this just comes from teaching students for almost 40 years now, I wouldn’t really judge what anyone does with their lives. Some people are going to just really go for it and some people won’t. But I think it comes back to this question about self-awareness, really. If you’re really working on your productivity threads, you’re building mastery, you’re working with loads of people, you’ve got your AI really working for you, you know a great deal, there’s four threads of productivity. If you’re really focusing all your effort on that, then you have to acknowledge that your other threads, the nurture threads about your friendship, your calm, they’re probably becoming fragile and you need to think about what you’re going to do about that. And so I think the wonder of a long life is we can all live it in our own ways and I’ve stopped making judgment calls about how other people live their lives. But I do think we need to, in terms of personal agency, take responsibility for how we’re living our life and the implications of that. What I’ve noticed in the diagnostics, lots of people have already completed it, that people in their 40s are saying, “The weakest thread I have is calm and what could I do to bring more reflection into my life?” And that’s a question we could ask at any stage in our life. ADI IGNATIUS: Yeah. Well, you write that people should revisit some of these questions repeatedly throughout their lives. LYNDA GRATTON: Yeah. ADI IGNATIUS: What are the signals that it’s time to revisit yourself and ask those questions again? LYNDA GRATTON: Well, for me, it just happened three years ago when I was walking actually in France and just feeling really down. I’m wondering to myself, “What the hell is going on here? Why am I walking and crying?” Walking and crying, we’ve all done that. And I think it could be a moment like that when you think, “I have no idea why I’m doing this.” I talked to someone earlier today and they said, “I just got on the Northern line,” which is one of the undergrounds in London, “and I’m thinking tor myself have I got to really do this for the next 20 years?” So I think your body tells you when it’s time to ask yourself those three questions, the three guiding questions in the book which are, “Who am I? Where am I now? And what actions can I take now and promises to my future self?” ADI IGNATIUS: So yeah, driving and crying is a red flag for me. LYNDA GRATTON: Oh, if you’re driving and crying … ADI IGNATIUS: Driving and crying, yeah. LYNDA GRATTON: I can’t drive and cry. If I cry, I’d better stop. ADI IGNATIUS: I’d recommend it. LYNDA GRATTON: Oh, no, no. Okay, driving and crying. Yes. ADI IGNATIUS: Think about it. Now, crying on an airplane doesn’t count because there are atmospheric things, yeah, yeah, that make us all … LYNDA GRATTON: Everybody cries. We all, everyone cries on … Yeah, I agree. We can’t count the aircraft crying, but we can certainly walk and cry or drive and cry. Yeah. ADI IGNATIUS: All right, so back to the practical advice. Again, from an executive level, from a leadership perspective, you feel like managers … First of all, there are tons of layoffs out there these days. A lot of the hiring I see is people trying to bring in starting level people who are AI conversant, who’ve grown up with it, who know what to do with it. It doesn’t necessarily, on the surface, order well for an older workforce that is trying to take agency in their career. What are ways that executives should think about everything you’re talking about in ways that benefit the company by engaging with people who have the potential to be productive in their 70s, 80s, 90s even? LYNDA GRATTON: First of all, Adi, I absolutely agree with you, that this is a very tough labor market. It’s tough for people who are young, it’s tough for the middle people and it’s tough for old ones. So I don’t want to be Pollyanna about any of this and say, “Look, there’s this magic bullet or magic pill that’s going to somehow make it right for everyone,” because it is really tough. I have kids in their 30s, I feel it. I think many of us do who are listening right now. It’s the adult to adult really point I would make, which is to say you got to take control of your working life. Nobody else is going to do it for you. The marvel about the parent-child is the parent took control for you, and they might not have done a great job of it and they probably didn’t. But at least they pretended to, but they’re not doing that anymore now. And I think you’ve got to decide what working life you want. And also, understand where the world is going and what skills you might need. For example, we know that AI is going to take 20% of the tasks you currently do so you got to think about, “Well, what tasks do I do that AI isn’t going to be able to do? How could I become more human?” And we know that being more human is about the relationships you build, the friendships you build, the judgment you have, the way you think about information, the way you think about knowledge, the adventures that you have, the stories that you have. AI I know does a marvelous job of telling stories, but we all know it isn’t a storyteller. It’s humans who are storytellers. So I think we are in an enormous transition. I’m in my 70s, we’ve been around a long time. I’ve talked about, written about work now for 50 years. This is a truly astonishing moment to be at work and it does require us to really reimagine what it is we want from work and what organizations are there to do. I ran a pilot with three companies, executives from three companies, it went over 10 weeks. We transcribed everything they said to each other and these are the three things that really came out in terms of the new way that they were thinking about their careers when they realized more about who they were and what was happening to the world. Number one, they really understood that you’ve got to prepare before you need to. There’s no point in letting yourself get burnt out. Prepare before you need to. Number two, commit to what lasts. For example, friendship is something that’s going to last, mastering a skill is going to be something that lasts. So think about your future self when you’re making commitments. And thirdly, protect time for judgment. If we’re saying personal agency is so important, you need time to be able to think. And all of those executives said, “We don’t have any time to think.” And the program actually gave them an opportunity to legitimately talk about themselves, and talk about their lives, and living a 100-year life and thinking about it. And that, for me, came out so clearly. People are yearning to have an opportunity to think and talk to each other about this incredibly important topic. ADI IGNATIUS: So I love this optimism, I love the agency. Again, I feel like institutions, laws, practices have to adapt because I think age bias, it’s not allowed, but it is or it happens. It’s evident, it’s in front of our face. It’s something companies do all the time, they shuffle out the older people and they find legal ways to get away with it. So I think something has to shift in addition to the inner sense we have that we want to live these productive lives. LYNDA GRATTON: Yeah. Well, and you know very well I’ve written extensively about what organizations should do. I wrote Redesigning Work, it was one of your covers a couple of years back. So it’s not that we haven’t told organizations what they should be doing. I don’t think any company is naïve about what they should be doing. The question is are they going to do any of those things? And so what I’ve decided to do with the next decade of my life is just to show what the benefits are when you encourage people to think about the fabric of their life to help people develop personal agency. And we’re launching, at London Business School, an institute for longevity, work and careers, and that also will do that. So I do feel as if there’s a sea change and it takes institutions an awfully long time to move. But there’s a lot of really positive signs. You see people working into their 60s and 70s and being great. You see freelancers building, you see dads taking paternity leave. All the things that you hadn’t seen before are now beginning to come and so it’s good news for everybody. It gives us more freedom, more variety. ADI IGNATIUS: All right, well, we’ll have to get you back in your 90s, maybe for your centennial, to give us a perspective. But, Lynda, thank you for the conversation. LYNDA GRATTON: Thank you so much, Adi. Thank you. ADI IGNATIUS: That was Lynda Gratton, professor of management practice at London Business School, founder of HSM Advisory, and author Living the 100-Year Life: How to Build a Career that Lasts and a Life You Love. Next week, Alison digs into how we can better leverage indirect influence in our organizations. If you found this episode helpful, share it with a colleague, and be sure to subscribe and rate IdeaCast in Apple Podcasts, Spotify or wherever you listen. If you want to help leaders move the world forward, please consider subscribing to Harvard Business Review. You’ll get access to the HBR mobile app, the weekly exclusive insider newsletter and unlimited access to HBR Online. Just head to hbr.org/subscribe. Thanks to Senior Producer Mary Dooe and to Senior Production Editor Kristin Murphy Romano. And thanks to you for listening to the HBR IdeaCast. We’ll be back with a new episode on Tuesday. I’m Adi Ignatius.
