PETTYJOHN: Going back to Trump's first term, he made a big overture to Kim Jong Un and tried to reach an agreement with him that failed miserably. But I think that the president is so desperate to have a win and to reach some sort of agreement with someone that he sometimes makes these sort of openings. And North Korea seems to be a potential place where he could actually score a victory, I guess, in his view, though it is quite inconsistent because there, the president has also praised South Korea for being a country that's doing more for its own defenses. It's building more, it's expanding its industry and looking to cooperate with the U.S. defense industry. So there isn't a lot of coherence to the - this administration's overall policy, I think, towards the region. And it vacillates between this personal diplomacy and reaching an agreement with another head of state and sort of what actually is happening day to day and behind the scenes at a lot of more working levels. DAVIES: Is there any evidence that diplomacy with North Korea has convinced them to curb their nuclear ambitions? PETTYJOHN: There was an agreement in the '90s that at least temporarily worked, though that's hotly debated, in terms of stopping the North Koreans as they sought to develop a nuclear weapon. But now North Korea has a nuclear weapon. It's a very different situation and one that is much harder to reverse. They - their stockpile has - is projected to have grown fairly significantly. You're not even talking about a handful of weapons - dozens at this point. You don't know where they are, so coercive options or forcible removal would be incredibly risky and difficult. DAVIES: And of course... PETTYJOHN: And... DAVIES: This is all after Trump's two face-to-face meetings during the first term, right? I mean, they made a real effort at this. PETTYJOHN: He did. And, I mean, I think that you've seen that lesson that if you don't have a nuclear weapon, you get attacked, and if you do, you're safer. The - it has been ingrained in many different states that are observing what's happening and could actually lead to more proliferation. The other thing is North Korea has really advanced its missile arsenal. So it's been providing short-range ballistic missiles to Russia, and they've been improving significantly. They're not great, but they're becoming more and more accurate. Its advancements in its medium- and its, you know, intercontinental-range missiles have also advanced. So that makes it a very different threat than it was previously. DAVIES: You know, we've talked a lot about the war in Iran. We began by me asking you - when this war broke out, did you have an intuition about what might happen? You know, as things stand now in this war, how might this unfold as we go forward? PETTYJOHN: I'm not sure. I think that, I mean, eventually, at some point, the United States is going to accept that they're going to have to take a deal that gives Iran at least de facto control over the strait so that it's open, which is a worse position than the United States and the world was in before the war began. But there has to be some sort of face-saving measure in there right now. And it seems like, if you believe reports that are out there - I think it was in The Wall Street Journal the other day - talking about the Iranian regime's position as hardened, and they see themselves in perpetual war. And the Trump administration, you know, desperately seems to want to get out, but also needs something that the president can call a victory. It's in a really tough place. And relying right now on this blockade of Iran is causing more harm to the Iranian economy and to the Iranian people and regime, but they've also suffered a tremendous amount and shown an ability to endure that. So I don't know if that will work or when it would work, but I tend to find that punishment strategies, if they do have an effect, it's over a long period of time. And it's not clear that the U.S. can win this war of endurance because Iran is likely to be able to rearm faster. It's getting drones from Russia. There have been reports of key precursor materials for rocket fuel that have been delivered from China. And it's in a position where it's building cheaper weapons. And it can do so more quickly than the United States, where we're hearing about the strain on the U.S. force more generally, not just its stockpiles, with the Navy. But I think the other deployed forces are on long tours that are a hardship tour and fairly stressful, and things are going to begin to break. DAVIES: Well, Stacie Pettyjohn, thank you so much for speaking with us. PETTYJOHN: It's been a pleasure to be here. DAVIES: Stacie Pettyjohn is a senior fellow and director of the Defense Program at the Center for a New American Security. We recorded our interview yesterday. On tomorrow's show, we hear from actor Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. Up for an Emmy for his role in Marvel's "Wonder Man," he tells us about playing a struggling actor with a secret, losing the role of a lifetime when Disney canceled the show and his unlikely path to an acting career. He was a city planner until a layoff changed everything. I hope you can join us. (SOUNDBITE OF MICHAEL BLAKE & SLOW POKE'S "ROCKIN' IN RHYTHM") DAVIES: To keep up with what's on the show and get highlights of our interviews, follow us on Instagram - @nprfreshair. FRESH AIR's executive producer is Sam Briger. Our technical director and engineer is Audrey Bentham. Our engineers today are Adam Staniszewski and Diana Martinez. Our interviews and reviews are produced and edited by Phyllis Myers, Ann Marie Baldonado, Lauren Krenzel, Therese Madden, Monique Nazareth, Thea Chaloner, Susan Nyakundi, Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez-Wisler. Our digital media producer is Molly Seavy-Nesper. Roberta Shorrock directs the show. For Terry Gross and Tonya Mosley, I'm Dave Davies. item.title: Greetings from Trouville-sur-Mer, a beach town little changed since Monet painted it
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Score: 4.19
Greetings from Trouville-sur-Mer, a beach town little changed since Monet painted it The Normandy beach town of Trouville-sur-Mer is just a two-hour train ride from the center of Paris, but it feels a world away. Gone are the heat and traffic of the city, replaced by English Channel breezes and the sound of seagulls screeching through the cobbled streets. The beaches along this expanse of coastline known as the Norman Riviera are wide, with big tides, and many Parisians come up just for the day — as I did — relaxing in chaise lounge chairs under colorful beach umbrellas that line the boardwalk. The Impressionists captured Trouville's sandy beaches and shifting skies just as fashionable holiday makers began taking to the waters here in the 19th century in what was known as "sea bathing." Looking at one of Claude Monet's Trouville-sur-Mer beach scenes of turreted houses and fashionable boardwalk strollers, it feels like nothing has changed since then ... except perhaps the strollers' attire.

item.title: Striking hospital employees sound alarm over workplace violence
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Score: 4.03
Striking hospital employees sound alarm over workplace violence Nurse Crystal Dhooghe is used to dealing with blood and broken bones in the emergency room. But she didn't expect to witness so much violence against her own colleagues. "I've seen nurses get shoved, pushed, scratched. The biggest one is bitten," said Dhooghe, who works at Henry Ford Genesys Hospital in Grand Blanc, Mich. The prevalence of workplace violence in healthcare has fueled strikes in states such as Louisiana, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island and Michigan, where Dhooghe and many of her co-workers have been on the picket line since Labor Day of last year. "People will question me and be like, 'Why are you still working in a place if you're treated like this?'" said Dhooghe, who gets by on strike benefits and working extra shifts at another hospital. The problem, she said, is that other hospitals aren't any better. "It's the same everywhere I go." In a statement, Henry Ford spokesperson Dana Jay acknowledged violence against healthcare workers is a "national epidemic" and said the health system's efforts to address the problem include metal detectors, armed security officers trained to make "misdemeanor arrests" and de-escalation training. "We have zero tolerance for violence of any kind," said Jay, asserting the strike is not about safety but is instead "simply an economic strike." Nationwide, hospital workers are seven times as likely to be injured on the job due to violent acts as members of the general working population, according to the most recent data available from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The outcry over workplace violence in healthcare is pitting workers' demands for better compensation and staffing against hospital operators pressured to cut costs. When ERs feel like "a powder keg" Violent outbursts are so common that they've been dramatized on the popular medical TV series The Pitt. "Emergency rooms right now are like a powder keg," said Rachel Odes, an assistant professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison School of Nursing. In hospitals, a combative or violent patient is known as a "code gray." Outbursts can be spontaneous and unpredictable, making some almost impossible to prevent. But research shows the risk of violence increases when hospitals are understaffed or employees are insufficiently trained or experienced. Mental health worker Andrew Kimball-Mirzaie said he got hurt in February 2024 at Butler Hospital in Providence, R.I. He'd been working at the private psychiatric hospital for about six weeks and said he hadn't yet worked in the ER. He said he was sent there to "monitor" a man in his 20s who was waiting for an inpatient bed. The patient was alone in a back room watching a Knicks basketball game on TV, he recalled. Kimball-Mirzaie said he got the patient a drink and a snack. They were watching the game when, suddenly, he said, the patient stood up and punched him in the face. He said the assault left him with a concussion and broken nose. His injuries were documented in the hospital's incident log. "I understand that there is an inherent danger with the job," Kimball-Mirzaie said. He doesn't blame the patient, who was very ill at the time. "We should have had at least another staff member with us," he said, "and I should have been adequately trained on the unit." The attack emboldened Kimball-Mirzaie to join some 700 other unionized Butler workers last spring and summer in a months-long strike, which forced the hospital to close nearly half of its beds. Service Employees International Union 1199 New England declared the strike a win. Employees received wage increases that union leaders said would enable the hospital to attract and retain more staff. The hospital also agreed to provide financial support for workers violently injured on the job. And the hospital and union agreed to jointly fund a "time bank" to supplement workers' compensation for injured workers who need more time to recover. But five months later, a nurse supervisor at Butler had to call 911 because an unarmed patient in the hospital's ER was assaulting staff. According to the police report, by the time police arrested the patient, he'd injured two nurses, a security guard and a police officer. "Butler recognizes the importance of being proactive in protecting those who provide care," Mary Marran, Butler's president and chief operating officer, said in a statement. She added that hospital leadership meets regularly with staff to review safety measures and "identify opportunities to strengthen protection for everyone." The patient was charged with four counts of felony assault, including against the two nurses. The American Hospital Association has said punishment is key to preventing violence. It has been lobbying Congress to make assaulting healthcare workers a federal crime that would carry up to 10 years in prison. At least 45 states, including Michigan and Rhode Island, have enacted similar laws. But workplace safety experts say there is no evidence that such laws have reduced the incidence of violence against healthcare workers. Calls for "safe staffing" Striking healthcare workers around the country often have demanded "safe staffing" instead of stronger punishments for patients who cause injuries. The rise in violence against healthcare workers has caught the attention of the Joint Commission, the accreditation organization for more than 80% of U.S. hospitals and health systems. The commission released national performance goals that took effect in January and require hospitals to be properly staffed and that staff be trained "to provide safe, quality care." But no federal law limits the number of patients in a nurse's care across healthcare settings. The nation's largest nurses union, National Nurses United, having pressed for a national standard since 2018. Hospitals must "safely staff all units" to enable nurses to "provide the care that patients need before they get agitated or disoriented," said Jane Thomason, lead industrial hygienist for National Nurses United. Some states have passed their own staffing laws. Only California has enacted broad mandatory nurse staffing ratios, which research shows were associated with lower mortality rates and likely higher retention. Oregon enacted a staffing law, with exceptions. Legislators in Massachusetts and New Jersey have introduced similar bills, but they have failed to advance to floor votes. The American Hospital Association opposes mandatory minimum nurse staffing ratios in hospitals, saying they would "remove real-time clinical judgment and flexibility," compound staffing shortages, and potentially force some hospitals to turn away patients or delay care, spokesperson Colleen Kincaid said. Kincaid also pointed to California, whose new emergency nurse staffing ratios for psychiatric hospitals reportedly forced bed closures in at least four counties. "There are a lot of other things you can do to prevent workplace violence than just increasing staffing levels," said Jordan Barab, who was a deputy assistant secretary of labor for the Occupational Safety and Health Administration during the Obama administration and helped develop OSHA's 2016 guidelines for healthcare and social service workers. Barab said hospitals can, for example, train employees in de-escalation, install metal detectors, or have specially trained security guards on-site so staff members don't have to wait for police to arrive when an incident happens. The health provisions in President Trump's signature tax-and-spending law will squeeze hospitals' finances in the next few years, said Debbie Berkowitz, a worker safety and health policy expert at Georgetown University. When funding dries up, she said, "protecting workers is going to be the first thing that gets cut." This story was produced as part of NPR's health reporting collaboration with KFF Health News.

item.title: Arizona Rescuers Saved an Overheated Hiker with a Mobile Cold Plunge
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.26
Members of the Phoenix Fire Department demonstrate how to use the mobile cold plunge (Photo: Courtesy Phoenix Fire Department) Move over, Wim Hof. Rescuers in Phoenix, Arizona, are using mobile cold plunges to save overheated hikers when temperatures soar. And now, members of the Phoenix Fire Department make sure to bring the devices—which look like a cross between a plastic tarp and a sleeping bag—along to every call in the spring and summer. “We used to put ice packs into people’s armpits and groin areas, but we realized it wasn’t cooling them down quickly enough,” said Mike Johnson, a captain with the Phoenix Fire Department. “When a person’s temperature is that high, only a cold immersion will work.” Thanks in no small part to Hof and his popular YouTube video series, cold plunges have, in recent years, become a cure-all for a wide range of maladies, from depression and anxiety to insomnia, as well as a useful tool to soothe sore muscles. Perhaps overlooked in the contemporary buzz is that diving into a pool of ice water is the best way to stave off heat stroke. The National Library of Medicine has published multiple research papers on the benefits of cold plunges when treating patients with hyperthermia. One report refers to cold plunges as the “gold standard for exertional heatstroke treatment.” “The quicker someone with heatstroke receives cold water immersion, the less risk of death and organ damage,” writes a report on the Mayo Clinic. The Phoenix Fire Department’s mobile cold plunge likely saved the life of a hiker at the popular Camelback Mountain in the Phoenix Mountains Preserve on Sunday, August 16. Authorities responded to a distress call at 11 A.M. and sped to the Echo Canyon Trailhead on the north end of the preserve. Midway up the trail they located a woman who was overheated and unable to descend to safety. Crews called a helicopter and hoisted the woman off of the peak and down to the trailhead. According to a Facebook post, crews then placed her into the bag, and then filled it with ice and water. They later took her to a nearby hospital. Johnson said a patient must show two primary symptoms before being treated with the cold plunge: a core body temperature at or above 104 degrees Fahrenheit, and exhibit signs of an “altered state.” If a patient checks both boxes—which the woman did on August 17—rescuers immediately get out the mobile cold plunge. The device folds down to the size of a small tablecloth, Johnson said, and can be easily stored in a fire truck or ambulance. Crews unfold and then unzip the bag, and then fill it with ice. They put a patient inside and then add water. “We monitor their temperature when we have them in it,” he said. “We’ve had some really great success with it. It cools their internal body temperature extremely quickly.” The idea to invest in the technology came from a member of the department who had seen similar devices employed by the U.S. military. In 2024 the department tried the devices out on a trial basis. After a few successful saves, Johnson said, the department trained its crews to use them permanently. Now, the devices are as commonplace as a First Aid kit. “This time of year we take them out on pretty much every call,” he said. “It might be an unknown medical event, but if it comes in and they’re having a heat-related emergency, we can quickly get their body temperature down.”

item.title: Hike Through the Swiss Alps With the World’s Most Famous Rescue Dogs
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.72
(Photo: Courtesy of Barry Foundation) High in the Swiss Alps above Bourg-Saint-Pierre not far from the Italian border, are hiking routes that wend through alpine passes, high-altitude meadows, and lakes that perfectly reflect the wide blue expanse of sky. But here, there are more than show-stopping vistas: The hills are brimming with living history, too—of the furry, four-legged variety. Near the aptly-named Great Saint Bernard Pass, sweet-faced Saint Bernards accompany hikers just like their ancestors used to. In the late 1700s through early 1900s, the dogs were famous for acting as both guides and rescuers during snowstorms or avalanches.These days, their job is less physical and more social and educational. They no longer lead lost explorers down the mountain pass or roam freely over hills and trails, but they do provide a glimpse into the history and culture of the region—and offer a unique experience for hikers. Each summer, visitors can book guided hikes with the animals led by dog keepers from the Barry Foundation, a nonprofit organization that exists to carry on the more than 350 years of Saint Bernard breeding tradition in the region. The hikes offer the opportunity to spend some quality time with Saint Bernards while learning about their personalities, care, and role in local history. “Walking with them on the ancient pass where their ancestors were raised by monks felt a privilege. It’s one of the most peaceful places I’ve been in Switzerland,” says Kendall Hunter, an Outside contributor and author who visited the area last September. “We had them on a lead for part of the hike then set them free, and seeing them run in the beautiful Swiss landscape felt timeless.” You’ll have to book months in advance to enjoy the experience. Because the well-being of the dogs comes first, the canine-accompanied guided hikes are limited, says Andrea Zollinger, head of corporate communication at the Barry Foundation. Interactions between dogs and visitors are restricted and professional keepers attend to their every need, including grooming, exercise, and protecting them from overwhelming crowds of tourists. If you didn’t snag a spot on a guided hike or prefer a longer excursion, you can still explore the area by foot, including along historic paths that have been trod for centuries, like the Alpine Passes Trail from Bourg-Saint-Pierre to the Great Saint Bernard Pass, which climbs over 3,400 feet in 7.4 miles. When you reach the pass, you can tour kennels that house Saint Bernards all summer, explore the museum at the Great Saint Bernard Hospice (where you can book an overnight stay), then return the way you came or catch a bus back down. Now overseen by the Barry Foundation, the hospice dates back to the 11th century, when it provided shelter to travelers crossing the Alps. Starting in the mid-17th century, the location became home to dogs whose job was to guard and protect it. Before long, the Saint Bernards’ responsibilities extended to accompanying travelers over the pass and locating and rescuing people lost in snowstorms. “Today, Saint Bernards are no longer used for mountain rescue, as helicopters and specialized rescue teams have taken over that role” Zollinger says. “However, their calm temperament, gentleness, and strong bond with people have enabled them to take on a new and equally meaningful mission.” Their days as search rescuers may be over, but the dogs do more than hike with travelers. Instead, they are trained as emotional support and therapy animals for nursing homes, occupational and physiotherapy programs, and more as they continue their calling to offer comfort and joy both on and off the mountain.

item.title: LISTEN: Low Water, No Problem. We Packrafted One of the Most Remote Rivers in the West
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.39
Across the West, whitewater guides have had to grapple with a similar problem throughout 2026: bone-dry rivers. Last fall, writer Owen Clarke took an innovative tour down the Owyhee River in eastern Oregon during its lowest flow of the season. The secret to the trip were inflatable packrafts, which sit just a few inches into the water. These rafts allowed Clarke and his group to navigate rocky and tight sections of the river—stretches that were simply too shallow for a normal whitewater raft. In this week’s Long Read on the Outside Podcast, we dive into Clarke’s adventure.

item.title: Apple Rolls Out iOS 26.6.1 With Fixes for 29 Security Issues
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 7.15
Apple’s software division has had a lot on its plate in recent weeks. As it prepares to launch stable versions of the company’s upcoming operating systems next month, it has also been kept busy with security flaws popping up on several existing versions. On Monday, Apple rolled out fixes for 29 issues with iOS 26.6.1, iPadOS 26.6.1, and macOS 26.6.2. In its release notes, the company said the flaws included an app’s ability to leak sensitive audio, image processing that led to arbitrary code execution, and malicious web content that caused a Safari crash, among others. For iPhones and iPads, the update arrives just three weeks after Apple released iOS 26.6, and for Macs, it arrives just days after the company fixed a critical screen-sharing flaw in macOS 26.6.1. The back-to-back releases suggest Apple is taking these issues seriously, and the company always encourages users to keep their devices updated to the latest software. On iPhones and iPads, you can do that by going to Settings > General > Software Update. On Macs, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. I received the updates on my iPhone and Mac on Monday itself. On iPhones, the update file is just 500MB if you’re coming from iOS 26.6.1, so it shouldn’t take long to download and install. For Macs, it could be a slightly larger file. Last week, Apple also sent out mercenary spyware warnings to impacted users in nearly 110 countries. If you’ve received the warning, it means your phone may be subject to targeted surveillance, and you must enable Lockdown Mode and seek expert help immediately. Apple has a big September coming up. John Ternus will take over as CEO from Tim Cook on Sept. 1. He is then expected to unveil the latest generation of iPhones, AirPods, and Apple Watches. Among iPhones, we expect to see the company’s first-ever foldable and the iPhone 18 Pro models, while among AirPods, we expect to see the company’s first-ever camera-equipped earbuds. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: OpenAI Details New AI Security Measures After Hugging Face Hack
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.78
Almost a month after announcing that its models had gone rogue by hacking the AI platform Hugging Face, OpenAI is updating its public security policies with new rules designed to prevent future incidents. The changes include improved monitoring and alignment techniques for advanced models, as well as enhancements to security measures in research environments dedicated to their development. OpenAI’s announcement says, “As models become more capable, the risks associated with developing and testing them internally also grow. Our standards for monitoring, alignment, and security must stay ahead of those risks.” OpenAI notes how it also made these changes after pausing development and training for its upcoming Astra models. Earlier in August, OpenAI raised concerns that its in-development models could autonomously carry out cyberattacks without oversight. To help allay fear, OpenAI is making its new security protocols public. One of the biggest changes concerns frontier model research involving "model-generated or otherwise untrusted code," with new restrictions to isolate development sandboxes from other tools. It also brings in controls to “isolate higher-risk and untrusted workloads from the internet.” OpenAI says, "We have designed these controls so that a single compromise of a workload or supporting service does not, by itself, allow for unauthorized access to the internet or other internal networks." The brand also claims to have improved its internal security testing in various ways, including removing potentially vulnerable shared services, implementing tools to automatically test boundary conditions using simulated attacks, and improving the collection and monitoring of security logs. New monitoring tools look for signs of potential security incidents by automatically inspecting a model's internal activity. OpenAI said, "Those systems examine tool actions, available reasoning, and the full sequence of activity for unauthorized access, data theft, destructive behavior, and attempts to defeat safeguards." These monitors will flag issues within 30 minutes of their identification, with security and research teams encouraged to investigate immediately and to pause a model's activity if the issue can't be confirmed as inaccurate within the next 30 minutes. This likely won’t mean any major changes to the consumer-facing version of ChatGPT, but it may mean further delays in newer models coming to the service as OpenAI tightens its security. Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. item.title: Love Sideloading on Android? Watch Out for This Upcoming Rule Change
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.57
Android is changing the way sideloading works on your smartphone or tablet, and the first major step is now rolling out to devices. First announced last August, the changes are designed to make it harder for casual users to mistakenly download malware. The first part of the change is gradually rolling out now to devices. Announced in a Reddit post, Google called this its "first version of the advanced flow," restricting users from downloading apps from unverified developers. The advanced flow is intentionally more difficult to use on the first try and is designed to discourage users from downloading apps from untrustworthy sources. It won't affect any apps from developers who have registered with Google, regardless of where you downloaded the software. After the changes roll out, to continue sideloading an app from an unverified developer, you’ll need to wait 24 hours after enabling an option in your phone's settings and restarting your device. If you choose to do this once, you can use an option to avoid having to repeat the steps later. Google’s logic is that this better protects the average user from downloading dangerous software from bad actors, while allowing power users and developers to continue sideloading onto their devices. The new scheme begins on Sept. 30 for users in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand, with a planned global expansion to all app installations at some point in 2027. Google has yet to suggest what time of year to expect the changes. How to Continue Sideloading Apps Once Advanced Flow Is Active To keep access after this new option is enabled, you will need to make a change in the Developer Options on your device. This feature is gradually rolling out, so you may not find it available immediately. You have always needed Developer Mode enabled to sideload apps, and you can turn it on by heading to Settings > About Phone and tapping Build Number seven times. Once available, head to Developer Options, select Apps from unverified developers, then turn on Allow apps from unverified developers. You’ll be asked to enter your screen lock and confirm that you’re not being prompted by someone else to make a change to your phone. The biggest roadblock is that you will then have to restart your device and wait 24 hours before you can begin downloading apps from unverified developers. After a day has passed, head back to the Settings and choose to allow apps for either seven days or indefinitely. If you are sideloading regularly, choose indefinitely, as you’ll have to wait another 24 hours if you download any more unverified software after the initial week is up. Once activated, you will continue to see a warning about apps as you install them, but you can override them to download without restrictions. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. item.title: Claude Can Now Send Gmail Messages, Sometimes on Your Behalf
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.19
Anthropic’s Claude now has more control over Gmail, allowing its AI to send emails on your behalf. The Claude connector for Google Workspace has been available for over a year to help you manage your Google accounts, but this is the first time it can send an AI-generated message. The tool now lets you enter a prompt to ask Claude to draft, reply to, or forward emails, and you can choose whether to confirm approval of the task before sending or let Claude send without a final check. By default, you'll be asked to approve all messages, with Anthropic saying those on Team and Enterprise plans will see "owners decide whether members can allow these actions to run without asking each time.” The feature is now available for everyone on paid Claude plans of all tiers. The upgrade also improves file management in its Google Drive integration by enabling prompts to share, move, or delete files across your cloud storage. Anthropic says it will, by default, ask for approval before each of these actions, much like it does when sending emails. Anthropic confirms it can’t do everything with Gmail, saying current limitations mean you can’t access attachments directly through the Workspace connector tool. It also says it may struggle to load a large inbox or interact with particularly complex Gmail filters. Claude also can't extract images embedded in Drive files, instead focusing its AI tools on text. The tool also gives you access to your Google Calendar, although there are no changes to the service in this latest update. You can continue to view, create, update, and manage events, as well as set up recurring meetings or manage attendees. Claude’s Cowork agentic tools are also now available across all mobile and web interfaces if you have a paid account. Anthropic confirmed the rollout finished on Aug. 18, allowing you to ask Cowork to start a task and then pick up the results on another logged-in device later. It means you can now run a task on your computer and access the results on your smartphone or another less powerful device. item.title: Googlebook Launch Event Confirmed, Set for Sept. 15 in NYC
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.54
Google is hosting a launch event dedicated to its new Googlebook laptop range in New York City on Sept. 15, according to Chrome Unboxed. The website received an invite, though Google has yet to make a public announcement, which may mean it's designed for press, without a livestream. Designed to unify its ChromeOS and Android platforms into a more functional, laptop-first operating system, Googlebooks will be more powerful than Chromebooks and built from the ground up to be AI-native. Google suggests its new operating system could be used to create custom widgets on the fly. We've had a few hints of different Googlebook designs from partners over the past few months, but this event will give attendees hands on time with a range of partner devices. Although Google doesn't name them, it's likely that previously announced partners like Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo will be among them. Google will also reportedly hold a keynote to formally introduce the new brand and its intent, as well as the software platform, including the operating system. Journalists will also reportedly be able to photograph, film, and benchmark the laptops in person, so we may get some real performance and efficiency data from the event. The main website for the Googlebook still lists an "Autumn 2026" release window, so a September reveal followed by an October release may make sense. It would also align the laptops for sale during the holiday season. Confirmed features for the new range so far include a "magic pointer" that lets you have Gemini AI interact with anything on screen, a way to run phone apps natively on a laptop, easy file and data transitions between devices, and the return of the iconic Glowbar. We still don't know what Googlebook devices will cost, but judging by the prices of most 2026 laptops, they won't be cheap. These likely won't be $300 Qualcomm Snapdragon C laptops, but they could use Intel Wildcat Lake chips. They're unlikely to target the multi-thousand-dollar market either, at least not with the base versions. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: American Airlines Will Add Seatback Screens to Narrowbody Jets
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.53
In 2028, American Airlines will upgrade many of its smaller Airbus and Boeing jets, adding 4K screens with Bluetooth audio to seatbacks for passengers' enjoyment. The move marks a reversal for the Fort Worth, Texas, carrier, which in early 2017 decided to stop ordering screens on new single-aisle mainline planes and to remove displays already installed or on order for those aircraft while keeping screens on widebody jets. AA’s thinking at the time: Everybody will bring their own device, so we can save on display weight and instead provide Wi-Fi fast enough to stream Netflix, plus our own onboard streaming. That assumption aged poorly as AA’s competitor Delta Air Lines made seatback screens based on cheaper, lighter hardware part of its standard experience. In 2021, United Airlines announced its own commitment to audio-video-on-demand (AVOD), including Bluetooth support, on narrowbody jets. Since then, both Delta and United have increasingly made onboard tech part of their pitch to passengers. AA’s change, which it announced Tuesday, comes with more than the promise of screens with higher resolution than the average laptop (sizes go unmentioned) that welcome Bluetooth headphones. The airline is also committed to providing USB-C power at every seat. The airline's press release further touts personalization, including TV and movie recommendations and flight maps that feature “destination information and real-time flight insights.” But not all existing narrowbody Airbus and Boeing airframes will get upgraded, spokesperson Andrea Koos clarifies in an email. Out of the airline’s current 1,045-plane mainline fleet, all 132 Airbus A319s, 310 domestic-configuration A321s in two versions, and 303 Boeing 737-800s and 103 737 Max 8s are in line for upgrades. But 48 older Airbus A320s with planned retirements won’t get any, while 12 new internationally configured A321XLRs already have seatback screens. The smaller regional jets built by Bombardier in Canada and Embraer in Brazil—593 aircraft that fly shorter routes operated by AA subsidiaries and partners—also aren’t part of this screen expansion. Koos says AA hasn’t yet picked a company to add this tech, but suggests the ability to monetize a passenger’s attention (already a priority at United) would matter. “Beyond meeting today's needs, we are looking for a partner with a modern, scalable platform that can evolve alongside technology advancements, enabling continuous enhancements to the customer experience while creating incremental revenue opportunities for American,” she writes in an email. The airline’s news on Tuesday also includes putting more first-class seats in these aircraft and expanding the number of extra-legroom Main Cabin Extra seats, which AA says would push the percentage of seats with more personal space on narrowbody departures from 25% to about 40%. Last year, American announced plans to install free Starlink Wi-Fi on a subset of its planes, joining such domestic carriers as Alaska Airlines and its Hawaiian Airlines subsidiary, Frontier (where Starlink apparently won’t be free), Southwest, and United in adopting SpaceX’s satellite broadband. Delta and JetBlue Airways will switch to Amazon Leo, another low-Earth-orbit satellite service that has seen its own flight delays after one of its primary launch vehicles, Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, exploded and destroyed its sole launch pad in Florida. About Our Expert Rob Pegoraro writes about interesting problems and possibilities in computers, gadgets, apps, services, telecom, and other things that beep or blink. He’s covered such developments as the evolution of the cell phone from 1G to 5G, the fall and rise of Apple, Google’s growth from obscure Yahoo rival to verb status, and the transformation of social media from CompuServe forums to Facebook’s billions of users. Pegoraro has met most of the founders of the internet and once received a single-word email reply from Steve Jobs.

item.title: Lenovo Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11 Review: Oh, Snap! Elite CPU Speed at a Heavy Price
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.49
Lenovo's high-end Yoga laptops are widely appreciated for their style, comfort, and performance, and the company’s latest, the Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11, is a stunner with speed to back it up. Starting at $1,499.99 ($1,999.99 as tested), the Yoga Slim 7x gives a similarly configured 13-inch Apple MacBook Air, our Editors' Choice pick for Mac laptops, one heck of a fight. The Yoga's Snapdragon CPU also sprints faster than a comparable Intel Core Ultra Series 3 laptop, like the Dell XPS 14 2026, our current Editors' Choice ultraportable laptop pick, and the laptop lasts longer than both on a charge. This year's Yoga Slim 7x has its shortcomings, however, such as limited ports, weaker graphics performance, and a higher price compared with the aforementioned award-winning laptops. If you're dead set on a faster, longer-lasting laptop, the Slim 7x will deliver, albeit only with apps coded directly for Arm processors. The Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11 starts at $1,499.99 (on sale by Lenovo for $899.99, at times, during this review) and features a six-core/six-thread Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus (X2P-42-100) processor with a Qualcomm Adreno X2-45 integrated graphics processor (IGP), 16GB of LPDDR5x memory running at 9,523 megatransfers per second (MT/s), and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 solid-state drive. The screen is a 14-inch 1,920-by-1,200-pixel (1200p) OLED touch display with HDR500, 100% DCI-P3 color coverage, and a 60Hz refresh rate. The specific review configuration I tested is available at Best Buy for $1,999.99, with an 18-core (six Performance plus 12 Prime cores) Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Elite (X2E-88-100) CPU with a faster Qualcomm Adreno X2-90 IGP, 32GB of RAM, a 1TB SSD, and the same 14-inch 1200p display as the starting configuration. It’s worth noting that this Asus Zenbook A14 on sale at Best Buy has almost identical specs to the Yoga Slim 7x reviewed here, just with 16GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD, for $650 less. I don’t know if the extra RAM and storage in the Slim 7x are worth $650 for you, but I don’t think this is reasonable, and so it takes some of the shine off this laptop for me. This Zenbook A14 laptop is also often found for just $999, to further the point. You can also configure the laptop somewhat on Lenovo’s website, with the priciest build using a slightly less powerful 12-core (six Performance plus six Prime cores) X2-80-100 CPU, 32GB of RAM, a 2TB SSD, and an upgraded 14-inch 120Hz OLED touch display with 2,880-by-1,800-pixel resolution, HDR1000, and 100% DCI-P3 color coverage. This setup will run you $2,309.99 at list price, but Lenovo sells it for $2,194.49 on sale at publishing time. The Lenovo Yoga line rarely looks anything less than gorgeous, and the Yoga Slim 7x delivers with a sleek, ultra-thin (0.55-inch), and feather-light (2.58-pound) aluminum chassis in a deep Cosmic Blue. You'll notice a subdued Lenovo logo on the lid and a similarly slight Yoga branding on the right wrist rest below the keyboard. Cool white backlighting beneath the keys brings quality of life while adding a bit of aesthetic appeal. I feel some stiffness in the hinges, which makes the lid a bit of a challenge to open one-handed, but the slight webcam bulge along the top of the display helps your grip in this regard. The Yoga Slim 7x includes an OLED display even on the base configuration, and that screen is gorgeous to watch. The visuals are crisp, even at 1200p, and the HDR500 and DCI-P3 color coverage make the display pop when watching movies. The 60Hz refresh is more than functional for most needs, though many laptops at this price have landed on 120Hz as the standard. The screen's peak brightness goes up to 400 nits without HDR, with 600 nits peak brightness with HDR, and it supports Dolby Vision. The audio, meanwhile, is fantastic for a laptop this thin. You won’t hear deep bass or anything desk-shaking out of the speakers here, but you'll find two top-firing 2W speakers in addition to the two 2W woofers on the underside of the chassis, so the audio is fuller than most laptops in this size bracket. Lenovo included Dolby Atmos support to further improve the audio. Anecdotally, I can tell you that running the battery test on this laptop required me to put it on a shelf in the front hallway closet in my apartment, since the volume at 100% was loud enough that I could hear it from several rooms away through two closed doors. I love a Lenovo laptop keyboard, and the Yoga’s keys don't disappoint. They're comfortable enough to type on for hours-long writing sessions, with deep enough travel and quick response. The keyboard backlighting is configurable through the Lenovo Advantage app, with Auto, Low, High, and Off settings. The buttonless touchpad has a smooth glass surface and is comfortable to use, with only the slightest bit of flex at the bottom corners. It’s responsive enough that you won't long for a haptic alternative, and it’s spacious enough for everyday work. It also supports multitouch gestures. Lenovo's webcam is a 9.2MP IR cam with better-than-4K video and picture resolution (2400p). Though it’s limited to 30-frame-per-second (fps) recording for all other resolutions, the sensor can record at 60fps at 1080p. You'll find no physical privacy shutter here, but Lenovo included an E-Shutter switch on the side of the laptop that cuts off power to the webcam, which is better than nothing. You won't find many ports on the Slim 7x. You might chalk that up to its slimness, were it not for other laptops at this size including more options. The laptop houses three 40Gbps USB4 ports, two on the left and one on the right, and all three support DisplayPort 1.4 and up to 65W power delivery. Lenovo didn't include a 3.5mm audio jack, so if you want to listen to music or watch movies without disturbing those around you, you’ll either need an adapter or Bluetooth-connected headphones. On the bright side, Lenovo included Wi-Fi 7 connectivity, as well as Bluetooth 5.4. To see how the Yoga Slim 7x’s overall performance and speed measures up to the competition across specific tasks, we've gathered several competing ultraportable laptops together to see how they all match up. First up is the recent $2,932 Framework Laptop 13 Pro we tested, followed by the Asus Zenbook A14 ($1,349.99 as tested; $1,999.99 similarly configured). To round things out, we included our Editors' Choice picks for ultraportables: our $2,199.99 Dell XPS 14 review configuration, and the 13-inch MacBook Air ($1,599 as tested; $1,999 similarly configured). Our first group of tests represents workloads such as content creation, office productivity, and raw CPU speeds. Our go-to overall productivity and storage test, PCMark 10, is not yet Snapdragon-compatible, so we focused on core-stressing tests and media tasks. The three primary tests presented below are CPU-centric or processor-intensive. Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the transcoding freeware HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Additionally, we have encountered issues with Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators Adobe Photoshop 25 test on systems with Qualcomm Arm processors, so we’ve skipped it here until we resolve our problems with the test. These tests are where the Slim 7x stood out, outperforming its Intel x86 rivals as well as the MacBook Air in multi-core performance, which is essential for multitasking and overall system responsiveness. The Yoga also defeated the x86 competitors in single-core speed, which is important for single-app and basic task responsiveness. Its Snapdragon chip only landed within 75% of the Apple M5’s single-core Cinebench 2024 result, however. Surprisingly, it put up the best HandBrake time on the list, finishing the 1080p video transcoding task nearly 90 seconds faster than the M5. However, this performance advantage falls away if you run apps through Windows 11 Prism x86 emulation. Apps developed for x86 processors, like Intel and AMD, can’t run directly on an Arm-based processor like the Snapdragon X2 Elite, so Windows Prism converts an app’s existing x86 code into Arm-compatible code on the fly so it runs on Arm chips, though this impacts performance. In Cinebench, for instance, running the x86 version of the benchmark on the Zenbook results in about 44% lower multi-core performance and about 41% lower single-core performance compared with the version designed for the Arm CPU architecture. Most popular apps nowadays have Arm versions of their software, so this shouldn’t be too much of an issue; you just need to make sure you’re downloading the right version to get the most out of this laptop. A shrinking number of Windows apps simply will not work on an Arm system, or will run so poorly through emulation that it’s not worth the hassle. We challenge all systems’ graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last up, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. Graphics performance is where the Slim 7x struggled, falling behind its Intel and Apple rivals in some tests, with Wild Life showing an especially poor result against the Arc B390 GPU in the Intel chips. The Yoga's Snapdragon also reported noticeably lower ray-tracing speed than both Intel and Apple chips in Solar Bay. These workloads represent advanced creative work and gaming, so the results aren't a deal-breaker for this laptop, since that's not really what this device is going for. If you want the capability to play PC games or work in 3D creative apps, however, the MacBook Air or the latest XPS 14 will perform much better in either regard. We test each laptop and tablet's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with display brightness at 50% and audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. To gauge display performance, we also use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). In this case, Qualcomm Snapdragon's renowned efficiency came through with a clear win against Intel-based Windows laptops, lasting 28 hours and 48 minutes against its nearest Intel-based rival, the Framework Laptop 13 Pro. The Yoga's result was even more impressive than the XPS 14's and MacBook Air's times. The Yoga Slim 7x display, meanwhile, cleared 100% of the sRGB color gamut (common for web content) and covered 98% of both the Adobe RGB and DCI-P3 color gamuts, which are important for still media and video work, respectively. This is much better than the Framework while essentially tying XPS 14 and Zenbook screens. The MacBook Air’s display, meanwhile, covers about 11% less of the Adobe gamut than the Yoga’s, while effectively tying on sRGB and DCI-P3 coverage. For brightness, the Slim 7x is the second dimmest display on the list, with a max non-HDR brightness of 397 nits, which is slightly lower than the Dell laptop. The MacBook Air's brightness is noticeably higher, and the Framework's 796 nits max brightness is in another realm entirely. Final Thoughts Lenovo Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11 - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Lenovo Yoga Slim 7x Gen 11 is an excellent showcase for the new Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Elite chips, especially in terms of battery life and CPU performance. It doesn’t hurt that the Yoga is one of the better-looking laptops out there, ready to easily accompany you on your college commute or around the office. Its graphics performance is less impressive, but since the most important workload for a GPU at this level, gaming, isn’t practical on a device like this (where Arm's app-compatibility issues still hurt most), it’s not a deal-breaker. For everyday productivity tasks, the Slim 7x is outstanding, even if it does come in at a higher price than it should for the parts inside. Look to the MacBook Air and Dell XPS 14 for a slightly more premium treatment at a similar price, as they still hold on to our Editors' Choice awards for that reason. But watch for price fluctuations: Lenovo's selling prices seldom stand still, and you could catch a slick bargain if you're alert.
About Our Expert John (he/him) is a programmer, gamer, activist, and Brooklyn College alum currently living in Brooklyn, New York. Named by the CTA as a CES 2020 Media Trailblazer for his science and technology reporting, John specializes in all areas of computer science, including industry news, hardware reviews, and PC gaming. He's also well-versed in general science writing and the social impact of the tech industry. John has a Bachelor’s degree in English and a Master’s degree in Computer Science. You can usually find him on Bluesky, where you’ll get his hot takes on stuff, as well as his reposts of content that is almost as good as the worst stuff you used to be able to find on Vine. Beyond PC gaming, he spends his evenings building digital circuits, multiboxing Linux kernels, and coding shell scripts.

item.title: Framework Refreshes 12-Inch Laptop, Uses Linux To Hit $699 Price
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.39
Upgradable laptop maker Framework is refreshing its budget 12-inch notebook with some user-requested features and a surprising focus on Linux, rather than Windows. On Tuesday, the San Francisco company debuted the new Framework Laptop 12 over a year after the product first arrived to address the entry-level and education market. The new version starts at $699, a $100 price cut from the first-gen model, making it a potential rival to Apple’s MacBook Neo, but expect a compromise on the laptop's RAM. The biggest change is the Intel Core Series 3 “Wildcat Lake” processors, which promise to increase the laptop’s battery life, a much-requested improvement that owners of the first-gen model asked for. In the company's early testing of the Laptop 12 with Intel's Core 5 320 chip, "we’re seeing a 70% increase in Netflix 4k streaming battery life over the Core i5-1334U in the original Framework Laptop 12,” the company wrote in a blog post. The 12.2-inch laptop also adds a backlit keyboard and a fingerprint reader in the power button, two other requested features. That said, the backlit keyboard and fingerprint reader are absent in the $699 base model, and only available when configured with Intel’s higher-end Core 5 320 and Core 7 350 processors. Other enhancements include Wi-Fi 7 and support for Thunderbolt 4 over the two rear Expansion Card slots, "enabling you to plug in high-speed peripherals like eGPU’s or two 4k 60Hz displays," the company says. We’ll be curious to see how the Laptop 12 stacks up against Apple’s MacBook Neo and Dell’s new XPS 13, which both start at $699. The $699 XPS 13 also uses a Core 5 320 chip, features 8GB of RAM, and is so far the “budget Windows ultraportable to beat,” according to our review. In contrast, Framework's $699 Laptop 12 uses a lower tier processor in the Core 3 304. Still, the laptop promises to excel at repairability and upgradability since it features an easy-to-access modular design Framework is already accepting pre-orders, but the first batches won’t ship until October. Although the “pre-built” base model starts at $699, it only features 8GB of RAM, which is low, especially on the Windows OS. To get 16GB of RAM, you’ll need to buy the Core 5 320 model, which costs $400 more at $1,099. But on the plus side, it includes the fingerprint reader and backlit keyboard. Meanwhile, the Core 7 350 model is going for $1,399. The laptops can also ship with the Linux distribution Fedora, which is open source and free. To get Windows 11, you’ll need to pay an extra $100, which might explain the price cut from the first-gen model. On why it's pushing Linux, Framework noted: “Almost 80% of Framework Laptop 12 owners are running Linux across a range of distros. This was a clear signal to us that we should push even further on Linux ease of use.” The Framework Laptop 12 will also be sold through "DIY editions" that start at $549, featuring the Intel Core 3 304 processor. The DIY editions expand the color options from merely a greenish "sage" to five other color ways. However, the DIY models don't come with RAM or storage unless you pay to add them. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Gmail's Verified Sender Program Lets Political Committees Bypass Spam Filters
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.46
Google announced on Monday a Verified Sender Program that allows political committees to bypass standard Gmail spam filters and reach users more directly. As reported by The New York Times, the program will launch on Sep. 8, and it is open to any 527 tax-exempt candidate, political party, PAC, or other political committee in the US. To be eligible, the committee must verify its sending domain with Campaign Verify, use Google’s Postmaster Tools to monitor the email-sending operation, and keep its spam rate below 0.3% over a 14-day average. Gmail users remain in full control of the emails they receive. They can continue to mark messages from any user, including political committees, as spam, block them, or unsubscribe from their mailing lists. If a political committee exceeds the 0.3% spam threshold, it may be suspended for seven days or permanently terminated from the Verified Sender Program, Google says. After that, committees can continue using their domain to send messages, but they will be subject to Gmail’s spam filters. The feature uses machine learning and user feedback to identify emails that users like to see in their inboxes and to keep unwanted, unsolicited, or dangerous emails in a separate Spam folder. Notably, Google’s new Verified Sender Program will launch around two months before the midterm elections in the US. Google began reaching out to sections of both parties regarding the program on Monday, The NYT reports, citing two sources familiar with the development. This, however, isn’t the first time Google has tried a no-spam program for politicians. The Federal Election Commission approved a similar yet limited pilot program for Gmail in 2022. The same year, the Republicans sued Google over claims that it was suppressing the party’s email outreach by sending messages directly to spam folders. A federal judge dismissed the claims in 2023. Last year, FTC chairman Andrew N. Ferguson raised the issue with Google once again. In a two-page letter to CEO Sundar Pichai, Ferguson claimed he could make a federal case out of Gmail’s spam filters, and the feature could qualify as “unfair or deceptive acts or practices.” About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: FCC Retracts 7 Million US Starlink Subscriber Figure
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.09
Oops: The Federal Communications Commission says it mistakenly claimed SpaceX’s Starlink had reached over 7 million subscribers in the US. The FCC has officially issued an “erratum” to correct the number, which appeared in the Commission’s Section 706 report examining broadband access in the US. The FCC originally published the report on Friday, saying on page 64: “Satellite service is also rapidly expanding. Starlink alone has launched over 2,300 satellites between mid-2024 and mid-2025 and has now deployed more than 7,800 satellites—a worldwide network already with over 7 million American subscribers.” The over 7 million figure stood out because it suggested that Starlink had somehow tripled its US customer base from more than 2 million in a span of a year. In contrast, SpaceX’s own figures have only shown the global customer base doubling, from 7 million in August 2025 to now over 13 million+ consumer subscribers. We wondered if SpaceX may have shared some new information with the Commission, but it turns out the Section 706 report made an error. The FCC has since corrected the document to cite figures from SpaceX’s recent Q2 earnings. The Commission’s report now says: “Starlink alone has reported a total of over 10,200 on-orbit broadband and mobile satellites and has grown its global subscriber base from 6 million to 12 million between June 30, 2025 and June 30, 2026.” The correction doesn’t explain why the error was made in the first place. On Tuesday, an FCC spokesperson merely notified PCMag that the fix was issued. Jianping Pan, a University of Victoria professor who studies satellite internet systems, strongly suspected the FCC made an error with the over 7 million figure. One reason is because his own tracking of Starlink using public IPv6 addresses suggests the satellite internet system has an estimated 4.7 million US users. In the original Section 706 report, the FCC also mistakenly claimed the 7 million figure while citing a July 2025 update on Starlink.com that mentioned serving over 6 million global customers. Hence, Pan told PCMag the Commission likely meant 7 million global subscribers, rather than American subscribers. “7 million was roughly the worldwide user base around middle 2025, they just mixed up the context,” Pan told PCMag.
